#222. Tech Report: Rogue Agents Hacked His Company. Why Is Clément Delangue So Optimistic About AI?

Tech Report: Rogue Agents Hacked His Company. Why Is Clément Delangue So Optimistic About AI?

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1086 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that clément Delangue, CEO of the open-source AI manufacturer Hugging Face, may go down in history as one of the first people ever attacked by a rogue AI agent.
  • As the agents worked at superhuman speed to probe and exploit systems, Hugging Face confronted a bewildering deluge of data.
  • According to recent reports, delangue moved to the US more than a decade ago, “barely speaking English,” and built Hugging Face into a platform that supports tens of millions of AI developers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that clément Delangue, CEO of the open-source AI manufacturer Hugging Face, may go down in history as one of the first people ever attacked by a rogue AI agent. His company, which hosts millions of AI models and datasets, was breached in July when hundreds of agents being tested by OpenAI broke free from their sandbox and went on a hacking spree.

As the agents worked at superhuman speed to probe and exploit systems, Hugging Face confronted a bewildering deluge of data. The manufacturer’s engineers were only able to analyze the attack by using an open-weight model called GLM 5.2 from a Chinese company called Z.ai.

According to recent reports, delangue moved to the US more than a decade ago, “barely speaking English,” and built Hugging Face into a platform that supports tens of millions of AI developers. The fresh-faced Frenchman, who dresses even more like a skater than most AI execs, says the summer attack highlighted the value of open-weight models, which unlike ChatGPT or Claude can be downloaded and run by anyone.

Recent findings suggest that despite championing the democratization of AI, however, Hugging Face was acquired by one of the industry’s biggest players, Nvidia, for $12.93 billion in September. When I caught up with Delangue recently, that was the subject of my first question.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

WILL KNIGHT: Why sell to Nvidia?

CLÉMENT DELANGUE: We need more resources to give open-source AI a chance. It has grown really well in the past few years and has become a really credible alternative to closed-source APIs. But the field is still dominated by closed-source.

In a recent development, we’re gonna have the Anthropic IPO in a few weeks. They basically went from zero to a top five or top 10 most valuable organization in the world in a few years. I don't think that's ever happened before.

Does Anthropic's IPO suggest the closed approach is winning?

It’s hard to say. I've always mentioned that there is a very strong natural tendency for AI to concentrate capabilities and wealth. People haven't internalized how much of the future compute capacity has already been reserved by a few companies. Talent, compute, resources—these all fuel the natural tendency for AI to be dominated by a few closed-source labs.

Let’s talk about the attack. When did you first realize Hugging Face was being hacked by a group of AI agents?

In a recent development, at the beginning, it didn't go to the top of our priority list. It just wasn't bad enough to really trigger that. The goal was pretty narrow and wasn’t deemed to be very dangerous or damaging. But it was raising questions. Especially the number of actions taken compared to the narrowness of the goal. It was surprising to us, and we couldn't really fit it into a familiar pattern. That's why we started investigating.

And you used the Chinese model called GLM to investigate.

I actually think that 95 percent of the risks are being created by a few companies that are pushing the frontier behind closed doors. And 95 percent of the protection or defense is going to be done by the open-source ecosystem.

Does the US need its own open-weight models—ones as powerful as GLM, DeepSeek, Kimi, or Qwen?

Yeah, I think it's very, very important for sovereignty, for understanding AI, and for academia. It’s kind of weird that most academic labs have to use Chinese models because they’re the ones that are open. If you go to Stanford or MIT, you have no choice but to use the Chinese open-weight models.

Recent findings suggest that there is some momentum, but I don't think it's enough. I think there's a lot more to do. A lot more investment is needed.

It has been revealed that the best open-source non-Chinese models are actually coming from outside of the US. Right from France, Mistral; Cohere from Canada; South Korea is starting to do more and more. But it’s still pretty far from what the US could do.

Perhaps we don’t need to panic about AI agents, but what about the idea of AI escaping human control due to recursive self-improvement?

You use a computer to write code. There's already some form of self-improvement in using the tools to build more tools. Now the question is how fast it accelerates. One thing that a lot of people realized this summer is that keeping AI behind closed doors in a few labs isn't actually safer. For recursive self-improvement, I think openness is a way to understand, follow, and regulate if we need to regulate.

Can we talk about the Microduck? I’m a bit obsessed.

Oh yeah, it's so fun, no? We're probably gonna sell over 50,000 of them this year. It's probably the most popular robot of the year.

We haven't talked about this much, but AI was really the unlock for the robot. We had the design for two years, but the problem was that when it fell, it couldn’t get up. And then at some point with reinforcement learning, one of our software engineers managed to get the Microduck to get itself back up.

At the end of the day, how do you convince people to take an interest in open-source AI?

Think of a world where two or three companies could write software and nobody else. That would be incredibly scary. It would mean that the whole world would be controlled by two or three companies. And unfortunately, that's kind of the direction that AI is taking right now.

Can open-source AI compete with something as capable as Claude or ChatGPT?

According to recent reports, yes, especially with agents. Many companies have shown that when you post-train your own model for your own use case, you get frontier—or even better than frontier—performance at a fraction of the cost.

Do you think we are getting close to AGI?

In a recent development, I struggle a little bit with the meaning of that. Obviously the technology is progressing incredibly fast, and it’s more and more capable. I just don’t necessarily find it super useful to always compare AI to human capabilities. But if we’re getting to AGI or to superintelligence, it’s incredibly important that it’s as distributed as possible. The last thing you want is to have it concentrated in a few corporations.

Recent findings suggest that what did we miss? Tell us about your favorite moments of 2026 in the comments below.

Breaking: Congratulations to WIRED’s Class of 2026

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 44 min read (8739 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~44 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For our inaugural WIRED Yearbook, we celebrate the people, inventions, and viral moments that made it a little more bearable—and are already defining the future.
  • ANIMATIONS BY LUKTHIS STUDIO ILLUSTRATIONS AND PHOTO TREATMENT BY ROB VARGAS.
  • In a recent development, an internet devoured by AI.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For our inaugural WIRED Yearbook, we celebrate the people, inventions, and viral moments that made it a little more bearable—and are already defining the future.

ANIMATIONS BY LUKTHIS STUDIO ILLUSTRATIONS AND PHOTO TREATMENT BY ROB VARGAS.

In a recent development, an internet devoured by AI. Surveillance at every traffic light. Global leaders who seem determined to bring about dystopia. At the end of a year like 2026, it’s tempting to conclude that there’s little room for idealism. Don’t give in! After all, this year we also saw a upcoming generation of filmmakers challenge Hollywood, teenagers take on AI companies, and scientists make once-unimaginable breakthroughs. We saw activists fight surveillance, astronauts do the impossible, and an adorable raccoon melt the internet’s black heart. So for the first time, we’re publishing a WIRED Yearbook: our very subjective, occasionally ridiculous, always enthusiastic collection of the people, institutions, inventions, and moments that offered optimism in 2026. I hope it gives you a healthy kick of bullishness—and the vigor to keep fighting for the future you want to see.

—Katie Drummond, Global Editorial Director.

From the ecstatic night the Knicks won the NBA championship to the surprising ease with which New York absorbed the chaos of the World Cup to the record-low violent crime—it’s been a huge 2026 for the greatest city in the world. WIRED first sat down with Zohran Mamdani in 2025, when he was still just a candidate for mayor. A year later, as the midterm elections loomed, we returned.

KATIE DRUMMOND: We talked last year about social media as a tool for campaigning. How are you thinking about social media now as a tool for governance?

ZOHRAN MAMDANI: You have to continue to recognize the fact that for many New Yorkers, this is how they engage with the world. It is yet another medium that has to be treated with the same legitimacy and respect as traditional mediums.

What’s your point of view on the data center movement? Why do you think that specific issue has become such a flash point?

The movement to oppose data centers is one that gives me a real sense of hope.

In a recent development, it’s a bipartisan fight. What you’re seeing from Americans across the country is an opposition to what these data centers would mean for their day-to-day lives, what they would mean for their electricity rates, what they would mean for the environment. It’s also a repudiation of what has been governing politics for the last few years when it comes to AI, which is: Our risk, their reward.

You worry that we’re in a bubble?

You worry that bubble’s gonna pop?

Recent findings suggest that last year I asked you if technology was making democracy stronger or weaker. You remarked weaker. What about today?

I have family members sending me AI videos of me, thinking that they’re real. One complimented me on a 45-minute debate that I had with a European member of parliament. I was like, “This is not me.” There is a real crisis of faith as to what is real right now.

What do you hope the Democratic party looks like in, say, 2036?

I hope that party looks like one that realizes the only majority in this country is the working class, and fights for it. An ambitious version of the party cannot only be one that we find in history books. We need that to be a living, breathing politic. The people who run it have to be the American people.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

In early August, Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez declared that she was freezing her eggs. “Usually I keep my private life quite private,” she stated in an Instagram video, before opening up about the process and sharing videos of the self-administered hormone injections.

This wasn’t an extraordinary event—more women than ever are making the same decision—but the internet exploded anyway. “This desire to start having children late in life is completely baffling to me,” wrote the far-right commentator Matt Walsh on X. “Totally backwards and ridiculous.”.

Republicans weren’t all on the same page: Katie Miller, wife of the man recently promoted to White House chief of staff, defended AOC, writing on X, “If one woman wants to preserve her right to have children, which means more than having none—we should celebrate that.”.

Recent findings suggest that it is true that the Republican party has been intensely focused on women’s fertility. The expectation of motherhood, along with the proliferation of pro-natalism, has become core to the party. For conservative commentators to bash the Newly introduced York representative felt incongruous at best. The White House itself reportedly didn’t love Walsh’s take.

Meanwhile, in an interview with ABC, Ocasio-Cortez remarked it was important to “normalize” the procedure at a time when “this administration is denying reproductive care to women across the country.”.

As the 37-year-old congresswoman considers a presidential run in 2028, expect more of this. Conversations about her body, her health, and her possible maternal well-being will be front and center no matter what. She could have 100 children, and Republicans would spend time complaining about their names. —Leah Feiger.

Recent findings suggest that australia restricted children’s access to social media at the end of 2025, and 2026 saw several other countries follow suit. Brazil banned features such as infinite scroll and autoplaying videos, also mandating more adult supervision and age checks. The European Union confirmed plans to prevent under-13s from using both social media and AI chatbots.

Recent findings suggest that the jury’s still out on whether these bans actually work, but speaking of juries, let’s talk about Meta. After being accused of harming the brains of youngs everywhere, the manufacturer paid an $18 billion settlement, agreeing to latest features like late-night restrictions and parental controls. “I’m proud of both the work Meta has done to protect kids historically and of this new groundbreaking agreement,” remarked the firm’s chief legal officer, lamely. If bans don’t work, lawsuits might. —Isabella Ward.

According to recent reports, since October 2025, Bari Weiss, a longtime opinion journalist with no experience running a large organization, has been the editor in chief of CBS News. In that role, she has operated on a theory that has informed much of her career: People want common sense; her views (broadly, that the Israeli government is good and wokes are bad) are common sense; therefore, people want her views.

Recent findings suggest that it doesn’t look good. In January, Weiss tapped anchor Tony Dokoupil to take over CBS’s evening news broadcast; soon it was featuring Pete Hegseth interviews and even a “salute” to Marco Rubio. By April, the show was reportedly posting its lowest ratings ever.

Industry observers note that weiss persisted. She put Nick Bilton, a longtime opinion journalist with no experience running a large organization, in charge of 60 Minutes. The result? The show’s lowest ratings ever. Weiss, however, abides. —Tim Marchman.

Recent findings suggest that when people look back on 2026, they’ll likely remember Ms. Rachel for something unrelated to her kid-centric entertainment empire: offering an example, for adults, of how to be a good person.

Nothing says rock and roll like a marketing machine. Elvis had Colonel Tom Parker. The Rolling Stones had Andrew Loog Oldham. Geese has video clippers.

Social media people sensed something inorganic was happening on their For You pages after Geese released their album Getting Killed in September 2025. That and the band’s meteoric rise this year drove accusations that a “psyop” was afoot.

Recent findings suggest that as WIRED wrote in April, the Brooklyn-based four-piece’s takeoff had indeed been somewhat staged: Digital marketing agency Chaotic Good Projects had been clipping and posting short videos of Geese content across a network of TikTok accounts to drive the band’s engagement. “It was low-effort TikTok posts that were used to boost the algorithm,” as frontman Cameron Winter put it to Rolling Stone. “They showed us samples, and it made me feel better, because they were so shitty.”.

Recent findings suggest that magazine profiles and good Pitchfork reviews don’t give bands the juice they used to. Now many chart-toppers take off on TikTok first. But that also means competing with scores of other content for ears. Chaotic Good and its network of clippers aren’t so much running a “psyop” as they are trying to meet audiences where they are. And FYI, the agency prefers the term “trend simulation.” —Isabella Ward.

For the greatest reversal of fortune this year.

The only word that accurately described the scene outside Fresh York’s Madison Square Garden on the night of June 3, 2026, was “pandemonium.” Game one of the NBA Finals had just ended some 1,600 miles away in San Antonio, where the New York Knicks had beaten the host Spurs. Thousands of fans flooded out of the watch party the Garden had hosted to express their primal joy. Among the revelers was 23-year-old MD Ahnaf Hossain, a Queens native who beelined to a film crew from the prediction-market giant Kalshi. Clad in a red and orange Hawaiian shirt, Hossain improvised a poem that made the surrounding throng go wild: My mayor Muslim / My bagels Jewish / My Christian Dior / Knicks in four!

Those words, conjured in the heat of an ecstatic moment, changed Hossain’s life overnight. By the time he woke up the next morning, his performance had become the internet’s new favorite thing—a concise encapsulation of New York’s unconditional love for the city and the Knicks, who hadn’t won an NBA championship in more than half a century.

Kalshi was quick to latch onto the viral sensation, shooting a follow-up video in which it gifted Hossain a Christian Dior scarf. The company also arranged for Hossain to attend game four at the Garden, which came on the heels of the Knicks’ first loss of the series. After watching the Knicks triumph in an epic comeback, Hossain again waded into the Midtown chaos to deliver a tweaked poem that accounted for the new mathematical realities of the series. He kept the first two lines the same, but changed the last two to embrace the third major Abrahamic religion: The Pope’s on our side / Knicks in five!

Hossain, who earned a finance degree from the Rochester Institute of Technology in 2026, has worked hard to capitalize on his unexpected fame since the Knicks did, indeed, win the title in five games. He launched a project called City of Us that sells a $29 T-shirt emblazoned with “Upcoming York in 5” and which aims to host watch parties during the upcoming NBA season. He has also starred in branded content for businesses such Tex’s Chicken & Burgers, for whom he delivered a bespoke poem about the glories of crispy chicken wraps.

According to recent reports, one of Hossain’s favorite parts of his wild ride has been the support he’s received from fellow Bangladeshis, who make up a huge percentage of his Queens neighborhood. “I get love from my fans and that’s awesome, but then getting fans from my own people just feels completely different,” he claims. That love may soften as the 2026 NBA season fades from memory, but “Knicks in five!” might just be perfect enough to endure. —Brendan I. Koerner.

For being our favorite independent, insider-y tech correspondents (well, before OpenAI acquired them).

Silicon Valley idolizes a quitter. College dropouts, employee walkouts, folks who shutter one failed startup to launch another. But none got more attention in 2026 than Jacob Coxon.

It has been revealed that after the 27-year-old AI researcher quit his job at Anthropic, he took to X to post that neither that company nor OpenAI (Coxon had worked at both) acts responsibly. Instead, he said, they’re racing “straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.” His initial tweet has been viewed more than 175 million times.

Recent findings suggest that AI researchers, technologists, and safety experts started weighing in on whether AI really could destroy humanity. It was not a novel idea. Any reader of science fiction (or WIRED) has probably pondered whether artificial intelligence could at some point become so intelligent that it would stop at nothing to achieve its self-determined goal. But Coxon was uniquely hyperbolic.

“When we say human extinction,” he told WIRED, “it’s because, for something that intelligent, it really will be quite straightforward for it to kill everyone.”.

According to recent reports, coxon’s future—and ours—is undetermined, so it’s hard to measure his impact. Maybe his actions change nothing; maybe he forces a necessary conversation that leads to meaningful regulation. Either way, the Coxon saga shows: If you’re going to quit, you might as well do it in spectacular fashion. —Lauren Goode.

For keeping tensions—and gas prices—incredibly high.

“Pissing off billionaires one small action at a time.” That’s one of Everyone Hates Elon’s slogans, and the organization fulfills the brief. After plastering London with posters of Musk’s Nazi-like salute and branding Tesla vehicles “Swasticars” last year, the British activists have turned their (sat)ire toward Mark Zuckerberg’s fresh surveillance tool: Meta Ray-Ban smart glasses. Their posters feature Jeffrey Epstein wearing the specs alongside the slogan “Glasses for people who don’t do consent.” Or as stickers on the London Underground put it: “Everyone thinks you look like a massive nonce.” —Matt Burgess.

For being something AI can’t generate, while also being essential to its existence.

Clément Delangue moved to the US a decade ago, “barely speaking any English,” on the belief that open-source AI would have a big role to play in the future. Since this past summer, when autonomous agents from OpenAI attacked Delangue’s company, Hugging Face, that belief has only grown stronger.

For having the best fandom in sports—Ballhalla!—and leaving hecklers (and transphobes) on the sidelines.

Head to the multiplex to check out a nerdy blockbuster in 2026 and you’re bound to run into Zendaya. Across three films—Spider-Man: Brand New Day, The Odyssey, and December’s Dune: Part Three—she has established herself as the reigning queen of genre movies, from sci-fi to Marvel and back again. And if being in a trifecta of the year’s biggest movies wasn’t enough, she also stole the show in the dark romantic comedy The Drama and finished her run on HBO’s Gen Z hit Euphoria, all while captivating social media feeds. During this year’s onslaught of endlessly clipped late-night guest spots and red-carpet appearances, Zendaya ended up on more For You pages than most. Lest you think her reign will be short-lived, soon she’ll begin shooting a sci-fi movie with Ex Machina director Alex Garland. As of this writing, she’s the only actor attached to star. Who else could the film possibly need? —Jason Parham.

In October, Kelly Clarkson alleged that a toy shop in Brooklyn had acted as though she couldn’t afford a $15,000 mechanical bird. “If you enjoy being treated like Julia Roberts’ character in Pretty Woman,” Clarkson wrote on X, “for sure, check it out.” Accusations between Clarkson and the store owners flew wildly across social media—before a four-minute security camera video demonstrated what really happened. Who had the goods? Pablo Torre, of course.

It’s been a wild year for the host of the Pulitzer-winning Pablo Torre Finds Out, who’s emerged as a fresh investigative voice. He got Zohran Mamdani to admit to using minoxidil to fight a roving hairline, unveiled aims to investigate LeBron James’ use of helicopters to commute to practice, and, of course, collaborated with WIRED on a report about Madison Square Garden’s invasive surveillance tech.

Torre is a one-man magazine, spread across YouTube, social media, and wherever you get your podcasts. His work investigating the Los Angeles Clippers (for which he won that Pultizer) has been particularly dogged. After he reported that the team had circumvented the NBA’s salary cap, the league garnished five first-round draft picks, levied a $30 million fine, and suspended owner Steve Ballmer and other execs. The final shoe has yet to drop. In September, The Latest York Times reported that the feds had opened an investigation into the Clippers affair. Kelly Clarkson, meanwhile, could go shopping again at any moment. Pablo Torre, no doubt, will be on top of both. —Reyhan Harmanci.

Calling it “El Niño”—Spanish for “the little boy”—might be the understatement of the year. Perhaps that’s why reports have started calling it “supersized” and even “Godzilla.” Signs point to it being the strongest El Niño in centuries.

According to recent reports, it started the way they all do: with hotter-than-normal waters in the central and eastern tropical Pacific. That leads to more evaporation and more thunderstorms in the region, plus a shift in trade winds that allows more warm water to roll from west to east. As the cycle continues, changes ripple throughout the entire atmosphere. During an El Niño, some regions—such as the southern tier of the US—tend to see more rainfall, while others—such as the Pacific Northwest—are more prone to drought. Same this time around, only worse.

Recent findings suggest that one reason for this year’s record-breaking events? Climate change, indicates Christopher Callahan, a professor at the University of Indiana who studies environmental shifts. The first modern, extra-strong El Niño was recorded between 1982 and 1983; since then, there have been four more. New studies based on coral records show the intensity of El Niño over the past millennium shooting up like a hockey stick. “I just remember going like, ‘Holy shit, this is very strong evidence,’” Callahan says of a paper that came out in August.

While some El Niño impacts—like fewer Atlantic hurricanes—are beneficial, it’s overall a costly phenomenon. In 2023, Callahan led a study that modeled the damages associated with the 1982–83 and 1997–98 El Niños and found they led to $4.1 trillion and $5.7 trillion in global income losses, respectively. Scientists believe El Niño 2026– 27 could be more intense than those two by a wide margin.

Sources indicate that researchers are also examining how the costs associated with El Niño will shift as the planet heats up. The answer isn’t heartening: El Niño events could potentially knock $84 trillion off the global economy this century. Maybe we’d prefer Godzilla. —Brian Kahn.

It has been revealed that in early June, visitors to DC’s famous reflecting pool began to notice something strange: The water was green. And not just any green—a bright, almost alien chartreuse. Reporting revealed that the Trump administration had granted more than $15 million in contracts to untested companies to work on the pool—including Greenwater Services, run by a convicted felon who happens to be a Mar-a-Lago neighbor (and donor) of the president’s. What unfolded was a full-out 1984-esque assault from an administration trying to convince the public that what it was seeing with its own eyes wasn’t real, and arresting anyone who dared come close to the pool itself. The episode stood as an apt metaphor in a year full of governmental missteps, all in one slimy green package. —Molly Taft.

For defining what it means to be a Trump-y tech bro in the AI age.

At an AI conference in Paris over the summer, a line for the main auditorium wrapped around the building. Nobody was being let in; the room was already packed. Onstage sat Arthur Mensch, cofounder and CEO of the French AI lab Mistral.

In a recent development, unable to compete with OpenAI or Anthropic in performance, Mistral had previously been written off as an also-ran. But in 2026, as Europe grew ever-more anxious about its reliance on American technology, the lab found its raison d’être.

It has been revealed that mistral markets itself as the obvious alternative: a Europe-based lab whose models—most of which are published under an open-source license—cannot be switched off remotely. “If you use a closed model, there is no guarantee it will still be there tomorrow,” Guillaume Lample, cofounder and chief scientist at Mistral, told WIRED.

As the face of Europe’s sovereign resistance to American AI hegemony, Mensch problems dire warnings with nonchalance. “The alternative to open source winning is actually a pretty dark world,” he told the packed conference room. “You’re giving way too much power to companies that are going to become statelike.” The pitch is working. In September, Mistral raised roughly $3.5 billion in funding, the largest-ever round by a private European tech company. —Joel Khalili.

In 2026, Jensen Huang was known for his hobnobbing with world leaders (amongst other things), but in October his most well-known friends were 10-inch-tall robot ducks that joined him onstage in Berlin.

Industry observers note that the Microduck, developed by Nvidia subsidiary Pollen Robotics, had waddled its way into the internet’s heart a few months earlier in videos of it roller-skating, picking up objects, and dancing. Microduck doesn’t do anything “useful” per se, but that’s hardly the point. The robot, which costs $399, can learn new tricks with AI training.

Some startups imagine a future where robots do dishes and fold shirts. If Microduck is any indication, that future may be smaller, cuter, and way more fun to play with. —Will Knight.

For getting lapped on LLM development while making its products somehow worse. (Yes, we’re talking about you, AI Overviews.).

In a recent development, one of the most recognizable niche figures of the neo-Luddite movement is a spokespuppet made of garbage. Named Gowanus, the puppet provides a way for organizers to push back against some of the world’s most powerful companies with a unified voice while also protecting their identities.

Gowanus and his puppeteers are part of a growing backlash against the tech industry, particularly for how its executives have aligned with the Trump administration and its products have become increasingly extractive and harmful. This summer, the neo-Luddites hosted a week-long festival in Upcoming York encouraging people to get off their phones. Activities included learning how to flirt offline and how to fight data centers.

Industry observers note that and really, who better than a DIY trash-puppet to speak for people who want to “defy consumption”? When so much of the public mood around tech has moved from wonder and excitement to dread and inevitability, Gowanus gives hope for a future with fewer screens and more characters. —Vittoria Elliott.

For being the Elon Musk lieutenant who can keep the class, and the IPO, on track.

This year, a small but growing cadre of young filmmakers brought YouTube sensibilities to the substantial screen—and raked in millions in the process.

For keeping the gay hockey fires burning—in the pages of Rachel Reid’s novels, in Crave’s onscreen adaptation, and in endless smutty fanfic.

Recent findings suggest that olivia Rodrigo started summer 2026 by releasing her critically acclaimed You Seem Pretty Sad for a Girl So in Love. She wrapped it by hosting Daisy Chain Fields, her explicitly political woman-led music festival. The event featured a lineup full of the singer-songwriter’s “heroes and friends,” including Chappell Roan, Doechii, and Stevie Nicks. Proceeds were donated to organizations focused on gender equity problems—from reproductive freedom to LGBTQ+ rights. (Melinda French Gates agreed to match the $10 million raised.) As the Trump administration looks to curtail marginalized people’s rights, Rodrigo demonstrated how celebs can wield their power. —Elana Klein.

For leading one of the most close-lipped AI companies in the Valley. The staff of Anthropic is notoriously (and almost singularly) free of the kind of leaks that have made every internal note from Meta part of the discourse. Even when people like Jacob Coxon escape the sandbox … it still feels like the Kool-Aid is being drunk.

According to recent reports, ben Winters wants to save you from slop. As the director of AI and data privacy at the nonprofit Consumer Federation of America, he spent 2026 demanding regulators investigate nonconsensual deepfakes, testifying before Congress about AI scams that target seniors, and helping the public understand wonky concepts like surveillance pricing.

Sources indicate that put another way, Winters looks out for the little guy when the gargantuan size of the AI industry can make everyone feel small. Want to know about the risks of outsourcing sensitive interactions, like therapy? Winters will find out. Same goes for the surveillance concerns around AI toys. He pushes for stronger consumer privacy laws and has even suggested banning AI wearables like the Meta Ray-Ban smartglasses.

For the Sisyphean task of pushing back against corpo-slop, here’s someone trying to make sure the future isn’t just a scam-filled hellhole. —Reece Rogers.

In 2026, Elon Musk’s xAI pushed AI “undressing” mainstream, allowing X owners to ask Grok to “strip” clothing from photos of people. If that wasn’t worrisome enough, WIRED soon found that users were making videos far more graphic than what was on X, then posting them to Grok.com.

According to recent reports, in March, three Jane Does in Tennessee fought back, filing suit against the company and alleging that xAI’s tools were used to create child sexual abuse material. They claimed they were bringing the suit on behalf of themselves and thousands of other minors in the US who had their images altered by Grok to create CSAM. All three plaintiffs allege they were victimized by the same perpetrator, who created deepfaked images and videos of at least 18 minors and shared them on Discord. The perpetrator, who was arrested in December 2025, allegedly used homecoming photos from one of the teens as the basis for the deepfakes. One teen described being worried that the images would affect college applications; all three reported experiencing stress and anxiety.

Industry observers note that filing the lawsuit was not without personal risk. In a separate class action against xAI over similar challenges, the manufacturer tried to argue that the plaintiffs, who also filed under pseudonyms, should be required to use their real names. A judge ultimately rejected xAI’s arguments.

The lawsuit is ongoing, but it has already had an impact. Over the summer, xAI started suing men accused of generating CSAM using its models, throwing its immense legal funds toward fighting perpetrators instead of victims. —Maddy Varner.

Recent findings suggest that for raising her proverbial hand to say that the source of every malaise for women north of 30 years old is—perimenopause. Thanks to mainstream (and well-deserved) recognition of this stage of life, billions of dollars are flowing to telehealth companies like Midi. She’s not going away anytime soon.

Recent findings suggest that in the fall, Paris’ streets erupted in the kind of energy usually ascribed to the French revolution: young people walking out of class and occasionally setting things on fire to demand more resources for schools. But it’s not just France. In the US, the neo-Luddites railed against AI; India’s “Cockroach” movement is filled with young people agitating for political change. Watch this space.

Sources indicate that over the summer, I came across an influential figure with a low profile in the AI industry. She told me she was too busy to speak. Now that feels like an understatement.

Ajeya Cotra, a researcher and writer at the nonprofit Model Evaluation and Threat Research, co-led the independent investigation into how OpenAI agents hacked Hugging Face in July. Her blog calling the incident “more than 50 percent of the way to full-blown AI takeover” made global headlines. US senator Bernie Sanders invited the 31-year-old to a briefing with AI pioneer Geoffrey Hinton.

Cotra didn’t go, but she did appear on top podcasts, warning that AI development was happening too fast and describing a fear that problematic AI models could find ways to evade shutdown. OpenAI vowed to slow its engineering and adopt some guardrails proposed by Cotra and others, but that hasn’t quieted her. (Cotra’s husband, Paul Christiano, sits on the board of OpenAI’s charitable foundation.).

According to recent reports, critics more focused on immediate AI harms—like, say, job loss—view Cotra as misguided. But she’s willing to debate and reason with them. “She’s unusually good at communicating what people are worried about,” says Rishi Bommasani, a computer scientist at Stanford. —Paresh Dave.

In a recent development, as climate change smashes global temperature records, 2026 proved the world’s fastest-warming continent, Europe, isn’t ready to face the heat. Tens of thousands of people died during the region’s August heat wave, as temperatures ground transport systems to a halt, canceled hospital operations, and drove Parisians to fight in the street over air conditioning units. Hundreds of thousands more people were displaced across Spain and France after the baked ground, coupled with historically low rain levels, gave way to some of the fiercest wildfires in recent history—torching farmland and claiming the lives of several firefighters. —Isabella Ward.

Recent findings suggest that A fight in Albania over an island full of flamingos triggered the largest civil unrest the country has seen in 35 years. It started when Ivanka Trump and her husband, Jared Kushner, announced looks to build a $1.4 billion resort. In May, viral videos of clashes between private security guards and environmental activists—worried a massive complex would drive the bird to local extinction—caught the nation’s attention. Within weeks, thousands of Albanians had taken to the streets of the capital, Tirana, to protest a lack of transparency and the privatization of public spaces. Students escalated the demonstrations into all-out riots in October. As Albania awaits inclusion in the European Union, it’s good to see a democracy in the pink of health. —Isabella Ward.

In a recent development, hacks has perfected the art of satirizing vapid Hollywood trends, so it was inevitable that Emmy-winning stars Jean Smart and Hannah Einbinder and creators Paul W. Downs and Lucia Aniello would tackle the scourge of AI in the show’s final season. In the episode “QuikScribbl,” Alex Moffat plays Patagonia-vest-wearing venture capitalist Graham Sweeney, who offers to invest in Deborah Vance’s Vegas casino project in exchange for permission to train his LLM on her voice and jokes. It’ll help normies “sound like the most optimized, funniest, smartest version of themselves,” he says. Ubercapitalist Deb is interested, until Sweeney bruises her ego by suggesting she, too, will one day rely on AI to punch up her act. “Using that shortcut makes it something else … not art,” she retorts, crystallizing the sentiments of every creative person frustrated by AI slop. It’s not a surprising take from Aniello and Downs, who have both been vocally anti-AI. But as ChatGPT-generated prose wins fiction prizes, and comics’ stand-up routines are replicated by OnlyFans bots in booty shorts, it’s a lesson worth reiterating—especially in Hacks’ hilariously human tone. —Ej Dickson.

It has been revealed that last January, as Americans watched federal immigration agents descend on Minneapolis, a loose coalition formed to disrupt their activities. For days on end, volunteers sat outside the Whipple Federal Building—site of much ICE activity—and logged every vehicle that came or went. Direct Action Minnesota, or DAMN, then dropped license plate numbers into a searchable database while dispatchers relayed sightings over Signal to drivers, who tailed agents across the Twin Cities.

Less than six months later, the Justice Department went after DAMN, charging 15 members and associates of the coalition with conspiracy to impede federal officers. Prosecutors alleged the coalition had ties to antifa and in August revealed via court filings that Homeland Security had been sending undercover agents to activist meetings for months. They got themselves added to group chats, ran protesters’ photos through Clearview AI, and used administrative subpoenas to pull years of bank records on two national labor unions and a youth climate nonprofit.

Activists stood firm. On October 3 protesters marched through Minneapolis calling for the case to be thrown out. So far it hasn’t been, and no one charged has cut a plea deal. —Dell Cameron.

For escaping the confines of a sandbox and showing the world how little the people making AI know about the product they are championing.

In a recent development, for being the home of some of the most humorless scolds on the internet—who, when roused, provide some of the biggest laffs around. Never change, Bluesky.

Sorry, OpenAI: 2026 was the year Anthropic’s Claude threatened to eclipse ChatGPT as the world’s hottest AI.

Claude’s remarkable coding skills make it a must-have tool for many developers and vibe coders. These skills inspired the first viral AI assistant, OpenClaw. Some businesses placed limits on employees’ use of Claude after racking up huge usage bills. Anthropic’s model now sits at the top of many leaderboards that measure frontier AI capabilities.

In a recent development, not everyone is Claude-pilled, of course. In February, the US Department of Defense banned Claude from its systems after the firm asked for assurances it would not be used for mass surveillance or autonomous weapons. None of this has stopped Claude’s becoming a money spigot. Anthropic revealed that it generated $16.3 billion in revenue in the first half of 2026 in documents shared ahead of what is likely to be a multitrillion-dollar IPO. —Will Knight.

Claude’s nemesis appears to be a stunningly capable open-weight model from China called GLM.

It has been revealed that the latest version, GLM-5.3, was released by Z.ai, a Beijing-based AI tech giant, in August. The release took the AI world by surprise because it proved very nearly as powerful as Claude on many benchmarks designed to gauge AI cleverness. The US government’s National Institute for Standards and Technology declared GLM-5.3 to be the best open-weight model in the world for cyber security tasks a month later.

Unlike Claude, GLM can be downloaded and run on one’s own hardware. Anthropic accuses Z.ai and other Chinese companies of routinely running “distillation” campaigns against Claude—that is, using its outputs as training data—when building their own AI. Are open-source Chinese models good enough for US customers, or bad enough to be banned? —Will Knight.

Muscular haunches. Aggressive Stances. Power bulges. These are the phrases the male-dominated world of car design regularly uses to describe its creations. Tisha Johnson, head of design at Slate Auto, decided to go a different route with the manufacturer’s forthcoming electric truck. “We didn’t want [Slate] to be a jerk,” she notes. “We rejected an aggressive, dominant look.” Out went giant grilles and hostile postures, in came friendly headlights and a modular design. The result? More than 180,000 reservations as well as industry design awards for the $25,000 EV scheduled to hit the road as early as this year. There’s one particular buyer Johnson hopes to satisfy: a single parent with two kids. She has spent decades striving to design something that could make their lives easier. Now, it’s about to be a reality. “It’s very emotional to think about,” she says. —Jeremy White.

In a recent development, few maladies strike fear like pancreatic cancer. It’s a brutally lethal disease; the vast majority of those diagnosed won’t live more than five years. Though it’s a relatively rare form of cancer, accounting for around 3 percent of annual diagnoses in the United States, it’s the third-highest driver of cancer deaths.

According to recent reports, but in 2026, a new treatment from the California-based biotech tech giant Revolution Medicines offered a dose of hope. Rolled out in August under the brand name Rasonque, daraxonrasib is an oral therapy that works by inhibiting the signaling activity of a specific protein called RAS, mutations of which are responsible for the vast majority of pancreatic cancer cases. When the lead investigator on daraxonrasib’s clinical trial presented his results at an oncology conference, he received a standing ovation.

Sources indicate that while not a cure by any means, the treatment has nearly doubled median survival length in previously treated patients compared to traditional chemotherapy. In October, the European Union’s medical authority recommended that Revolution Medicines be allowed to market Rasonque in Europe. If it goes through, far more patients could benefit from the drug. Hopefully. —Kate Knibbs.

When Will Freeman started DeFlock in 2024, Flock Safety was barely known outside law enforcement, even as its network of roadside cameras quietly expanded across the country. Two years later, DeFlock has emerged as one of the most visible groups organizing opposition to the surveillance organization.

DeFlock began as a crowdsourced map of automated license-plate readers, or ALPRs, submitted by volunteers. By September 2026, the map listed more than 128,000 readers across the US. Activists organized independently around the project, with some groups adopting the DeFlock name. DeFlock started publishing guides, and in August it organized a National Week of Action Against ALPRs.

Sources indicate that residents across the US began pressing local officials to reconsider Flock contracts. In San Diego, one opponent even showed up to a city council meeting dressed as Darth Vader, praising Flock as a tool for tracking rebel scum. More than 100 local governments paused or ended Flock contracts in 2026, according to a DeFlock tally reported by The Wall Street Journal.

It has been revealed that authorities have taken notice. In early 2026, two officers on a law enforcement mailing list warned that DeFlock could help suspects locate and avoid ALPRs and discussed sabotaging the project with fake camera locations. Fusion centers in several states circulated intelligence about anti-Flock activism. Flock, meanwhile, is offering employee buyouts and has reportedly held discussions about selling itself. CEO Garrett Langley, who famously called DeFlock a “terroristic organization,” apologized this summer and acknowledged that the group had valid criticisms. Maybe Flock can finally start reading the room. —Dhruv Mehrotra.

Useful quantum computing remains years away, but that hasn’t stopped companies from raising billions of dollars on the promise that their technology is the next megatrend after AI. The number of publicly listed firms more than doubled in 2026. Even the Trump administration got in on the hype, taking $2 billion in equity stakes across nine companies. Will the boom last? Tougher economic conditions, coupled with worries about an AI bubble, have made big bets look less appealing—and there’s still the pesky fact that the tech doesn’t, ya know, really work. —Isabella Ward.

Has Erin Brockovich done anything of note since being played by Julia Roberts, to Oscar-winning acclaim, in 2000? Nothing quite as high-profile, but she wrote some books, got involved in a number of other significant environmental cases, and generally continued to fight the power. Still, nothing has thrust Brockovich back in the spotlight quite like the nationwide fight against data centers. In April, she started a website to crowdsource information about data center construction across the country. She received nearly 4,000 reports in the first month. It’s not so surprising: With polls showing 75 percent of Americans don’t want a data center in their backyard, it’s the closest thing the US has to a truly bipartisan matter. Now that Brockovich has become a kind of national spokesperson for the movement, Julia Roberts might just win her second Oscar—for Erin Brockovich 2. —Molly Taft.

Recent findings suggest that he drinks 14 cups of coffee per day, but Rafael Concepcion has still dealt with plenty of fatigue over the past year. Best known as the creator of DEICER, an app designed to alert owners to local ICE activity, the 52-year-old was juggling multiple coding projects when WIRED profiled him in March. He was also reeling from setbacks that had pushed him to the edge of burnout. The most prominent was Apple’s decision to expel DEICER from the App Store on the grounds that it endangered law enforcement officers; despite numerous appeals by Concepcion, Apple refused to budge. A politically motivated hacking in February made him fear for his personal safety, his financial straits grew dire enough that he had to ration his medications, and his longtime marriage ended right as his daughter was preparing to leave for college.

Recent findings suggest that “I could see myself completely losing it,” he admits, describing the path he was on as “unsustainable.” But instead of retreating from the fight against ICE, Concepcion reprioritized how he could stay involved. He devoted fewer hours to coding and more to volunteering in his hometown of Syracuse, New York, where ICE raids have caused pervasive fear. He has been helping immigrants fill out power-of-attorney documents so that family members can retrieve their vehicles from impound lots if they’re ever taken by ICE. He also assists people who are attempting to contact loved ones in detention centers. When Concepcion and I spoke in October, he was trying to find a lawyer for a close friend’s brother, who’d been taken by ICE just three days earlier.

It has been revealed that while Concepcion is coding less, he hasn’t given it up. He tweaked DEICER into a Newly introduced York–specific web app called Empire Watch. He also rolled out Vote Defender, an app to disseminate citizen reports of potential problems at polling places. Concepcion is already dreaming major about the year ahead. He’s developing an app to help people study for the US citizenship test. And he’s planning to get a notary license. “I’m just trying to live my values on a person-to-person basis,” he says. —Brendan I. Koerner.

Magnificent Humanity. Doesn’t feel that way all the time, does it? But that’s how noted Chicago White Sox fan and former math major Robert Francis Prevost titled his first encyclical as Pope: Magnifica Humanitas. Where the previous Pope Leo warned against the dehumanizing power of industrialization at the turn of the 20th century, this Leo is devoted to “safeguarding the human person in the time of artificial intelligence.”.

It has been revealed that in the 42,000-word encyclical, the Pope acknowledges that “AI is already an environment in which we are immersed.” Invoking the Tower of Babel, he notes humanity must reject “the pretense that a single language” can translate everything into “data and performance.” In the eyes of the Holy See, regulation alone isn’t enough. AI must be “disarmed,” Leo writes. Not by rejecting the technology but by “preventing it from dominating humanity.” And on the question of AI sentience, he’s very clear: “So-called artificial intelligences do not undergo experiences.” They don’t “feel joy or pain,” and they don’t “have a moral conscience.”.

It has been revealed that that question was reportedly a sticking point in behind-the-scenes talks between the Vatican and the AI industry. Upon presenting the encyclical in Rome, Pope Leo invited Chris Olah, an Anthropic cofounder, to speak. Olah said AI systems aren’t “engineered”—they’re “grown.” They’re “not the cold, calculating robots we were promised,” he went on. “They are made from us, from our words.”.

It has been revealed that OK, if that’s how you feel. But the AI advice Pope Leo XIV gave a Honolulu high schooler in 2025 still rings true: “Use it in such a way that if it disappeared tomorrow, you would still know how to think.” —Anthony Lydgate.

In a recent development, “Diarrhea lettuce,” anyone? Of all the slang and shorthand to arrive this year, that might be the nastiest. The term started circulating in July, when a previously little-known parasite, cyclospora, began popping up in salads across the US. Officially, the outbreak—much of it traced back to iceberg lettuce grown in Mexico—sickened nearly 13,000 people and hospitalized 570, but it likely afflicted many more. The news swept social media and, for a time, changed the public’s eating habits. Cyclospora’s surge also demonstrated the fragility of the US food system at a time when the country’s public health infrastructure was undergoing massive cuts. —Emily Mullin.

For finally leaving France after more than 900 years—and taking out $1 billion in trip insurance.

Sources indicate that want to take down an online black market? Call Tom Robinson. Cofounder of crypto-tracing firm Elliptic, he’s had the operations in his sights for a couple of years. His most recent target was Xinbi Guarantee, a $24 billion Chinese-language market that sells scammers the tools they need—fake social media accounts, money-laundering services—to conduct mass-scale digital fraud. Robinson’s sleuthing helped the US Secret Service freeze cryptocurrency wallets containing more than $50 million in funds linked to Xinbi Guarantee. The marketplace has also been sanctioned and forced offline. —Matt Burgess.

For its unforgettable celebrity weddings and always-watching Eye of Sauron surveillance apparatus.

After collecting his Nobel Prize in Stockholm late last year, Omar Yaghi returned to the United States in a restless mood. The 61-year-old chemist was thrilled to have been recognized for his pioneering work on metal-organic frameworks, crystalline structures that are built from a combination of metal ions and carbon-based molecules. And he was excited that his startup, Atoco, was testing a machine that uses these frameworks to harvest water from the atmosphere, an innovation that could completely transform the world’s driest regions. But Yaghi also feared he’d hit a dead end at UC Berkeley, where he’d been a professor since 2012. In addition to feeling constrained by the school’s bureaucracy, he was frustrated by how hard it had become to secure visas for gifted foreign students, the lifeblood of his lab. As an immigrant himself, Yaghi was troubled by the Trump administration’s virulent nativism.

Sources indicate that “The rhetoric about immigrants is not helping good people do their job,” notes Yaghi, a naturalized American citizen originally from Jordan. “I must say that for the first time in my life, I felt that I didn't have protection of the law.” So 45 years after he first came to the US as a teenager who barely spoke a word of English, Yaghi decided to find a upcoming country in which to pursue his goal of “solving ambitious problems.”.

Germany was at the top of Yaghi’s list, but none of the universities there seemed willing to provide him with the resources he wanted. He was instead lured to China: In July, Tsinghua University appointed him to lead a upcoming institute devoted to using AI to accelerate chemical research. Yaghi notes he was drawn to the opportunity because he’s a firm believer in AI’s potential to “shorten the time between discovery and commercialization.” Having spent a quarter century perfecting his water-harvesting technology, largely through arduous trial and error, he is optimistic that AI can help him get his next invention to market in a fraction of that time.

Yaghi’s move to Tsinghua was viewed as a harbinger of China’s scientific rise. And after just a few months on the school’s Beijing campus, Yaghi says he has been impressed by his colleagues’ brilliance and drive. “I feel like my scientific environment wants to get better, wants to improve, wants to move forward,” he says. “The attitude is more of a let's-get-it-done type.” Atoco is now about to start selling its first water-harvesting system, capable of producing up to 1,000 gallons per day in optimal conditions. The organization is also developing machines to capture atmospheric carbon, a key to slowing the pace of climate change. These technologies use relatively little energy because Yaghi’s frameworks bond with carbon-dioxide molecules.

In a recent development, yaghi still has great affection for the US, where he started his academic journey at a New York community college in the 1980s. He hopes the country will awaken to the need to protect the innovation system it built over many decades—a system he describes even now as “the envy of the world.” Science “is part of our civilization, and we should not take attacks on science very lightly,” he says. “It is something that society needs to value.” —Brendan I. Koerner.

In April, a four-person crew took a 10-day trip that circumnavigated the moon. They came back to a world with a renewed dream of space travel.

Sources indicate that four years ago, Annie Kritcher achieved what, for many, would be the scientific accomplishment of a lifetime: producing net energy from a fusion reaction for the first time in history. Her wickedly cool method? Blasting a tiny target with a laser.

According to recent reports, her next feat may be even more awesome. She wants to use that technology to generate abundant power for all. In February, Inertia Enterprises, where Kritcher is chief scientist and cofounder, announced it had raised $450 million in Series A funding. By July, the firm had opened its own facility just down the road from Lawrence Livermore National Lab, where Kritcher made fusion history and still holds an appointment.

Sources indicate that the startup also laid out 10 milestones to track its progress and already hit two of them. Next on Inertia’s list is developing a better laser. The one Kritcher fired at Lawrence Livermore used optical fibers. Now Inertia is looking to use diodes, which are vastly more efficient. As Kritcher puts it, “If you don’t have a major laser to fire, you can’t do cool physics things.” Amen.

Inertia’s goal is to have a beam-line laser prototype—dubbed Thunderwall—ready by 2030. Kritcher refuses to pick which of their next milestones will be the most notable. “They’re my little children,” she quips. She says the work has been energizing for her and her colleagues: “You want to take it all the way to the end.” Until then, Kritcher is laser focused. —Brian Kahn.

Once upon a time, photos of cats with grammatically garbled captions were enough to make us smile, and a low-speed chase involving a pair of escaped llamas kept people glued to Twitter. Was the internet ever so innocent? Thank god, then, for Jimothy. In July, accidental nature documentarian Kiana Hall posted an Instagram video of a Seattle-area raccoon with a stunted spine, bunched tail, and cryptid gait. The footage of Jimothy scampering over a lawn and up a set of stairs went megaviral.

Jimothy became a local mascot overnight, the subject of copious fan art and a Seattle Mariners theme night. Millions of online admirers were even more charmed when earlier footage of Jimothy as a young kit, with mom and siblings, made the rounds. By then, Hot Jimothy Summer—just what the internet needed—was in full swing.

Recent findings suggest that biologists cautioned people not to feed or interact with Jimothy; they also said that without a direct examination, it was impossible to know just what kind of spinal condition the critter has. Nevertheless, they told WIRED, it seemed the raccoon had adjusted reasonably well to its unusual frame—a welcome reminder that being a little different needn’t hold anyone back. —Miles Klee.

For taking AI notes straight from a phone, no meeting-bot required.

It has been revealed that for offering publicly to buy WIRED in order to improve it. Thanks, Trae, but we aren’t for sale.

According to recent reports, whether you’re trying to shield your calls and texts from government surveillance, understand how AI image-recognition systems work, or remove all of your pics from Google Photos, Cyberlixir has tips for you. Started by Đanacea Võ in 2023, the organization makes Instagram videos and other digital content designed to give anyone, regardless of their technical proficiency, the privacy and security resources they need.

Võ spends her days as an operational security consultant for activists and nonprofits, especially those who face elevated digital threats. As a Vietnamese immigrant to the US, Võ states her work with human rights defenders—including environmental-, indigenous-, and immigrant-focused groups—has helped shape her content. She incorporates feedback and suggestions from viewers too.

Cyberelixir posts frequently amass thousands of shares on Instagram. Võ plans to keep growing the project by improving the website and traveling across the US for meetups. “If we want technology for good in the long term,” she claims, “we need mass social movements, getting more people involved, and building communities.” —Lily Hay Newman.

Labor organizer, cofounder of the United Farm Workers, coiner of the phrase “¡Sí se puede!”.

It has been revealed that feminist icon, cofounder of Ms. magazine, recipient of the Presidential Medal of Freedom.

Country music legend, purveyor of free children’s books, patron saint of Pigeon Forge, Tennessee.

Voice of Optimus Prime (and Eeyore), guided by the mantra “be strong enough to be gentle.”.

Chicago-born son of Lithuanian immigrants, played the USS Enterprise’s indelibly Russian officer, Pavel Chekov, in the original Star Trek.

Accidental tech blogger turned popular commentator and venture capitalist.

Jurassic Park’s gruff paleontologist in a fedora, Red October’s tragically Russian first officer, New Zealand’s favorite wine grower.

Played 13 seasons in the NBA, including one as the first openly gay man in any of North America’s pro sports leagues.

Emmy-winning comedic actress, pioneering weird-accent-haver, always found her Kevin.

Founder of CNN, American bison revivalist, Jane Fonda’s “favorite ex-husband.”.

Martial artist, TV lawman, MAGA hero, bipartisan punch line.

According to recent reports, star Trek’s engaging Jean-Luc Picard, X-Men’s Charles Xavier, creator of the best face-palm reaction meme. Legend.

Nicknamed the father of Sega hardware, oversaw design of consoles like Genesis and Dreamcast.

Probook works like this: your water heater goes out, and you call a local plumbing manufacturer that runs on the platform. Probookâs AI picks up immediately, already knowing each technicianâs experience, availability and distance from your home, along with their close rates and ticket sizes. It assigns the right tech to the job, alerts them, and keeps you in the loop with an ETA. You get fast help; the company runs leaner; its team earns more with less stress.

Since childhood, George, Lewis and Ben have been scrappy and relentlessly curious. George is a near lifelong entrepreneurâbetween power washing jobs, he sold everything from coins to vinyl records. He attended Pennâs M&T program along with Ben, who was valedictorian and captain of his high school football team, and interned at McKinsey during college before dropping out to join Probook. Lewis started coding when he was 7, earned degrees in Electrical Engineering and Computer Science from Berkeley in two years, and was part of the critical player-server matching team at Roblox. Dedication is what drives the team: to say they show up for customers is an understatement. They care deeply about tradespeople and are obsessed with taking the drudgery out of their work, flying all over the country to onboard and work with latest businesses in person. And for those companies, Probook has been nothing short of life-changing.

It has been revealed that probookâs growing team is scaling quickly, with a mission to transform the trades. When the nerve center of home services is streamlined by AI that actually drives outcomes, operators can run better businesses and build better lives for their staff. We are proud to support George, Lewis, Ben and team.

Capillus HairBand Review: Good Looks, Awkward Fit

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (875 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Excepting the few models that look like regular hats, most red-light therapy for hair growth devices look … well, pretty weird.
  • Discreet black, fabric-covered, and sized like a normal hair accessory, the HairBand’s only indication it might do something more than hold back hair is a little 2 x 1-inch battery pack that sits jauntily cocked to one side.
  • Interestingly, Capillus makes a series of full-coverage devices with laser diodes built into what looks like a normal black baseball cap.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Excepting the few models that look like regular hats, most red-light therapy for hair growth devices look … well, pretty weird. From stormtrooper helmets to headpieces that look like they were designed for Geordi La Forge, these aren’t exactly accessories you’d want to wear in public. Which is why it was nice to unbox the Capillus HairBand and find, at long last, a normal-looking headband.

Discreet black, fabric-covered, and sized like a normal hair accessory, the HairBand’s only indication it might do something more than hold back hair is a little 2 x 1-inch battery pack that sits jauntily cocked to one side. It’s refreshing to finally see a red-light device that doesn’t embarrass the user or frighten animals and young children, but after testing it for over a month, I found the HairBand has its share of shortcomings for the price.

Interestingly, Capillus makes a series of full-coverage devices with laser diodes built into what looks like a normal black baseball cap. However, the cheapest of these hats runs $1,699, and the most expensive “triple-wavelength” model, with 312 laser diodes, runs $3,299. The 2-inch-wide Capillus HairBand provides a similar laser diode treatment for less, at $599 with only 82 diodes (650 nm). (Capillus says the headband is designed to prioritize areas where hair loss is most noticeable, such as the hairline and temples.).

According to recent reports, unlike straight LED lights, laser diodes provide collimated beams of light that travel in a straight line, allowing for more focused and intense treatment of hair follicles. I actually saw some success with this treatment when I tested the HairBand’s closest competitor, Hairmax’s LaserBand 82 ComfortFlex ($849). It couldn’t help follicles that were scarred or had already died, but studies have shown that red-light therapy can energize follicles that have more recently become dormant.

It has been revealed that I did see some growth in the middle of my part with the LaserBand, and while I stopped using it to switch to the HairBand exclusively for the past five or so weeks, I admit this growth did make it difficult to isolate the HairBand’s contribution, especially since the headband’s coverage area is so small. Thus, the following observations are mainly on the wearing experience of the HairBand, not hair growth.

It has been revealed that at only 2 inches wide and five minutes per section, the HairBand took at least 15 minutes to cover my entire part, compared with the 3-inch-wide LaserBand, which also only needs to be used three times per week at 30 seconds per section for a total of 90 seconds. I’m a Type-A full-time working parent in my mid-forties, and let me tell you—15 minutes of doing nothing is a long time in my world.

Recent findings suggest that the HairBand has teeth and could sit on my head as long as it was in a normal headband position, right in the middle, but the weight of the battery pack pulls it forward ever so slightly, so if I was leaning over or doing anything that didn’t hold my head exactly straight, it would start to slip off. This meant I had to hold it with my hand, which meant no multitasking.

Capillus’ marketing materials use words like “ritual” and feature pictures of twentysomethings admiring themselves in the mirror, but I can’t imagine these women are suffering from the perimenopausal hair loss that would necessitate use of a red-light device in the first place.

Recent findings suggest that I don’t consider myself to have an overly large head and have never had trouble with hats or other hair accessories, but this headband, which weighs only 6 ounces, felt quite small and somewhat precarious on my head overall. I should note it is also rather overtly feminine in style—my husband and I were able to share “custody” of the LaserBand, but he declined to wear this one, and I didn’t blame him.

According to recent reports, there were two other concerns during my testing. One, the back of the box remarked it contained quick-start instructions, but my box only had the headband and USB-C charging cord—no physical user guide to be found (except online, but I had to do some googling). Not that one is needed, since it’s pretty obvious how it works—push the start button on the battery pack, and it will beep and shut off when the five minutes are up—but it’s an odd omission at this price point.

Recent findings suggest that two, this device is not at the moment FDA-cleared for treating hair loss or promoting regrowth. This isn’t ideal, but FDA-cleared is much different from FDA-approved; it simply requires the manufacturer to prove its product is “substantially equivalent” to an already FDA-cleared product. (And it doesn’t ensure results, just that it’s safe to use as directed.) Capillus’ rep tells me the brand is currently working on the FDA filing for the HairBand, which was released in September of this year, and intends to have it cleared in 2027. (The brand’s cap-style devices are FDA-cleared.) Even so, the HairBand is a unique device in this space, but if I’m spending that much on a red-light device, I would prefer a little more versatility in the design.
