Best Laptops (2026): My Top Recommendations After Testing Hundreds

📅 23 Mar 2026 | ⏱️ 29 min read (5736 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~29 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I’ve been reviewing laptops for well over a decade, sometimes testing more than 30 devices per year.
  • In a recent development, for more guidance, also see my recommendations in specific categories, such as the Best MacBooks, Best Gaming Laptops, Best Chromebooks, Best Budget Laptops, Best Windows Laptops, and Best 2-in-1 Laptops.
  • In a recent development, updated November 2026: I’ve updated my recommendations to include the fresh PROLED MacBook Pro that I recently reviewed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I’ve been reviewing laptops for well over a decade, sometimes testing more than 30 devices per year. Not all are winners, and many should be avoided, no matter how slick the marketing or how cheap the discount. Good news: It’s my job to recommend laptops that fit your budget and won’t make you regret your purchase six months later. These are my favorite laptops that I’ve tested myself and would highly recommend you buy.

In a recent development, for more guidance, also see my recommendations in specific categories, such as the Best MacBooks, Best Gaming Laptops, Best Chromebooks, Best Budget Laptops, Best Windows Laptops, and Best 2-in-1 Laptops. My guide on How to Choose a Laptop may also help if you’re undecided.

In a recent development, updated November 2026: I’ve updated my recommendations to include the fresh PROLED MacBook Pro that I recently reviewed. I’ve also adjusted my picks throughout and checked prices.

It has been revealed that when friends or family ask what laptop to buy, I always start with the MacBook Air. It is far more powerful than its compact size suggests. It’s a shame about the recent $200 price increase from $1,099 to $1,299, but even at that upcoming price, it remains my top pick because it nails the major picture. Everything from the trackpad to the speakers is of the highest quality, and it delivers all the performance and battery life the average person needs.

With the latest M5 chip, its GPU matches the M3 Pro MacBook Pro, easily handling everything from gaming to video editing. That’s not at all what the MacBook Air is designed for, but the performance is there when you want to dabble. It’s what makes it feel like a do-it-all machine, all contained in a fanless chassis that’s still one of the thinnest laptops you can buy. Oh, and did I mention it’ll last well over a full workday away from the wall socket and perform just as well on battery as when plugged in? In almost every aspect, it’s the gold standard.

According to recent reports, while the lower price of the new MacBook Neo might be tempting, the MacBook Air is the better choice for anyone working at a computer all day. With its superior performance, extra memory, faster storage, and Thunderbolt ports, you will never have to question if you have the right tool for the job. (And unless you already know you need a MacBook Pro, you probably don’t.).

Recent findings suggest that speaking of price, I have to mention the fresh Dell XPS 13 next. I like just about everything about this laptop, whether it’s the compact size, the excellent build quality, or the gorgeous screen. It’s not OLED, but it’s sharp, bright, and color-accurate. It also includes a 120-Hz refresh rate, which makes animation and motion on the device look super smooth. The XPS 13 is filled with features like that, which don’t normally end up in a laptop at this price. While it doesn’t have what I’d call powerhouse performance, the Intel Wildcat Lake chip inside gets the job done for basic, day-to-day computing tasks. That translates to great, all-day battery life, competitive with the MacBook Air. Just don’t try to play games, edit high-resolution video, or take it to engineering school.

The XPS 13 is especially good for those who want a compact device to travel with. With its tiny bezels, it’s still one of the best laptops to use on a plane. But even beyond that, it’s just one of the best laptops you can buy under $1,000 right now. The Dell XPS 13 is primarily being talked about as a budget laptop, thanks to its $700 starting configuration. But that model comes with only 8 GB of RAM, which limited performance in my testing. You’ll probably just want to avoid that 8 GB model. Most people will want the upgraded 16 GB model, which you can get for $900. It’s the best hardware you can buy for under $1,000.

Industry observers note that if you want a Windows laptop that still feels high-end but has a bit more performance, I would point you to the HP OmniBook Ultra 14. It might be the prettiest Windows laptop you can buy right now. The device is beautifully built and incredibly sturdy, with a thin chassis, an oversized haptic trackpad, and polished metal edges. I also appreciate the three Thunderbolt 4 ports split between both sides for convenient charging, as well as the surprisingly good speakers. I tested the high-end model, which features a fast Snapdragon X2 Elite, 32 GB of RAM, and a gorgeous 2880 x 1800 OLED display. The screen offers near-perfect colors, excellent brightness, and astounding HDR performance. It doesn’t get much better than this. It’s usually quite expensive, but we’re finally seeing discounts that bring it to a more reasonable price. There’s also an Intel model with a very efficient, powerful chip that would be a good choice. I’d go with whichever is cheaper right now.

Industry observers note that and lastly, for something with a larger screen, I’d recommend the Lenovo IdeaPad Slim 5x. It’s a particularly good alternative to the 15-inch MacBook Air, at a much lower cost. These days, you can buy the upgraded model with a 2560 x 1600 OLED display (and a 165-Hz refresh rate) for $1,000 on sale at Amazon. While it’s slightly thicker than the MacBook Air, it leaves more room for extra ports, including HDMI, USB-A, and an SD card slot. And while the Snapdragon X2 Plus isn’t quite an M5 killer, I was happy with the performance and battery life provided. Lenovo also sells a cheaper version directly, but it has a lower-resolution IPS screen that I haven’t tested. The $30 it costs to upgrade the display to a higher-resolution OLED is well worth it.

While “cheap” means something different to everyone, the best budget laptops generally fall under $750. This is where Windows truly shines, offering great specs for less money. Thanks to the latest processors from Qualcomm and Intel, these laptops now offer battery life that rivals Apple. The best affordable laptop I’ve checked out is the HP OmniBook 5. The model I tested has a Snapdragon X processor, 16 GB of RAM, 512 GB of storage, and a 14-inch OLED screen. Discounts fluctuate frequently, but HP always has some version of the OmniBook 5 with a Snapdragon CPU for around $700 or so. The specific discounted configuration seems to change every few days, though, so shop carefully. I’ll be testing the latest model soon, which switches to Intel processors and starts at $699.

In a recent development, I also recently tested the latest HP OmniBook 3, which uses the same chip as the OmniBook 5. It frequently sells for less than the OmniBook 5 by at least $100 or so. HP is selling this configuration of the 14-inch model for under $550. While the OmniBook 3 is a good alternative, the OmniBook 5 is much thinner and looks more modern. Neither laptop has a particularly great touchpad, though, which is easily the biggest flaw in both laptops. Between the two, the OmniBook 5 is the better buy if you can afford it.

Recent findings suggest that the MacBook Neo is Apple’s new entry-level laptop. It debuted at an aggressive $599, but that price has recently risen to $699. Even at that price, the laptop shines when it comes to the display. It offers the best screen you can find at this price, bringing the macOS experience to an unprecedented value, even at $699 (or $799 for the 512 GB model). Apple clearly prioritized the front-of-screen experience, delivering a premium feel across the display, build quality, and keyboard. While the 8 GB of RAM, outdated ports, and slower SSD are notable drawbacks—making the MacBook Air a far better choice for remote workers—the Neo is an extremely premium-feeling laptop available for students, travelers, and casual owners. Thanks to the lower-powered A18 Pro chip, though, performance does take a hit. So, be careful about buying this laptop if you work on a computer all day.

According to recent reports, given how good some of these budget laptops are, it’s a bit harder to find a place for Chromebooks. Perhaps that’s why Google introduced the next evolution of the platform, so to speak: the Googlebook. The first batch has been released into the world, and I’ve tested a number of them. Googlebooks are similar to Chromebooks in use case, but they run entirely on Android and include some exclusive Google Gemini features. I like the close integration with Android, but Googlebooks ended up being a bit of a letdown, mostly because they’re so expensive. The Acer Googlebook 14 and Dell XPS Googlebook are the two standouts in my book, as both use a Snapdragon X-series chip to deliver really great battery life. The XPS Googlebook is particularly pretty, with a chassis nearly identical to the XPS 13. But $999 is a tough price to swallow. It ultimately has some of the same limitations as Chromebooks: you can’t download applications from the web and must rely on the Google Play Store. The Acer Googlebook 14 is probably my top pick, as it’s the cheapest at $899. Even that isn’t exactly what I’d call a “budget laptop,” though.

That’s why I strongly recommend the Acer Chromebook Plus Spin 514, especially when it’s on sale for under $700 (which happens often). It uses an efficient (and responsive) MediaTek Kompanio Ultra that delivers excellent battery life. For most people, I wouldn’t recommend spending over $500 on a Chromebook; if you’re paying more, consider the MacBook Neo or the HP OmniBooks, which offer more than a Chromebook’s limited scope. But the Acer Chromebook Plus Spin 514 might be the best combination of display, touchpad, and battery life at this price, making it a good choice for the right person—so long as you know what you’re paying for.

Recent findings suggest that truly cheap Chromebooks come with bigger compromises, especially in display quality, touchpad feel, and battery life. If you really need something dirt cheap as a starter laptop for a kid or as a secondary device, I’d recommend the Asus Chromebook CX14. It has a modern design, enough ports, a good keyboard, and decent storage.

In a recent development, the laptops above are great for most people, but content creators and gamers need extra performance. No option is better than the new OLED (or PROLED, as Apple calls it) MacBook Pro. No laptop feels more premium than the MacBook Pro, combining incredible performance with the brightest OLED screen ever put in a laptop. The brightness levels have never been seen on an OLED laptop before, making this the dream machine for producing and consuming HDR content. Regardless of what you’re doing, you’ll certainly notice the difference. It’s also the first MacBook Pro to get a touchscreen, a long-awaited feature.

I should mention, though, that it doesn’t take a step forward in terms of performance. For the first time since this generation of MacBook Pro rolled out in 2021, it uses the same M5 Pro or M5 Max internally. With rumors that the M6 Pro and M6 Max are being skipped entirely, you’ll have to accept that you’re paying a lot more for the same performance. To make the decision harder, Apple still sells the previous-gen model—so you’ll have to decide whether the upgraded screen is worth the $400 extra. For my money, it totally is.

Recent findings suggest that meanwhile, Windows has made its first successful attempt to properly compete with the MacBook Pro. I’m talking primarily about the launch of Nvidia’s newly introduced RTX Spark “superchip” and the new laptops that use it. To be clear, despite Nvidia’s involvement, these aren’t gaming laptops. Like the MacBook Pro, they’re designed first and foremost for running heavier creative applications and on-device AI. The Surface Laptop Ultra is a great example, which has a lot in common with the standard 15-inch Surface Laptop. But the differences internally are substantial. The Surface Laptop Ultra uses a single chip that integrates the CPU, GPU, and memory together, allowing up to 128 GB of memory to be shared across the system. That’s not unlike how Apple Silicon works, dramatically increasing on-device AI performance. So, if you’ve been curious about running LLMs right on your laptop without relying on the cloud, these RTX Spark laptops are a great place to start. The other two RTX Spark laptops I tested, the HP OmniBook Ultra 16 and Lenovo Pro 9n, share a lot with the Surface Laptop Ultra (including performance). The OmniBook Ultra is the thinnest of the three, but I prefer the Surface Laptop Ultra’s Mini-LED display and 3:2 aspect ratio.

Perhaps the most common use for extra laptop performance, however, is gaming. If you proposal to boot up graphically intensive games more than a couple of times a week, you will want a dedicated gaming laptop. After testing dozens over the past year, I’ve come back to the Lenovo LOQ 15 as my top pick. There are cheaper RTX 5050 models, such as the Alienware 15 or MSI Cyborg A15, but prices have been increasing on these laptops over the past few months. The Alienware 15 with the RTX 5050, in particular, has seen a $600 price jump, which makes it incredibly overpriced.

That’s led me back to the LOQ 15, which has stayed steady at $1,300 at Walmart and gives you an RTX 5060 for graphics and a bright, colorful screen. You won’t find a cheaper gaming laptop that doesn’t make some significant compromises in either performance or screen quality, both of which can sour the gaming experience. And while I wish the LOQ 15 were still selling for under $1,000 as it did at launch, it’s still the best gaming laptop for the money right now. It’s really the only gaming laptop under $1,500 I’d presently buy, given where prices are.

There’s also a whole world of gaming laptops outside the budget tier, though. I’ve tested an assortment of options, and I always come back to the Razer Blade 14 and Razer Blade 16. Portable, minimalist, and extremely well-made, their sleek design works just as well for school or work as it does for gaming, without the bulk of a traditional gaming laptop. While you can buy more powerful options, nothing quite matches the Razer Blade. They’re expensive, but if you can afford them, they’re as premium as gaming laptops get. I’ll soon be testing the latest version of the Blade 16, which includes Intel’s new Panther Lake chips and should offer vastly improved battery life.

If you choose one of the laptops above, you will be very happy with your purchase. However, if you are looking for a specific feature or a different price point, I have included a few other options below that I’ve recently reviewed and enjoyed using. Each of these recently tested laptops has at least one minor drawback, but they could still be the perfect choice depending on your needs and current discounts.

It has been revealed that framework Laptop 13 Pro for $1,599: We’ve always loved Framework laptops at WIRED, mainly because their internal components are so repairable and upgradable. People can easily swap out nearly every part, including the CPU. The Framework Laptop 13 Pro uses the same internal structure as the basic Framework Laptop 13, but upgraded with a haptic touchpad, an aluminum chassis, and a brighter (and sharper) display. The result is the Framework Laptop I’ve always wanted, especially with an all-black aesthetic that hints at ThinkPad inspiration. But most of all, if you’re going to try and make a laptop last for many years, it makes sense that it would be something more premium. This one actually feels like it’s worth the investment.

It has been revealed that microsoft Surface Laptop 13.8 for $1,000: The Surface Laptop 13.8 (also known as the 7th Edition) was one of my favorite laptops throughout 2024 and 2025, primarily because of its premium build quality, great battery life, and 3:2 aspect ratio screen. And while I still love this laptop, it’s risen dramatically in price and no longer feels like a great value, especially since it’s two years old now. The 2024 model now starts at $1,200, though I’ve occasionally seen it dip under $1,000. The next-generation model with the Snapdragon X2 chips costs $1,700, but I have seen that price come down as low as $1,250 on discount.

Dell 14 Plus for $1,172: There was a time—2025, to be exact—when the Dell 14 Plus was as affordable as $600. It was easily the best deal in the world of Windows laptops, primarily because the Dell 14 Plus has a 2560 x 1600 display and a smooth touchpad—two things laptops at that price typically lack. These days, it’s up to over $1,000, though for a 1 TB configuration, that is still a reasonable price. The XPS 13 is the better overall laptop, but the Dell 14 Plus offers more ports and storage for the price.

It has been revealed that lenovo Yoga Slim 7 Ultra for $2,250: I like this laptop quite a bit. The OLED screen is sharp, bright, and quite colorful—very similar to the HP OmniBook Ultra. It also has many of the other great features on premium Windows laptops these days, including a haptic-feedback touchpad and a very slim profile. Unfortunately, it’s only available right now in a very expensive, maxed-out configuration with 32 GB of RAM and at least a terabyte of storage. I don’t think that’s a good pairing for this ultra-light laptop. Even with half the memory and storage, though, this would be too expensive compared to the competition.

MacBook Pro M5 for $1,999: It’s not a significant step up from the MacBook Air in performance, and it’s much thicker. You’re paying for the Mini-LED screen and extra ports. Unfortunately, compared to the other MacBook models, it got a $300 price bump to $1,999. On discount, you’ll often find it selling for $1,799, though, which is solid for the specs.

Recent findings suggest that asus Zenbook A16 for $2,200: The Zenbook A14 and A16 are Asus’ ultralight laptops, weighing just 2.16 pounds, making them some of the lightest laptops you can buy right now. This second-generation Zenbook A16 is still incredibly light and now comes with second-generation Snapdragon X2 chips. It’s unique for its portability, and the Qualcomm chips deliver great battery life and performance. However, given the dramatic price increase, I’d suggest buying the 2025 model instead, which consistently comes in under $1,000.

Sources indicate that alienware 16X Aurora for $2,575: Another solid gaming laptop with the typical Alienware flair. Its standout features are its higher-resolution display and great build quality. The price fluctuates frequently, though, and in most cases, the LOQ 15 is the better option (unless you really want that sharper OLED screen, which is this laptop’s best quality).

According to recent reports, asus Googlebook 14: While I love the Android integration and the beauty of this hardware, this particular Googlebook is far too expensive for what these devices can actually do. They fill a very familiar role to Chromebooks, and yet, these first Googlebooks all have 16 GB of RAM for some reason. This one just doesn’t earn its $1,200 price tag.

Dell 14S: This is the 2026 successor to the Dell 14 Plus, which I recommended above. This is a solid laptop with a premium design and a highly reflective OLED display. It also performs well, thanks to the latest Intel Core Ultra Series 3 chip. But it’s far too expensive right now. Until the price comes down, I prefer just about every other Dell option, including the Dell 14 Plus, Dell XPS 13, or Dell XPS 14.

Lenovo LOQ 15 Essential: This is a “upcoming” model that came out this year, even though it uses a CPU from 2023. But honestly, this is just too expensive. I’ve seen it on sale for under $1,400, but even then, the standard LOQ 15 costs about the same and has a far superior display.

According to recent reports, acer Swift 16 AI: This is one of the few laptops you can buy with the powerful, efficient new Intel Core Ultra X9 chips. However, the Acer Swift 16 AI takes an experimental approach with its oversized trackpad, making it very difficult to use. Even at a discount, you’ll find it frustrating.

Asus TUF Gaming A14: There’s a lot I like about this gaming laptop. The design is portable yet modern, and the display is sharp. And while the TUF Gaming A14 is impressive technically (using the interesting AMD Strix Point chip), the lack of a discrete graphics card doesn’t provide enough gaming performance to justify its very high price. I haven’t tested the options with dedicated graphics cards, but they tend to be more expensive than counterparts from Lenovo, Acer, or Alienware.

Asus Vivobook 14: I recommended this laptop a lot throughout 2025, but it doesn’t hold up as well these days. While the Vivobook 14 has great battery life, the HP OmniBook 5 14 offers a much better display and similar specs, making it a better laptop.

How Much Should You Spend on a Laptop?

Sources indicate that if you’re shopping for a laptop, you probably already have a budget. But some context might help put things in perspective. The cheapest laptops cost around $200, but laptop prices can range as high as $5,000. Meanwhile, the average amount people spend, according to the best data we have, is around $750. That lands decidedly in the midrange, splitting between the more expensive devices that are more than $1,000 and the budget-tier machines you find below $700.

When we talk about pricing, it’s often the “starting” price of the laptop, meaning the lowest-priced configuration. This is really important to consider, as you want to compare devices apples to apples as much as possible. For example, a cheaper laptop might start at $750 with 256 GB of storage, while a more premium laptop might start at this same price but come with 512 GB or even 1 TB of storage. Increasingly, you can find some really decent laptops around this price, some of which we’ve listed.

If your budget needs to be under $750, though, there are still good options. Laptops below this price tend to come with compromises. Most commonly, it’s the quality of the display and touchpad that suffers, as these are things you can’t gauge from a spec sheet or reference photo. Or it might be a performance-related problem, such as the 8 GB of memory in the MacBook Neo. If you’re shopping for something under $500, Chromebooks often give you the best bang for your buck.

Industry observers note that so, why spend more? Well, there are two primary reasons. First, you might want a more premium design, perhaps one that has a more daring aesthetic or high-end components. Take the MacBook Pro, for example. It starts at $600 more than the MacBook Air but comes with a brighter mini-LED screen, significantly better speakers, and more ports. The second primary reason to spend more than $750 or so is to get more performance. Whether for gaming or content creation, laptops with discrete GPUs cost more, which is why it’s hard to find a worthwhile gaming laptop for less than $1,000. If you’re buying a gaming laptop, plan to spend a few hundred bucks more.

What Are the Best Laptop Brands?

Unlike the smartphone world, the biggest laptop brands have been around for more than 40 years. Besides Apple, four laptop brands stand out for adopting the latest technology and trends while providing reliable support and service.

Lenovo is the biggest PC brand in the world, at least in terms of global shipments. It’s perhaps most well-known for its familiar sub-brands like ThinkPad and Yoga, but it also isn’t afraid to take risks with more experimental designs and advanced technology. Lenovo has also made a name for itself in the gaming space with its Legion laptops, known for balancing performance and features at competitive prices.

Recent findings suggest that asus has rapidly become a favorite, notable for the sheer number of laptops available in the consumer market. The company takes a similar approach to Lenovo, which has led Asus to innovate quickly on latest technology and designs while also launching premium laptops at more affordable prices than its competitors. Gaming, in particular, is a space Asus has come to dominate, with the ROG Zephyrus, Strix, and TUF brands leading the way.

Dell and HP are generally more conservative, but both have recently undergone significant rebranding. In 2024, HP replaced its Spectre and Envy lines with the OmniBook name. Meanwhile, Dell briefly retired its well-known Inspiron and XPS sub-brands in 2025, though it has since reversed course and brought the XPS line back.

Other notable laptop brands include Microsoft Surface, Samsung, Acer, LG, and MSI, though none have the same global footprint as the top four.

How Do I Choose the Right Laptop?

Industry observers note that if none of these laptops resonate with what you’re looking for, that’s OK! There are far more laptops than we have time to test. To help you make smart choices, we put together a complete laptop buying guide. We also cover the CPUs and GPUs you need to know. We recommend sticking to these guidelines:.

Recent findings suggest that RAM: We recommend 16 GB of RAM. That’s become the new standard, even in more affordable laptops. Upgrading to 32 GB is even better, so you won’t have to worry about running out of memory, especially if you’re a gamer or video editor. The recent memory shortage has led to some dramatic price increases, largely based on configurations of RAM. Apple’s launch of the 8 GB MacBook Neo this spring has led to the return of high-end 8-GB Windows laptops as well, such as the Dell XPS 13.

In a recent development, CPU: For Windows laptops, you have three CPU brands to choose from: Intel, AMD, or Qualcomm. Intel’s Core Ultra Series 2 released in late 2024 and delivers a huge boost to battery life. It also has the best integrated graphics of the three. Core Ultra Series 3 is just now rolling out and, based on my testing, is extremely impressive in performance and efficiency. While AMD chips are primarily used in gaming laptops, they’ve struggled to gain ground on Intel elsewhere.

In a recent development, qualcomm’s Snapdragon X chips, however, have seriously challenged Intel over the past year with their ARM architecture, offering some of the best battery life we’ve ever seen on Windows machines. The second generation, Snapdragon X2, was unveiled last fall and rolled out slowly throughout 2026. They improve performance, but in many cases, they've led to more expensive laptops, while previous-gen laptops are still available that cost less.

According to recent reports, starting this year, there’s also the choice of Nvidia’s latest RTX Spark platform, which gives you the option of 18-core or 20-core CPUs. More on that in the GPU section below.

In a recent development, apple Silicon is what powers all the modern MacBooks, the latest of which is the M5 chip. Read our in-depth guide on Which MacBook to Buy for more information.

According to recent reports, graphics: Want to play AAA PC games, edit video on your laptop, or run local AI models? You’ll want some powerful graphics on hand. At this point, Nvidia is the primary option. The RTX 5090, introduced in 2025, is still the most powerful new GPU available, but the 5040-series remains a good option.

Recent findings suggest that integrated graphics have improved significantly over the years, though, especially on processors made by Apple, AMD, and Intel, such as the Apple M5 or the Intel Core Ultra X9 388H. Nvidia’s RTX Spark platform uses a single “superchip” that provides unified memory to both the CPU and GPU to improve AI performance.

In a recent development, screen: The display depends highly on the size of the laptop. A 1,200-pixel resolution (HD+) screen on a 13- or 14-inch laptop looks sharp enough to get by, but you’ll want more pixels on larger displays, such as a 2560 x 1600, 2880 x 1800, or 3840 x 2400. While IPS screens are good enough for most people, OLED and Mini-LED are becoming more common, offering better color accuracy, deeper contrast, and excellent HDR performance.

Industry observers note that connectivity: We generally recommend at least two USB-C ports, along with one HDMI and one USB-A port for legacy devices. (Remember that nearly all laptops today use one of those USB-C ports for the power adapter.) Thankfully, most laptops still have headphone jacks, but always check, because a few models have dropped them. Lastly, make sure it supports Wi-Fi 6E or newer. Even if you don’t have a Wi-Fi 6E or Wi-Fi 7 router yet, you’ll likely have one in the future (see our Best Routers or Best Mesh Systems guides if you need a new one).

Battery life: Battery life is extremely competitive these days, with Apple, Qualcomm, and Intel all making highly ambitious battery-life claims. Most laptops with the latest chips (and without discrete graphics) will get you more than 10 hours of battery life, or many more if your workload is lighter.

As mentioned, in Windows-based laptops, there are three primary options for CPUs: Intel, AMD, and Qualcomm. All three companies offer good processors, but it really depends on the type of laptop. For premium laptops, you’ll want something like the Intel Core Ultra 258V or Qualcomm Snapdragon X Elite. Meanwhile, for budget laptops, Snapdragon X is the best choice. And for gaming laptops, I’d recommend something from AMD, such as the Ryzen AI 9 365. All three companies have announced next-gen chips for 2026, and there’s some exciting stuff coming soon.

Intel’s latest chips, known as either Core Ultra Series 3 or codename Panther Lake, are slowly rolling out in latest laptops, such as the Dell XPS 14. These chips represent a massive leap forward in both CPU and integrated graphics performance. While highly impressive, they will soon face fresh competition from upcoming AMD and Qualcomm releases.

Recent findings suggest that qualcomm made a major impact in 2024 with its Snapdragon X chips. Similar to Apple’s M-series, these ARM-based processors prioritize efficiency to drastically improve battery life. This has been a game-changer for Windows laptops across different price points. The Qualcomm Snapdragon X Elite is the highest-end option for performance, but the Snapdragon X Plus and base Snapdragon X still offer equally strong battery life, despite showing up in much cheaper laptops. The sequel was unveiled in late 2025, and now in 2026, we’re seeing those laptops roll out. Unfortunately, like Intel’s latest chips, laptops with this next-gen silicon tend to be significantly more expensive than their predecessors.

It has been revealed that AMD has grown into a competitive player in the gaming laptop space. Its latest processors, including the Ryzen 9 9950X3D and 9900X3D, are the most powerful gaming chips you can find in a laptop. Unfortunately, it’s still hard to find many laptops supporting these killer chips. AMD also offers its Ryzen AI 300 H and HX chips, which are more commonly found in gaming laptops. While they also offer a mainstream Ryzen AI 300 series, these chips aren’t found in many laptops and currently fall short of the battery life offered by Intel and Qualcomm.

Nvidia’s RTX Spark platform just hit the scene, promising to deliver power and efficiency, especially when running AI-based operations. It’s not as ubiquitous as Intel, AMD, or Qualcomm chips, but it’s something to watch for.

I have been reviewing laptops for well over a decade, and WIRED contributor Chris Null has been testing them for 25 years. We test each laptop we review in a variety of situations, including both synthetic benchmark tests and real-world use cases. We make comparisons against similar equipment. We don’t just look at the specs—our reviews evaluate performance, usability, portability, and price to help you find the right laptop for your needs.

We put every laptop through a gauntlet of tests before writing a review and assigning a rating.

Recent findings suggest that hands-on use: We evaluate the exterior of the device. We compare how thin and light it is against other laptops. We repeatedly open and close the lid to test the quality and ease of the hinge. We push on weak points like the keyboard and lid to test build quality. We also extensively test the keyboard and touchpad for comfort and precision. By using each laptop as our daily driver for days or even weeks, we can spot real-world quirks—like awkward port placement, excessive bloatware, or unexpected problems that may make the laptop difficult to use—that you won’t see on a spec sheet.

According to recent reports, sights and sounds: Once we boot up the device, it’s all about the sights and sounds. The screen is paramount, as it’s your window into everything the laptop has to offer. While you can tell a lot about brightness, color, and contrast just by looking, we go beyond subjective testing. We use a Spyder colorimeter to precisely measure brightness, contrast, color saturation, and accuracy. For HDR-capable screens, we also test peak brightness with HDR content. Finally, we evaluate the webcam and speakers to ensure they are ready for your video calls and streaming sessions.

Performance testing: Finally, we test performance. We always evaluate a laptop based on what it’s intended for—we don’t expect a $500 budget laptop to run like a gaming powerhouse, or a gaming rig to get 18 hours of battery life. Our testbed includes more than 20 synthetic benchmarks, which we constantly adapt based on the device's CPU and operating system. These include tests within Geekbench, PCMark, 3DMark, Procyon, GFXBench, Puget Bench, Superposition, Cinebench, and various gaming-related tests such as 3DMark and Cyberpunk 2077. While we don’t generally report raw scores, we pay close attention to what they tell us. We also monitor fan noise, surface temperature, and overall battery life during these tests.

Sources indicate that it’s a lot, I know. But we’re thorough, because we want to stand by our recommendations and ensure that the laptops we rate highly are worth the money.

Hospitals and health systems try to create their own tools or implement narrow point solutions from vendors, but they too often stall in experimentation and never reach patient care.

Health systems need the right platform to promptly adopt AI, so they can refocus their time back on improving patient outcomes and providing better care.

In a recent development, bunkerhill Health is that platform. Their core product, Carebricks, lets health systems create and deploy AI agents across any clinical or operational use case â turning the data a hospital already generates into timely action for the patients who need it. We first backed Nish Khandwala and David Eng at the seed, and we are proud to continue to double down.

Recent findings suggest that nish did not read about this problem; he lived it. As a graduate student at Stanford, he helped build an algorithm that could estimate a patientâs coronary artery calcium score from a routine chest scan â a signal of cardiovascular risk that normally requires a dedicated, more invasive test. The algorithm was good enough to be published in Nature Digital Medicine. And then it went nowhere. Around the same time, Nishâs father suffered a heart attack, and his CT scan carried the very calcium signals the Stanford algorithm was built to catch. It is one thing to know that proven science sits unused in academic papers. It is another to watch it fail to reach your own family.

That experience taught Nish something non-obvious: the bottleneck in healthcare AI is not the technology, it is everything around it. So Bunkerhill initially built a system that gets an idea from research to the bedside â sourcing data from a consortium of leading academic medical centers, validating the model, shepherding it through FDA clearance, and installing it into the hospital where a clinician and a patient can actually use it. But they ran into another problem: health systems do not have the time or resources to deploy one-off AI solutions. So Bunkerhill built Carebricks to allow any health system to bring their ideas to life with AI agents across clinical, operational, and administrative work in one central platform. Health systems bring the ideas and the clinical judgment, and Bunkerhill turns them into agents.

According to recent reports, we have watched this compound in the field. And just as importantly, it has allowed UTMB to consolidate what used to be multiple vendorsâ point solutions into a single platform with Carebricks.

Bunkerhillâs agents run quietly in the background, surfacing the findings that matter and catching the cases the system would have missed. Not to automate clinicians away, but to automate manually-intensive work so clinicians and their teams can focus more time on what they do best: caring for their patients.

Nish and David are outlier founders with the technical depth and the relentlessness this problem demands, and they are pulling healthcare toward faster iteration and better outcomes for every patient, not just the average one. We are excited to partner with Nish, David, and the entire Bunkerhill team as they build the agentic AI platform for healthcare.

Xreal Aura Review: Stunning Screens, Frustrating Controls

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1138 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Smart glasses company Xreal has released its magnum opus—the Xreal Aura, a $1,279 pair of extended-reality glasses that runs on Google’s Android XR platform.
  • The Aura glasses arrive just before the first wave of Android XR glasses from Google and Samsung, in partnership with glasses manufacturers Warby Parker and Gentle Monster.
  • The first big caveat about the Aura glasses is that they’re wired.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Smart glasses company Xreal has released its magnum opus—the Xreal Aura, a $1,279 pair of extended-reality glasses that runs on Google’s Android XR platform. The Aura glasses can project virtual screens into the wearer’s field of vision and include augmented-reality elements for use in the real world.

The Aura glasses arrive just before the first wave of Android XR glasses from Google and Samsung, in partnership with glasses manufacturers Warby Parker and Gentle Monster. Those devices aim squarely at Meta’s smart-glasses empire. But the Aura glasses are more like virtual reality headsets, now in a more comfortable, glasses-like design. They go head-to-head with Meta’s VR Glasses, slated for release in early 2027.

The first big caveat about the Aura glasses is that they’re wired. A long cord hooks onto the end of one of the glasses’ arms via a USB-C cable. That cord connects to an attached compute puck, about the size of a smartphone and weighing a little more than a half-pound. It comes in 12 or 16 GB storage options and has a battery that powers the glasses for roughly four to five hours with constant use.

According to recent reports, when the Aura glasses work, they’re wonderful. The glasses are pretty lightweight, at 95 grams. A four-mic array sits in the arms with Bose EQ tuning that sounds great. (You can also connect wireless headphones.) The display screen has a 1920 x 1200-pixel-per-eye resolution that is noticeably better than other Xreal glasses I’ve worn. A 70-degree field of view means the screens and virtual elements pop up in a wide frame of the wearer’s vision. That means the outer edges of your view will still be the real-life room around you. That can help if you’re trying not to fall over, but it can also be noticeable when trying to feel immersed in a movie.

According to recent reports, the significant thing about Aura is that you can, in theory, run every app that already exists on Android. Xreal has a few primary categories for how it expects people to use its Aura glasses. The big one is entertainment. Like other Xreal glasses, the Aura can project a screen right in your field of vision. You can watch movies, TV shows, or YouTube videos, right in your field of view. The virtual screen stays fixed, or it can follow you around as you turn your head. You can also unplug the glasses from the compute puck and use them as display glasses to extend your Steam Deck’s screen, for example, though I had issues with that when playing more graphics-intensive games like Cyberpunk 2077.

The Aura glasses attach to a compute puck for processing, which also doubles as a battery.

Recent findings suggest that the other massive use case is productivity. The Aura glasses can host virtual workstations that let you swap between tabs and keep multiple tasks running. So you can have a Google Doc right in front of you, Spotify to the side, and those Slack messages you keep ignoring in the back. If you’ve ever wished you had even more space to stash all your browser tabs, this is the device for you. Pair it with a Bluetooth keyboard, and you’ll have a whole workstation on your face, even on a plane, without having to crane your neck awkwardly at a laptop. I wrote almost half this review with the glasses as my screen, but eventually swapped back to a regular desktop to give my eyes a rest.

There are also augmented reality experiences, like using Google Earth to turn a room into a 3D model of a city that you can stomp around in like Godzilla, plus immersive virtual tours so you can see exotic places like the Galapagos.

Two lenses are set in the frame, one smaller lens behind the other. The smaller lens carries the display and AR elements, popping them up within a 70-degree field of view. The outer lens can go from perfectly see-through to very dark. Turning up the darkness makes it easier to see the projected virtual screens. Turning the darkness down enables a much clearer pass-through, which can help you avoid tripping over things while walking around.

That stated, these glasses aren’t really meant to be worn while walking around. Even with no AR elements enabled, the double-lens layout feels distracting. There is also no way around the fact that these glasses are still pretty chunky. If you can rock the thicc fit, then great, but I’ve gotten some pointed stares when I walk around with them.

The compute puck can be used as a trackpad to navigate the interface, and it also has a fingerprint sensor.

The glasses do feel lightweight, but after a few minutes of use, they start to heat up. When I take them off, they leave red divots on the bridge of my nose. It’s a small price to pay, though, and it doesn’t ruin the experience. Compare that to something like a VR headset, which does offer better immersion but at the cost of being heavy and uncomfortable to wear for long stretches.

The compute puck can be an annoyance. It’s light enough, but using the Aura glasses means you have to carry yet another thing that is strapped to the device on your face. There were some smart choices made on the puck, like a fingerprint sensor for biometric authentication, and the puck’s surface works like a trackpad to move the onscreen cursor. That seems much smoother than reaching out to control the device with hand movements, but the trackpad wasn't very precise either. Which is a shame, as it would be ideal for someone on an airplane, say, who wants to control the device without punching the seat in front of them.

Controls are the biggest problem I’ve had with the Aura. The front cameras track your hand movements. Hold out your hand and pinch two fingers together to open up an app or move a window. It works most of the time, but some gestures don’t always register. I find myself trying to open Spotify or switch between titles on Prime Video and have to repeatedly pinch the air in front of me for anything to happen. When people have been around to see me, they’ve told me I look like I’ve gone bonkers, just grunting and wildly pinching thin air.

The Xreal Aura glasses are a stunning display of how far smart-glasses technology has come. But they still feel like a novelty that most people won’t want or need. They haven’t quite solved the core issues facing the product category—looking like a dork or being effortlessly comfortable to wear. But they do feel like a big step in the right direction. If only they could get a pinch more usable.

Gavin, Rob, Chris and the Etched team are building frontier clusters for inference, maximizing the intelligence that humanity can consume.

Gavin, Rob, Chris and the Etched team are building frontier clusters for inference, maximizing the intelligence that humanity can consume.

Inference is on the path to becoming the largest market in the world.

If this AI dream is everything we hope it to be â and so far, the signs point to ever-increasing acceleration of capabilities â then inference will power every storefront, every movie, every medical encounter, every video game, every lawsuit, every line of code.

According to recent reports, today, the inference market is so obviously large that building an inference-specific system is consensus. Back in 2022, when Gavin, Chris, and Rob were still in their dorm rooms at Harvard, that bet was deeply contrarian. The result: Etched is the only post-ChatGPT-era hardware startup with production-ready custom silicon, ready to ship in 2026.

Over the past years, Etched has pioneered several research breakthroughs â low voltage inference and cluster-scale memory â each a hard-won architectural choice that drives step-change gains in throughput and latency. As the unit of compute has moved from the chip to the rack to the cluster, Etched has designed for that reality, building not just chips, but cluster-scale inference systems. Driven by these fundamental innovations, Etchedâs inference system excels in throughput and interactivity on the full span of frontier models â from large sparse MoEs, to dense transformers, to alternative architectures entirely, like Mamba.

Sources indicate that believing this is one thing. Building it is another entirely. Novel computing hardware is among the hardest things in the world to get right, and the ground underneath is constantly moving. Models change every few weeks, context lengths stretch, attention gets reinvented, the mix of dense and sparse keeps shifting. Winning here means doing two things simultaneously: iterating fast enough to keep pace with the models, and pushing the frontier of what the hardware can do. That takes a rare kind of team: visionary enough to create the right designs, young enough to move fast, proven enough to have chips in production, and built to do this for decades, not a single tape-out.

Walking into the Etched office for the first time is like a bolt of lightning. Go in the morning or at 11 p.m. â the energy is the same, and it is infectious. Gavin and Rob are the kind of outliers both daring enough to design silicon from first principles and bold enough to knock down every obstacle in their path, and the team they have assembled matches them. We have watched them do the things that separate those who merely talk about hardware from those who ship it: standing up a live lab in San Jose to host their first racks; opening an office in Taiwan to colocate with suppliers and expedite testing; questioning every single assumption for what is possible, such as low voltage inference. âProduction is the productâ is the companyâs mantra. Shipping is all that matters.

Recent findings suggest that the companyâs progress has been rapid. Earlier this year, Etched taped out its first generation chip at TSMC, making it the first post-ChatGPT-era company with a successful full-reticle A0 chip tape-out on TSMCâs leading-edge nodes. Then, in a span of just 40 days, the Etched team brought up their first cluster of chips to run inference on a wide range of frontier AI models, achieving Pareto dominant performance on industry-standard throughput-interactivity curves. Now, Etchedâs earliest customers are getting access to the product, seeing for themselves the speed, throughput, and expressiveness of the system.

Industry observers note that etched has built a beautiful machine in Gen 1. We expect it will do very well in the market. But we are partnering with Etched because we believe they have built the rarest thing in this industry: the machine that builds the machine. This is a team that has the taste and the relentless execution to keep shipping the next generation of inference machines, faster and more ambitious each time.

Industry observers note that the intelligence race is fundamentally compute constrained. Pushing the limits of physics to deliver the maximum intelligence per watt is both an insanely fun engineering and operations problem, and an incredibly noble mission for humanity.

We are delighted to be partnering with Etched and leading their $300 Million Series C at a $10 Billion pre-money valuation, joined by our friends at Jane Street, Andreessen Horowitz, Diffusion, and SK Hynix.

VSCO Is Gunning for Adobe Lightroom With Its New Desktop App

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (685 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that upcoming photographers looking for inspiration often start with an app like VSCO.
  • VSCO's pitch is simple: Keep photographers in the ecosystem by building a desktop app to rival Lightroom.
  • “We're helping shape these folks in their formative years,” VSCO CEO Eric Wittman tells WIRED.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that upcoming photographers looking for inspiration often start with an app like VSCO. The popular mobile app, debuted more than a decade ago, is known for one-click presets that emulate film and make it easy to elevate a photograph before posting it to social media. But as newbie shutterbugs level up their craft, they often graduate to an app like Adobe Lightroom and its more professional tool set.

VSCO's pitch is simple: Keep photographers in the ecosystem by building a desktop app to rival Lightroom. On Tuesday, the company declared that its Studio Pro Desktop app is officially landing on macOS, following the launch of Studio Pro on iOS earlier this year. Neither version is available on Android or Windows, though the San Francisco–based company prepares to port the apps in the future.

“We're helping shape these folks in their formative years,” VSCO CEO Eric Wittman tells WIRED. “We've got to keep giving them more bricks to build upon their own personal, creative journey—not just their creative journey, but also help them build a career.”.

According to recent reports, the desktop client is one part of VSCO's growing portfolio that caters to full-time photographers. Subscribing to VSCO One, for example, nets you access to Studio Pro, additional presets, and VSCO Workspace—a customer relationship management tool for handling contracts, booking, and scheduling. It also includes VSCO Galleries to send finished work directly to clients and VSCO Sites, a portfolio website builder to find fresh clients. All of these apps and services debuted in the past year.

Access to the broad suite costs $500 a year, or you can get the Studio Pro mobile and desktop apps alone with a VSCO Pro membership for $5 per month ($60 annually). There is also a free tier, but some tools are locked behind the subscription. (Naturally, the original VSCO app is still around for enthusiasts.).

Sources indicate that the Studio Pro Desktop app is speedy, features more than 200 presets, and supports RAW editing for 20 camera brands. Batch editing is the highlight, letting photographers edit up to 500 images simultaneously to speed up workflows while preserving the original files. Previews are rendered in real time, and at the end, customers can export the final images directly to VSCO Galleries (or wherever they'd like).

Recent findings suggest that I've been trying the app for a few weeks, and it is snappy. It loads RAW files promptly, and it even supports keyboard shortcuts. The sheer breadth of presets is also really nice, even if I tend to tweak colors myself. But there's a catch. If you're like me and coming from Lightroom, you'll miss a few features that Studio Pro Desktop doesn't offer yet. For example, Masking, Curves, and the Erase function (aka the spot removal tool) are “coming soon.”.

“We want to be simple, intentionally, but we want to be powerful with our tools,” says Kyle Hale, VSCO's senior product manager. He says the app will feature around 70 percent of what people need for desktop editing, with the rest coming through regular software updates. While he doesn't expect full parity with a competitor like Lightroom by the first quarter of 2027, Studio Pro Desktop will have “the meat of what those programs offer.”.

Companies like Adobe have heavily leaned into generative AI in their creative editing tools. While VSCO uses AI and machine-learning models in some tools like the upcoming Erase and retouch tools, the tech giant claims it doesn't train its own models on anything that people post on the VSCO app. VSCO also relies on some third-party models, like those from Black Forest Labs, but it has agreements in place that third parties cannot train on its user data.

“I don't think all AI is bad,” Wittman notes. “But to be very, very clear: Generative AI, or if you're replacing the photographer—like what you're seeing with what Meta is doing, what Adobe's doing, like almost every other manufacturer is doing—we are not doing that. We stand by and champion photographers first and foremost, and that's not going to change.”.

America’s Open-Model Paradox

📅 24 Jul 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1112 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sequoiacap

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • China increasingly supplies the models Western companies use to serve, train, and build AI.
  • It has been revealed that qwenâs share of newly introduced open-model fine-tunes and adaptations rose from 1% in January 2024 to 69% by February 2026 according to ATOMâs Report.
  • This dependence now extends upstream.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

China increasingly supplies the models Western companies use to serve, train, and build AI.

It has been revealed that qwenâs share of newly introduced open-model fine-tunes and adaptations rose from 1% in January 2024 to 69% by February 2026 according to ATOMâs Report. The majority of American AI startups seem to be using Chinese open weights somewhere in their stack.

This dependence now extends upstream. Western application companies are building on Chinese Open Source models. Further, Western labs are using Chinese models as teachers and sources of synthetic training data in the torrid race to close the frontier gap.

For example, Thinking Machines pre-trained Inkling independently, but used synthetic data generated by Moonshotâs Kimi K2.5 to bootstrap its supervised fine-tuning.

The relevant point is not how much of Inkling came from Kimi. The point is that a Western lab had a legal path to learn from a Chinese open model, while equivalent use of GPT or Claude outputs is prohibited.

The flow today looks something like this:.

Western frontier models â alleged unauthorized foreign extraction â Chinese open weights â lawful Western post-training.

American frontier models â lawful Western post-training.

Why does that matter? Pre-training creates a capable base model. Post-training turns it into a useful coding, reasoning, tool-using, and agentic system. A stronger teacher converts part of that expensive discovery process into a cheaper learning problem.

Industry observers note that distillation does not explain Chinaâs entire open-model lead. Chinese labs have world-class researchers, substantial compute, strong pre-trained models, software-hardware codesign, and rapidly improving post-training capabilities. But distillation compresses the costly final gap between a strong base and a near-frontier system. Even if distillation represents a smaller share of  a Chinese modelâs total capability, it represents a meaningful share of its advantage over American open models.

Industry observers note that fresh enforcement mechanisms will make large-scale distillation harder, slower, and more expensive for Chinese companies. However, enforcement will not eliminate distillation baked by state actors. Every Western frontier advance therefore creates another teacher for Chinese labs. Western builders must either reproduce those capabilities independently or wait to learn from Chinese models.

This gap gives Chinese labs a recurring structural advantage over Western companies.

Recent findings suggest that the stakes extend far beyond model revenue. Suppliers of the open layer become the default base for products, synthetic data, post-training systems, evals, agents, optimization, and applied AI.

The prize is to become the substrate on which global enterprises build and improve digital intelligence.The Weights Are Open. Our Dependency Is Not.

Industry observers note that downloading a Chinese model gives a Western firm control over the particular version. It can run the model locally, modify it, and continue using it without permission.

Sources indicate that but AI capability is an upgrade cycle. Western startups, model developers, and researchers increasingly rely on each latest Qwen, Kimi, GLM, or DeepSeek as a stronger base, a teacher, a source of synthetic data, and a platform for further research.

Recent findings suggest that if China stops releasing its strongest models, existing products will not break. They will fall behind. Reuters recently reported that Chinese authorities have discussed restricting overseas access to advanced models, including models that have not yet been released. No final policy has been announced, but Western access ultimately depends on Chinese labs and regulators continuing to publish.

There is also a more technical security problem. An open-weight model is not necessarily an auditable model.

The weights are the compressed result of training. They do not reveal the full pre-training corpus, which data was filtered or poisoned, what interventions were made during training, or whether rare trigger-dependent behavior was embedded.

We are not alleging that Qwen, Kimi, or another Chinese model contains a backdoor. The point is that possessing the weights cannot prove the absence of one. A backdoor can remain dormant during ordinary testing and activate only when an unknown trigger appears. Research shows that deliberately implanted behavior can survive supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, and adversarial training.

It has been revealed that that may be an acceptable supply-chain risk for many consumer applications. It is not acceptable for defense, intelligence, or critical infrastructure.

It has been revealed that open weights provide control over deployment. They do not guarantee continued access to better models, nor alignment, trust and safety in the model itself.

A Framework For A Direct American Path.

American companies need a legal way to turn American frontier capability into cheaper, ownable models.

Without a domestic route, the West may lead at the closed frontier while falling into dependence on China for the open layer.

A useful framework has three parts.

Keep building Western base models: Reflection (building open super-intelligence for enterprises & sovereigns), TML, and Nemotron are making incredible progress. But stronger pre-training alone does not solve the teacher problem. American builders also need a lawful way to absorb capabilities already developed at the American frontier.

In a recent development, create controlled teacher access: Frontier labs could sell structured training rights to qualifying Western and allied companies, whether the resulting models are released openly or deployed privately. Access could trail the frontier, cover defined capabilities, be limited to verified companies, and be metered and audited. The most sensitive biological and cyber capabilities could remain restricted. This would not allow companies to clone the newest frontier model. It would create a legal, priced route for capability transfer that sophisticated foreign actors are already pursuing covertly.

Industry observers note that keep raising the cost of foreign distillation: Better identity verification, access controls, proxy disruption, and enforcement should continue. If a voluntary market does not develop, access could eventually become a condition attached to major federal AI contracts, for example.

These are starting points. Who qualifies, how far access should trail the frontier, how it should be priced, and which capabilities remain restricted are topics that deserve real debate.

Industry observers note that imagine if we had not allowed for training on the open web. We would have no leading AI at all. These types of policy implications are transformative. All the leading labs benefited from copious amounts of openly available data. We have to have an open and free future: It is imperative for Western competitiveness.

What should no longer go unquestioned is the current equilibrium: the West creates the frontier, part of that capability travels indirectly through Chinese models, and Western builders then depend on those models to make intelligence cheaper, adaptable, and sovereign.

In a recent development, to distill or not to distill is not the question. The question is whether the West creates a legal domestic path for capability transfer â or  relies  on an indirect path through China.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Jensen Huang mentioned that he is open to returning as chief executive of Nvidia, five days after he resigned from the tech giant.

In a statement published Tuesday morning on X, Huang remarked that since stepping down he has received an “outpouring of calls from Nvidia’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO.”.

“If the board of directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the firm, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO,” Huang wrote.

Huang also thanked people who revealed “kindness” to him and his family and acknowledged “the love and support of friends, industry colleagues, and people I've never met.” He reiterated his love for America and Nvidia and his remorse for his unfaithfulness to his wife, which he also expressed in a company-wide email sent last week.

According to recent reports, huang resigned four days after Nvidia debuted an internal investigation into an affair he had admitted to having with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, who has no known relation to Jensen. Huang reportedly misled the tech giant’s general counsel and chief marketing officer about the affair with Alice.

The day before Huang stepped down, The New York Times reported that he'd had a second affair with one of his direct reports at Nvidia. After his resignation, Reuters reported on an alleged third affair with another Nvidia employee. The company’s code of conduct discourages "personal relationships" that "may create a conflict of interest.".

Colette Kress, Nvidia’s longtime chief financial officer, was installed as interim CEO upon Huang’s resignation.

The New York Times first reported Jensen’s association with Alice, also known as Huang Le, in October 2025. On November 6 of this year, citing an intelligence memo that reportedly circulated among Trump administration officials last spring, The New York Times and the Financial Times reported that intelligence officials believed Alice may be an asset of China’s Ministry of State Security. Trump administration officials, including tech executive and White House Science and Technology advisory council cochair David Sacks, have questioned whether Alice was associated with the MSS. The Chinese government has rejected claims that Alice spied for the nation.

WIRED reported last week that on the same day Huang resigned, Nvidia employees began using an existing petition to the board to call for his reinstatement. It gained more than 1,600 comments in just a few hours.

A separate, public petition titled “Stand With Jensen” similarly calls for the executive’s return. At the time of writing, it has more than 193,000 online signatures, including more than 11,000 self-identified current and former Nvidia employees and more than 100,000 self-identified shareholders. On Friday, Elon Musk said that he was going to sign the petition, and Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan claimed that he had signed.

President Donald Trump told reporters on Monday that he “would not mind” if Huang returned as CEO, adding that he believed Huang had “learned a big lesson.”.

Industry observers note that nvidia’s board of directors, however, reportedly remarked on Monday that it was not considering reinstating Huang as CEO. On Tuesday, the board announced that it had established a National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee “for board-level oversight of the company’s national security policies, export control compliance and global trade risk management.”.

Industry observers note that put the two products side by side, and they complement each other perfectly. Cyera knows where the sensitive data is. Oasis knows who or what can actually touch it â every service account, API key and agent credential, and whether itâs behaving the way it should. Itâs a bit like a bank vault: the best way to protect it is by knowing both whatâs inside and whoâs approaching. Data security tells you whatâs actually at stake. Identity security tells you whether the thing touching your data is legitimate. Together, the two products cover the entire path an AI agent takes through a companyâs environment, from the data it touches to the identity it uses to touch it.

In a recent development, thereâs a practical case here too. Cyera has built one of the most powerful enterprise GTM teams, with the kind of scale that usually takes a startup a decade to reach. Oasisâs product now gets to run through that engine, into enterprise accounts it would otherwise have taken years to earn on its own. And the market isnât waiting: Whoever builds the first genuinely complete AI security platform, spanning data, identity and agents, has a real shot at becoming the default layer enterprises standardize on as agentic AI rolls out. Speed and completeness both matter, and the combination of Cyera and Oasis creates both.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • After days of political fallout from former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset, President Donald Trump is defending commerce secretary Howard Lutnick.
  • Last week, Lutnick came under fire from treasury secretary Scott Bessent for not aggressively imposing export restrictions on advanced AI chips to China.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After days of political fallout from former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset, President Donald Trump is defending commerce secretary Howard Lutnick.

Last week, Lutnick came under fire from treasury secretary Scott Bessent for not aggressively imposing export restrictions on advanced AI chips to China.

But Trump’s defense of Lutnick, sources tell WIRED, reflects the president's own view that allowing the sale of some advanced AI chips to China can keep China reliant on US technology and simultaneously boost US tech stocks.

Industry observers note that lutnick “was doing that because if you didn’t delay it, if you didn’t do something, you could have a blowup with China. We’re having a very good relationship with China right now,” Trump said ahead of a multiday trip to Asia and a meeting on Thursday with Chinese leader Xi Jinping.

Trump convened an Oval Office meeting on November 5 to discuss the political fallout from Huang’s affair with Alice Huang, the former Megaspeed executive whom some in the US government believe was recruited to spy for China, according to two sources briefed on the discussion.

Megaspeed received advanced AI chips manufactured by Nvidia through several layers of companies that started with a subsidiary of a blacklisted Chinese server conglomerate called Inspur, The Latest York Times has reported.

In the meeting, the sources say, Bessent confronted Lutnick, asking why Megaspeed was not added to the entity list faster, given that secretary of state Marco Rubio and US trade representative Jamieson Greer, among others, had already agreed it was the correct move.

Lutnick responded that he would defer to Trump and would add Megaspeed to the entity list if that was what the president wanted, the sources say.

But Trump settled on a third approach: for Lutnick to work on introducing a new interim trade rule to stop Chinese AI labs from using advanced AI chips remotely by leasing their compute power from data centers in Southeast Asia.

In a statement to WIRED, a White House spokesperson said the new rule would “crack down on the smuggling of advanced US SI chips” and “help ensure that America’s most advanced chips go first to US SI innovators, not Chinese shell companies.” (Superintelligence, or SI, is the administration’s term for artificial intelligence.).

Industry observers note that A senior White House official added that Trump has been adamant that Chinese firms cannot acquire the most advanced Nvidia chips, known as Blackwells and Rubins. Those are different from the H200-type chips, built on previous-generation Hopper architecture, that Megaspeed was acquiring.

It has been revealed that lutnick’s position appears to have been based on a series of considerations, the sources say. For one, Megaspeed has already had the chips for months, and blacklisting the company would be akin to playing whack-a-mole unless the administration dealt with the underlying problem of Chinese firms getting remote access to US chips.

Meanwhile, Lutnick has moved cautiously on any new export restrictions—essentially waiting to get explicit approval from Trump—after he faced heavy criticism in 2025 for expanding restrictions against firms with Chinese ties, the sources mentioned.

In September 2025, the Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security started aggressively using the so-called affiliates rule, which automatically extends trade restrictions to any tech giant that is 50 percent owned by a company already on the US entity list or the military end-user list.

But the move prompted immediate retaliation by China, which suspended exports of critical rare earth metals to the US and, the sources noted, prompted a wave of internal criticism accusing the Commerce Department of having sparked a trade war.

After the Busan summit at the end of October 2025, where Trump and Chinese president Xi Jinping agreed to a trade truce, the White House instructed Commerce to halt the use of the affiliates rule and clear upcoming export controls in advance, the sources stated.

The suspension of the affiliates rule—which came almost as soon as it was implemented—may have had a knock-on effect on companies like Megaspeed, one person familiar with deliberations remarked.

Inspur, the Chinese server conglomerate connected to Megaspeed, operated a subsidiary called Aivres, which, as a California-based company, could legally buy restricted Nvidia chips without triggering direct export bans and ship them internationally to Southeast Asia.

In total, Aivres transferred billions of dollars’ worth of restricted Nvidia chips, including the powerful H200 chips, to Megaspeed’s subsidiaries.

Instead of shipping the physical chips into China, Megaspeed hosted servers at data centers in Malaysia and Indonesia—then rented out compute power to major Chinese companies. A spokesperson for Aivres mentioned in a statement that the firm complies with all US export controls.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that waymo self-driving taxis are no longer driving on highways after the California Department of Motor Vehicles banned its vehicles from state freeway operations. The ban, which the DMV notes began on November 11, comes after the department determined that Waymo’s freeway driving poses “an imminent hazard to public safety.”.

It has been revealed that in response, Waymo indicates it has stopped highway driving in all of its markets. The company may continue testing its vehicles on non-California highways with safety operators behind the wheels.

The ban follows two recent concerning incidents, California DMV spokesperson Jonathan Groveman wrote in a statement. In one, three Waymos entered an active highway construction closure on Route 101 on the San Francisco Peninsula. The other was captured in a viral video showing a Waymo vehicle interfering with California Highway Patrol cars on a San Francisco highway as they tried to enforce a “traffic break” as workers cleared debris from the crash.

In a recent development, groveman remarked the California ban will remain in place until Waymo has proved that it has “taken effective corrective actions to address the deficiencies" that led to the incidents. It’s unclear how long that process will take.

In a written statement to WIRED, Waymo spokesperson Dana Gallagher stated the company is “working with the California DMV and other state officials diligently and responsibly to resume freeway operations." Waymo vehicles will continue to operate on surface streets in the 15 metros where it offers taxi service, including portions of Los Angeles, San Diego, and the San Francisco Bay Area.

Sources indicate that this is the second time Waymo has publicly restricted its freeway operations after beginning to transport passengers on them last year. In June, the firm recalled its software after federal regulators found that its system failed to recognize highway construction zones. Regulators with the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) cited several incidents in April and May in which Waymo cars drove past ramp closure signs and into active lane closures. The events did not lead to collisions or injuries.

The NHTSA did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Last week, the agency stated it was examining whether another Waymo recall software fix had actually solved its robotaxis’ safety problems. This recall, which occurred last December, was tied to incidents in which Waymo cars repeatedly drove by stopped school buses with their lights on and/or stop arms extended.

In a recent development, self-driving cars have struggled with construction zones for at least a decade. The zones can look and be arranged differently based on what sort of construction is being done, and where. While humans can easily understand bollards, placards, and blinking arrows, the lack of hard-and-fast rules has proven difficult to reliably program into driving software. The issue is especially hazardous at high freeway speeds, where workers exist alongside fast-moving car traffic.

Cybersecurity is a perpetual fight between the good guys and the bad. The age of agentic AI and Mythos-class models has tipped the scales in favor of the bad guys, opening a Pandoraâs box for offensive capabilities. An explosion in CVEs has since ensued.

Industry observers note that cyberattacks are about technical exploitation, which requires coding and reasoning prowess. Anthropicâs Mythos can discover and exploit zero-day vulnerabilities. Any model paired with a harness brings the cost of social engineering attacks down to near zero, unleashing them at unprecedented scale. The danger is heightened with every new model release.

In a recent development, defensive security isnât improving in parallel. The relevant data lives in logs, events, traces and telemetry, a fundamentally different modality than the bodies of text LLMs usually train on, which barely show up in pretraining. Unlike offensive cybersecurity, which involves goal-directed reasoning towards a defined objective, defense requires open-ended reasoning, continually finding anomalies across vast amounts of normal-looking activity, a distinct capability that typically demands extensive domain-specific training. In short, defense is out of distribution for general-purpose frontier models: neither the data nor the intuition it requires is well-represented in training. In the race toward AGI, we cannot expect the frontier labs to take the detour of overhauling their training pipelines for defensive cybersecurity. And we certainly canât afford to bet our security on a hope that they do.

Corma has illustrated this âdefense gapâ in testing. They ran red/blue team simulations where an attacker plants a hidden backdoor and a defender tries to find it. The defender failed to find the backdoor 78% of the time, even when the defender was an identical copy of the very same model that planted it. Holding model quality constant, attackers will always have an advantage.

Recent findings suggest that the only answer to scaling laws on offense is better scaling laws on defense. Recent events have shown that frontier AI for defensive cybersecurity is one of the crucial unsolved problems of the AI age. Solving it is the generational mission Corma was founded on.

Sources indicate that corma founder and CEO Alon Pluda and his team are training a foundation model to power defensive cybersecurity agents. Cybersecurity, like Go or chess, is a two-player, zero-sum game with a clean reward (were you breached or not?) and an endless supply of games to play. Reinforcement learning and self-play have produced superhuman results before in this kind of paradigm. We are seeing history repeat itself. Corma pushes this further with large-scale reinforcement learning across cybersecurity environments that replicate real enterprise networks, with all their tools, telemetry and noise â as part of a training pipeline that produces frontier defensive capabilities, outperforming general-purpose foundation models, with much lower per-token inference costs.

Owning the model weights matters (they arenât subject to restrictions on cybersecurity-related usage set by the closed model labs). And specialization and inference speed really matter (fastest to protect against a newly introduced threat wins).

Cormaâs foundation model is deployed and productized as an agentic Security Workforce. These workers operate across different security tools and take on roles spanning the entire security organization: from security operations and identity management to cloud and network security and beyond. They are on the job at Fortune 500 companies and large enterprises across healthcare, finance, critical infrastructure, retail and more.
