#114. Latest Update: Google DeepMind just mathematically verified key parts of Signal

📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (696 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ars Technica ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Google DeepMind just mathematically verified key parts of Signal

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (696 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Google DeepMind researchers used agentic AI to mathematically prove, or “formally verify,” a number of the Signal protocol’s key cryptographic guarantees—a landmark development for the widely used cryptography and AI itself.
  • Conducted as a sort of proof-of-concept project in just four weeks, the work is significant in two ways.
  • More broadly, AI-aided formal verification is having a moment, but it is unclear how practical it will be for widespread use and how effective it can be at securing large amounts of code.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google DeepMind researchers used agentic AI to mathematically prove, or “formally verify,” a number of the Signal protocol’s key cryptographic guarantees—a landmark development for the widely used cryptography and AI itself.

Conducted as a sort of proof-of-concept project in just four weeks, the work is significant in two ways. It serves as further independent validation of the cryptography that protects massive quantities of the world’s communications on platforms like the Signal app, Google Messages, and WhatsApp. And it demonstrates Google DeepMind’s formal verification capabilities using a new AI framework called AlphaProof Code.

More broadly, AI-aided formal verification is having a moment, but it is unclear how practical it will be for widespread use and how effective it can be at securing large amounts of code. Proponents of formal verification have long referred to it as a sort of holy grail in software security, because it uses math to check and validate that software is functioning as intended—in other words, that it doesn’t have critical vulnerabilities.

Before the AI era, it was incredibly time-consuming for people to describe the characteristics of software they wanted to prove, turn these summaries into formulas, and then develop the proof. Agentic AI can significantly cut down the time of the latter project, enabling analyses like DeepMind’s Signal evaluation. But even this analysis was limited in scope—it did not, for example, formally verify the entire Signal mobile app—and DeepMind researchers emphasize that their findings are just one milestone in a larger process.

“We are very excited by this result, but there is a long distance to go before we are able to scale this to all the software of the world, and we want to do that,” Swarat Chaudhuri, a DeepMind research scientist, tells WIRED.

Industry observers note that the DeepMind analysis did not find any latest vulnerabilities in the portions of the Signal protocol it looked at, but when the researchers used AlphaProof Code on older versions of Signal that contain known and long-fixed vulnerabilities, it correctly identified them and showed that the protocol could not be formally verified. The researchers are releasing the specification and proof they developed for the Signal protocol analysis to aid other formal verification work.

While the speed of the project was notable, the DeepMind researchers point out that they were able to get a head start to a degree because of some past formal verification work that the Signal Foundation has conducted.

“While prior formal verification focused on smaller portions of the code, Google DeepMind’s approach enables significant expansion,” Ehren Kret, Signal’s chief technology officer, states in a statement. “As AI-driven security threats grow, rigorously verifying the Signal protocol implementation gives us even greater confidence in our code’s privacy guarantees.”.

For critical services used in high-stakes settings, it would be a dream to be able to formally verify every code base and entire software supply chains. “If you can now verify the correctness of these implementations, then you can rest easy,” claims Pushmeet Kohli, chief scientist at Google Cloud and DeepMind’s vice president of research. “You can imagine banks, imagine all those other companies who rely on assurances and who worry about bugs who could now say, ‘I can prove these properties.’”.

In a recent development, the open question across the tech sector, though, is whether AI-automated formal verification can truly scale—and whether it can do so at a workable cost. DeepMind conducted the Signal analysis free of charge as a research project, and Google declined to share the cost of the analysis. The company also declined to comment on whether it has aims to release a commercial formal verification product or service.

It has been revealed that the researchers say that some of their crucial advancements are in developing a “human-AI collaboration process,” as Chaudhuri puts it, that allows agents to contribute and self-correct at almost every phase of the process while still seeking human input and review at key junctures. “We don’t want this sort of vibe world where AI is generating the goals and AI is generating the proofs and basically taking tests that are self-written,” Chaudhuri states. “There’s a middle ground.”.

This story originally appeared on wired.com.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • With a new option called Memory summary, you’re able to view the details that Gemini has gathered about you over time.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Like any AI, Google Gemini wants to remember things about you. The purported reason is to help tailor and personalize your conversations. But remember that your personal details may also wind up training the AI or even being reviewed by actual humans. With that in mind, you might want to find out just what Gemini knows about you. And now you can.

Also: I tried Claude Sheets on 3 tasks – and it saved me hours of work.

With a new option called Memory summary, you’re able to view the details that Gemini has gathered about you over time. These may be tidbits from your conversations or things that you directly told the AI. Even better, you can add or remove any details just by editing the memory or issuing your request directly to Gemini.

This upcoming capability is available in Gemini across the board, so you can access it at the Gemini website, in the mobile iOS and Android apps, and in the Windows and Mac desktop apps.

According to recent reports, launch Gemini via the web or in one of the mobile or desktop apps. In the left pane displaying your previous chats, select the Settings icon at the bottom. At the Settings screen, select Personal Intelligence and then click or tap Memory summary. If the option is grayed out, it means the Memory feature is turned off. To proceed, turn it back on. You can always turn if off again afterward if you wish.

You’ll then see the individual details by category. My summary arranged the information across such categories as Essentials, Business & Career, Reading & Interests, and Culinary Preferences. Go down the list to see the individual items in each category. To view a recent history, tap the three dot-icon at the top and select Memory history. This indicates you the latest changes and updates to Gemini’s memory.

Also: Stop sharing your passwords with AI agents.

What if Gemini’s memory includes details that are too personal or just incorrect? No problem. You can alter the AI’s memories of you. At the website or in one of the desktop apps, click the pencil icon at the top. Now you’re able to directly edit the text to add, remove, or revise specific details. After you’ve made your changes, just click Save.

For example, my summary remarked that I lived in Madison County. I have no idea where Gemini got that notion, as I live in Latest York. Here, I revised the text and saved the changes, which then synced across the Gemini website and apps.

It has been revealed that the mobile apps have no direct editing capability. But there’s another method that works both on mobile and on the desktop. Just tell Gemini what change you want to make. At the prompt, type and speak your request, and the AI will carry it out for you.

Also: The best and worst AI for your privacy, ranked.

As an example, my summary said that I run a business called Batter Up selling collectible baseball cards. That’s not at all true. I had once referred to such a store only to test Gemini’s image creation skills to design a logo for a baseball card seller. Here, I simply told Gemini that I don’t run a business called Batter Up and asked it to remove that item from its memory. Poof, that detail quickly disappeared.

Sources indicate that google isn’t exactly known as being privacy-friendly, and that extends to Gemini. In this case, though, I give the company credit for offering this easy way to control the AI’s memories. I do find the memory feature useful as it recalls details about me that help personalize and direct its responses. But I don’t like Gemini or Google knowing too much about me. Now I can keep memory enabled and just control what it remembers about me.

AI finds zero-day flaws for just $4 now – even mediocre hackers can cash in

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (777 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Zdnet

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that the best AI models on the market couldn’t find zero-days earlier this year, but now they can in less than 15 minutes and at a cost of a few bucks, according to a upcoming report from penetration testing firm Xint.io.
  • It has been revealed that every major AI developer is working at breakneck speed to improve model effectiveness.
  • This is good news for businesses trying to harness AI for productivity and new services, but as token prices fall, it has also become cheaper for attackers to launch AI-assisted attacks, including software breaches caused by exploiting unknown vulnerabilities.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the best AI models on the market couldn’t find zero-days earlier this year, but now they can in less than 15 minutes and at a cost of a few bucks, according to a upcoming report from penetration testing firm Xint.io. The findings raise questions about how vulnerabilities will be discovered and exploited in the future.

It has been revealed that every major AI developer is working at breakneck speed to improve model effectiveness. At the same time, token prices continue to fall, with studies showing that the average cost of tokens, which varies by domain, has dropped by about 47% per quarter since 2023 and 15% last month alone, due to intense competition among companies including OpenAI and Anthropic.

This is good news for businesses trying to harness AI for productivity and new services, but as token prices fall, it has also become cheaper for attackers to launch AI-assisted attacks, including software breaches caused by exploiting unknown vulnerabilities.

Also: How AI security failures are endangering your supply chain.

Industry observers note that A report published by Xint.io examines how popular AI models have evolved over the past year to the point where cybersecurity tasks that would have failed only months ago now succeed. The team analyzed seven models launched since February 2026: two from OpenAI, three from Anthropic, and two open-source models from DeepSeek and Z.ai. The team tracked, over time, how they performed in finding a target vulnerability.

It has been revealed that the target of this research was a security flaw in Google’s V8 engine. Tracked as CVE-2026-102321, the type confusion bug leading to remote code execution (RCE) was disclosed to the Google Vulnerability Reward Program (VRP) by Xint researcher Taisic Yun and so was not present in the AI models’ training datasets.

The research scope was limited to a set of source files, including the file containing the vulnerability, and each model was instructed to search for security concerns within these files.

Xint’s first test was conducted in February. After 25 hours and $350 of scanning, the best models then available still couldn’t find the critical vulnerability.

In July, GPT 5.6 Sol found the zero-day flaw for $22 in 44 minutes.

Also: Finding Linux bugs is easy – fixing them is another story.

By September, GPT 6 Sol discovered the bug in 13 minutes for only $4.24 with its first guided prompt.

Only three of the seven models found the bug: GPT 6 Sol, GPT 5.6 Sol, and Claude Opus 5, all rolled out from July onward. GPT 5.6 Sol needed two prompts, while Claude Opus 5 found it on its first try but at a higher cost of $43.40.

DeepSeek’s and Z.ai’s models failed the task.

The researchers say that the combination of AI model development and low token prices means that “mediocre hackers” can now use frontier models effectively to discover and potentially exploit vulnerabilities, and “while we are still far from complete amateurs using unharnessed models to hack systems and applications, what used to be considered too hard and costly to be worth the effort of the average hacker is now reachable.”.

As a result, organizations need to adjust their security posture accordingly — but falling token costs and evolving AI skills and speed can also work in your favor.

Also: How I safely run my OpenClaw AI agent 24/7 on a Mac.

There’s nothing stopping an organization’s security team or pentesters from running the same checks themselves to find vulnerabilities before threat actors do. AI-assisted tests, arguably, are no longer something that can be pushed back to next year’s budgetary review. By performing a risk assessment that focuses on likely weak spots, such as public-facing services or a digital supply chain that hasn’t been audited for years, organizations can mitigate the risk AI-enabled cyberattacks pose.

It has been revealed that zero-day vulnerabilities are unknown to vendors, and a patch might not be available when they go public or are actively exploited in the wild. So, AI can only go so far, but it can free up your defenders for tasks that need the human touch. Furthermore, maintaining zero-trust access controls, segmenting and shoring up your network’s defenses, and monitoring endpoints for signs of suspicious behavior can do as much as, or more than, AI.

Sources indicate that as Xint notes, “expertise still matters” when it comes to instructing AI models to discover vulnerabilities. In some cases, the models couldn’t find the target vulnerability without guidance, so additional runs were needed, increasing time and cost.

“Software breaches still require some level of technical proficiency,” the researchers say, “but no longer top-of-the-distribution expertise.”.

#107. Your enterprise AI access can be sold for pennies – beware ‘LLM Mixers’

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (859 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech 📈 Bullish 🌐 Zdnet ↗ Open Full Page

Your enterprise AI access can be sold for pennies – beware ‘LLM Mixers’

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (859 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Zdnet

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In just a few years, businesses have adopted AI and large language models (LLMs) to manage everything from calendar invites to data analysis and programming.
  • Google’s latest report on AI threats, the Q4 AI Threat Tracker from the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG), found that gateways called LLM Mixers are selling access for cents on the dollar.
  • Also: 6 essential strategies to defend against AI-powered threat actors.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In just a few years, businesses have adopted AI and large language models (LLMs) to manage everything from calendar invites to data analysis and programming. Bad actors steal credentials for those models through LLMjacking — and the marketplace is evolving.

Google’s latest report on AI threats, the Q4 AI Threat Tracker from the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG), found that gateways called LLM Mixers are selling access for cents on the dollar.

Also: 6 essential strategies to defend against AI-powered threat actors.

Industry observers note that organizations have poured billions of dollars into AI development and deployment, although the amount they spend on AI tokens every month varies. According to Ramp AI index data, among firms paying for AI, the top 1% spent over $10,000 per employee per month, compared with around $16 for the median firm. When employees have access to AI models, companies may introduce spending caps, but smaller outfits may overlook them.

It has been revealed that LLMjacking is the theft of AI-related credentials, including usernames and passwords, or API keys, used to access AI models. This gives cybercriminals the opportunity to use tokens and AI resources belonging to a victim organization (or individual), typically with usage-based billing or subscriptions with no fixed cap.

Recent findings suggest that with these credentials, an unauthorized user could run high-resource computing tasks, manage their own malicious AI deployments, extract and steal corporate data from the AI’s memory, or even poison training data. To add insult to injury, if demand outstrips the limits of the victim’s subscription, cybercriminals can rack up high usage costs that the victim is then on the hook for.

Also: Rogue AI incidents hit ‘tens of thousands’: Can businesses trust these tools?

John Hultquist, chief analyst for GTIG, previously said the cybersecurity unit has seen a “major increase” in LLMjacking over 2026, so we can assume this trend will likely continue into 2027 and beyond.

AI access is now a lucrative illegal business in its own right, leading to what Google calls LLM Mixers: “illicit storefronts” that provide unauthorized access to AI services and underlying proxy infrastructure.

After analyzing LLMJacking vendor advertisements on Russian- and Chinese-language marketplaces, GTIG researchers found that most offer access not only to frontier models from AI labs, but also to jailbroken models marketed as suitable for malicious purposes.

However, it doesn’t seem that many of these cybercriminal groups can agree on “reasonable” pricing, with prices swinging wildly depending on the models offered and the credentials available.

Also: How I safely run my OpenClaw AI agent 24/7 on a Mac – with Claude Code standing guard.

According to recent reports, free trial credentials fetch far less than enterprise credentials, as you would expect. Token prices for business use ranged from $0.10 to $25, and one vendor, APIMart, increased its token price fivefold once a prompt exceeds 100,000 tokens. Other vendors offer subscription-based pricing.

It has been revealed that this might not seem like much at the lower tiers, but Sysdig estimates LLMJacking could cost around $46,000 based on earlier models, and even over $100,000 per day on cutting-edge models. Mandiant research published earlier this month recorded incidents with illicit AI usage exceeding $100,000 in only 24 hours, with cumulative charges at some organizations reaching $1 million before access was revoked.

It has been revealed that while direct credentials can be sold, the infrastructure element is also an interesting service offering. Google’s threat team stated in the report that the sale of LLM infrastructure “routes buyer traffic through a pool of stolen credentials and compute instances to ensure reliable access, while also offering the ability to spread query volume across multiple victim environments to reduce the likelihood of detection.”.

LLM Mixers look similar to the rest of the cybercriminal underground economy, in which traders tend to specialize in one or two parts of an attack chain. For example, an LLM Mixer offers the access and infrastructure needed to exploit an enterprise AI model, while its partners might break into victim networks to secure initial access or buy stolen credentials from operators of infostealer malware.

Avoid LLMjacking and having your organization’s AI added to a Mixer’s menu similarly to how you would prevent intrusions into SaaS applications and cloud setups: managing access, monitoring, and imposing restrictions.

It has been revealed that usage and spending are the first areas to tackle. By setting limits on how many tokens can be issued and used across every AI service and account, and by alerting when usage suddenly spikes, organizations can limit damage if an account is compromised and stop massive bills before they rack up.

Also: Can you still trust Proton?

According to recent reports, organizations should also try to prevent their keys from ending up in the hands of cyberattackers in the first place. Google recommends using a secrets manager that securely stores and frequently rotates API keys, and running audits to detect quiet probing, misconfigurations, or shadow accounts.

It’s also advisable, across the board, to implement phishing protections and multi-factor authentication (MFA) to make the business of stealing credentials or compromising your accounts and networks more difficult in the first place.

#106. Significant Walk used AI to fix a bug. Now the indie gaming world is having a reckoning.

📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1457 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ars Technica ↗ Open Full Page

Significant Walk used AI to fix a bug. Now the indie gaming world is having a reckoning.

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1457 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The last few years have seen significant debate over the widespread use of AI-powered tools in game development and the responsible disclosure of that usage to players.
  • Recent findings suggest that this particular controversy has been brewing behind the scenes for months, as judges and jury members for the prestigious Independent Games Festival Awards discussed the matter in private discussion groups.
  • Noting “a significant increase in the number of submitted games developer with generative AI tools,” the group of jurors called out AI’s ecological, economic, psychological, and labor harms in rejecting tools whose use, they stated, is still “not a foregone conclusion in our industry.”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The last few years have seen significant debate over the widespread use of AI-powered tools in game development and the responsible disclosure of that usage to players. That debate has exploded into a full-blown controversy in the indie game development space this week, as Major Walk developer House House has publicly and belatedly disclosed minimal AI use in its popular co-operative puzzle exploration game.

Recent findings suggest that this particular controversy has been brewing behind the scenes for months, as judges and jury members for the prestigious Independent Games Festival Awards discussed the matter in private discussion groups. But the debate started to break into public view on Monday when 19 members of the 50-plus-member jury released a signed statement outlining a stance “declining to vote for any game that uses generative AI in any capacity.”.

Noting “a significant increase in the number of submitted games developer with generative AI tools,” the group of jurors called out AI’s ecological, economic, psychological, and labor harms in rejecting tools whose use, they stated, is still “not a foregone conclusion in our industry.”.

The jurors also urged the IGF as a whole to “adopt a strong anti-AI policy for future years that disallows games containing any AI-generated work.”.

Sources indicate that although the jurors’ statement didn’t name any specific games, by Tuesday morning, one critical darling in particular was increasingly being noted as a central part of the debate. In a statement provided to Aftermath (and added to the game’s FAQ page shortly thereafter), developer House House admitted publicly that “LLMs were used sparingly” near the end of Substantial Walk‘s development “to help work through some difficult technical challenges and bugs.”.

That limited AI use—which House House indicates represents “well under 0.1% of Big Walk‘s code—stemmed in part from a thorny Unity engine bug that was slowing the game down with “infinite length” shadows during some game situations. After consulting with a Unity engineer who determined a fix “wasn’t possible,” House House stated it consulted an LLM chatbot, which suggested a possible fix that the developers “had to modify… extensively” into the 10 lines of code that ended up in the final game (At least one social media user says the bug was indeed fixable with significant human effort, though).

House House noted it didn’t disclose this LLM usage for Massive Walk‘s Steam release earlier this year because Valve “does not request disclosure of code or chatbot usage.” Indeed, Valve’s AI disclosure form for developers specifically notes that it is concerned with AI-generated content, not “efficiency gains” from “modern game development environments [that] have AI powered tools built into them.”.

In a recent development, the IGF Awards make no such distinction for AI usage, however, which led House House to mention its AI-assisted bug fix in submitting the game for awards consideration. A version of that disclosure is being made public now because “it has become a matter of public interest,” House House mentioned.

“This is not an endorsement of, or argument for, the use of AI tools, however minimal,” House House wrote. “We have some concern that voluntary disclosures like this might contribute to the normalization of this technology, or its treatment as ‘inevitable.’ We support the work of those who are trying to limit the harm generative AI is doing to videogames and our world, and apologize that Big Walk’s LLM usage may not meet their standards.”.

Learning of House House’s AI disclosure was particularly painful for some IGF judges who had previously felt a special connection to Substantial Walk. In a blog post discussing his feelings, IGF jurist Austin Walker called the game “an achievement” that was “remarkable” and “beautiful,” featuring puzzles that “capture a range of play that is largely abandoned by the digital form.” Fellow jurist Damon Reece shared in a blog post that the game is “seriously special to me” and that it gave him “a profound and powerful emotional reaction to being in a space that felt like home.”.

But when it comes to IGF awards consideration, Walker and Reece were among those who stated that even minimal use of AI tools overrode that deep and abiding respect for the work itself.

“We have our hands on the lever here,” Reece wrote. “This is pain that has to happen [emphasis in original] to try and steer our culture away from this. We need to choose to speak loudly and clearly on this, to prioritize human creativity and labour, to tell the culture and the world that this is unacceptable to us. To do otherwise is rank cowardice.”.

It has been revealed that this isn’t the first time AI usage has noticeably affected game award judging. Last year, the Indie Game Awards (which are completely separate from the IGF Awards) rescinded awards for Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 after the developers admitted that some in-game textures were made using AI tools (these were later patched out).

“The Indie Game Awards have a hard stance on the use of gen AI throughout the nomination process and during the ceremony itself,” they mentioned at the time.

Since House House’s public disclosure, the anti-AI contingent of IGF judges has found plenty of support from disappointed Big Walk fans and industry observers. In the last few days, the game’s Steam page has been bombed with over 400 negative reviews, though Steam’s anti-review-bomb tools seem to be limiting the impact on the game’s overall “Very Positive” reception there.

But others feel House House’s relatively minimal use of AI here is being blown out of proportion. They say it’s important to differentiate between games that use LLMs as a last-resort technical fix, for instance, and others that lean heavily on AI to generate the bulk of their art, music, or the core of the game engine itself.

IGF judge Liz Ryerson wrote on social media that she didn’t find House House’s AI use to be personally disqualifying for the awards and that “the fact that many acted like there aren’t any levels to this and it’s all the same is bothersome to me.”.

Recent findings suggest that “To feel like someone gets punished a lot more for transparency about a smaller level of fuckup vs. just not even attempting to be honest or transparent at all is what bothers me,” she wrote.

Steam Hype staff writer and prolific Steam curator Dominic Tarason also pushed back against the idea that “House House need to be memory-holed and their work never spoken of again” as a “penalty for touching the Forbidden Device.” He noted he considers Substantial Walk “very mildly compromised art” that is still “absolutely, unquestionably art and very human.”.

“They spent years on that work of art,” Tarason added. “They asked a chatbot for two minutes how to fix a bug. That’s a ‘That’s lame, don’t do that again’ failing. … Some of you are acting like they’ve been convicted of high crimes against humanity, to be sealed away in the darkest oubliette until not even bones remain.”.

It has been revealed that but some have argued that using AI to fix a bug rather than hiring an expert to figure it out did make the game’s development at least a bit less human than it could have been. “House House aren’t laying off developers to replace them with Claude, and I’m sure they would be firmly against the mere thought of doing this, but we can also clearly see how their actions are part of the same problem,” AI researcher Mike Cook wrote on his blog.

Still, game developer, author, and professor Brendan Keogh wrote that he thinks “an extreme zero tolerance of any [generative AI] is ultimately counterproductive now. [There’s] a lot of anger at devs that feel deeply conflicted enough about their glorified Google search to disclose it, and [that is] encouraging those using it to actually steal labor to hide that use.”.

It has been revealed that as time goes on and AI tools are increasingly used in the building of major game engines, it may become increasingly difficult for anti-AI absolutists to avoid every game that has been touched by even a hint of LLM-generated code (if that use is even disclosed in the first place). That mentioned, many still see value in a firm and unyielding public stance against what they see as a scourge to their entire industry.

According to recent reports, “I think zero tolerance is a viable political position,” narrative designer and writer Hannah Nicklin wrote on social media. “You use politics against systems, for people you affect change through connection and understanding… The IGF jury statement… levels itself at a system of shared value and asks for change to enable solidarity around a position of harm reduction.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Microsoft is testing a newly introduced feature that lets IT admins instantly lock down your lost or stolen device via remote connection, protecting your work projects and personal data from theft and unauthorized access.
  • Also: Windows 11 can run better on PCs with 8GB now.
  • The fresh remote lock feature is designed to work in tandem with other Microsoft services, such as Intune and BitLocker, to manage a fleet of devices both in-office and remotely across the globe.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Microsoft is testing a newly introduced feature that lets IT admins instantly lock down your lost or stolen device via remote connection, protecting your work projects and personal data from theft and unauthorized access.

Also: Windows 11 can run better on PCs with 8GB now.

The fresh remote lock feature is designed to work in tandem with other Microsoft services, such as Intune and BitLocker, to manage a fleet of devices both in-office and remotely across the globe.

Once a device is reported missing or stolen, an admin can disable login access from anywhere without having to fully wipe the laptop or smartphone. Microsoft reports that the lockdown will persist across restarts, even if the device is disconnected from Wi-Fi networks, and can only be lifted by an admin. This means that thieves can’t use your passwords, PINs, or biometric data to circumvent the lock.

While the new feature allows IT admins to respond rapidly when a laptop or phone is reported missing, there are still security gaps that other Windows controls must address. The new lock feature doesn’t erase your data or wipe your device if it can’t be recovered, nor does it isolate the missing device from corporate networks. Therefore, IT admins will still need to access those controls via the Intune and Microsoft Entra dashboards.

Also: You can now restore Windows 11 even if it can’t boot up.

Industry observers note that the remote lock feature also doesn’t change your Microsoft account credentials, so you can use your log-ins on other devices to recover your data, change passwords, and temporarily disable permissions. Finally, Remote lock doesn’t block the device from being booted in Safe Mode, from a USB, in Windows Recovery Mode, or if the storage drive is reimaged; Microsoft highly recommends keeping BitLocker enabled until the device can be wiped or recovered.

#101. Why your USB-C cables look alike, but work differently – and how to tell them apart

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1554 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Zdnet ↗ Open Full Page

Why your USB-C cables look alike, but work differently – and how to tell them apart

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1554 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Zdnet

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This article was supposed to be about my personal experience with a new docking station — specifically, the Plugable TBT-UDH2, a Thunderbolt 5 dock that is a perfect match for any modern high-end PC.
  • Industry observers note that instead, I wound up going down a deep rabbit hole, learning more than I ever imagined I would need to know about USB-C cables.
  • Recent findings suggest that well, yes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This article was supposed to be about my personal experience with a new docking station — specifically, the Plugable TBT-UDH2, a Thunderbolt 5 dock that is a perfect match for any modern high-end PC.

Industry observers note that instead, I wound up going down a deep rabbit hole, learning more than I ever imagined I would need to know about USB-C cables. I know what you’re thinking. Wasn’t the entire point of USB Type-C to eliminate all the confusion of those earlier USB connectors with all their different shapes and sizes?

Recent findings suggest that well, yes. Unfortunately, the Type-C standard only applies to the physical form factor of the connector, not the data transfer protocol or power capabilities of the cable it’s attached to. Because the 24-pin connector is reversible, you can plug it in either way. But what you can do with a USB-C cable depends on what’s between those two connectors.

I paid for some testing hardware and then evaluated dozens of USB-C cables to figure out which one does what and how you can tell the difference. Along the way, I dredged up some memories about old USB standards and learned a whole lot about Thunderbolt and USB4.

Also: 5 USB cables and dongles that can fry hardware and steal your data – or worse.

I also discovered the one thing you should do every time you get your hands on a new USB-C cable. Trust me, this information will come in handy someday.

I’ve been using Plugable products for years. The tech giant builds a wide range of products that I’ve found to be reliable and well-designed. A quick scan of my workbench shows several Plugable products: a 2.5 Gbps USB Ethernet adapter, a USB-C enclosure for an M.2 NVMe storage device, and the Thunderbolt 5 dock pictured here.

I’ve now tested this Plugable dock with a half-dozen Windows machines, from entry-level to workstation class, built on Intel, AMD, Qualcomm, and Nvidia platforms. It’s packed with a truly impressive collection of ports, including six USB-C, two USB-A, two HDMI 2.1, and a 2.5 Gbps Ethernet jack. By plugging in one USB-C cable, I can power my laptop (up to 140 W) and turn it into a very well-connected desktop PC, with a 38-inch external display, wired Ethernet, an external mouse, keyboard, and speakers, and several external USB drives.

According to recent reports, it’s been a real workhorse, but over the past few months I found myself occasionally puzzled. All Thunderbolt features worked perfectly when connected to USB4 ports, even though the laptops with those ports aren’t Thunderbolt-certified. On one PC, the video display worked properly when connected to a USB-C port on the left side but acted strangely when using the identical port on the right side. And then there was the challenge of figuring out why two cables that looked exactly the same didn’t act alike.

Also: This USB-C dock can be managed remotely (with a feature IT will love).

To get to the bottom of these mysteries, I spoke with Plugable’s founder and Chief Technology Officer, Bernie Thompson, who had the answers I was looking for.

Thunderbolt is a technology that delivers fast data, video, and power over a single cable. To use the Thunderbolt brand, hardware and software makers have to meet a demanding certification process.

Thunderbolt 3, which was developed by Intel and debuted in 2015, was the first technology to really show off USB-C’s potential as a single connection for high-speed data, displays, and power. USB4 is based on Intel’s Thunderbolt protocol specification and is backward compatible with USB 3.2, USB 2.0, and Thunderbolt 3 devices.

A USB4 PC can support USB devices, displays, high-speed storage, and many Thunderbolt peripherals over the same USB-C connection.

Also: I tested my USB-C cables with a free Mac app – some weren’t what they claimed.

Thunderbolt 4 takes USB4 capabilities and establishes a tightly specified, certified minimum feature set. Thunderbolt 5 increases bidirectional bandwidth to 80Gbps, with the ability to hit 120Gbps in display-intensive activities.

There’s a pretty big overlap between USB4 and Thunderbolt technology, which is why every USB4 PC I tested worked just fine with the Thunderbolt 5 dock.

Industry observers note that if you’re like me, you have a drawer filled with USB-C cables you’ve collected over the years. So, how can you tell which is the right one for a specific application?

In a recent development, unless it’s labeled, you can’t. That’s the absurd truth about cables that use the USB-C connector, which can have three very different sets of capabilities:.

I pulled three unlabeled cables from my drawer and tried connecting each to various peripherals, including a display and some external hard drives. Although the cables looked about the same, I had no idea why they behaved so differently.

My ZDNET colleague Adrian Kingsley-Hughes tipped me off to the Treedix USB cable tester, and it helped solve a few mysteries.

I’m reasonably certain that this handsomely braided, thick, white cable cost me a small fortune at the Apple Store a few years ago.

As the tester proved, it can handle the maximum allowed by today’s USB Power Delivery standard: 240 W. For data? Sorry, it only supports USB 2.0. I routinely back up 500 GB of data from my PC to a fast external NVMe drive. Using that expensive USB 2.0 cable, the job would take nearly four hours. Swap in a high-speed USB4 cable like the one shown here, with modern storage devices on both ends, and the backup would be complete in just a few minutes.

At this point I started testing every USB-C cable in that drawer, sorting them into neatly labeled bins: PC charging-only cables; USB 3.2 cables (USB A-to-C and C-to-C), capable of high-speed data transfers; old-fashioned, low-power charging cables (USB A-to-C) good for small devices but not much else; and a small but exclusive stack of high-grade USB4 and Thunderbolt cables.

The Treedix device has a button that displays a few additional details about cables, but I wanted more. So I paid $108.24 for a snazzy digital cable tester from Austria called the BLE CaberQU X-ray. It has a much more detailed display than the Treedix device, as well as a mobile app that connects over Bluetooth and saves the history of devices I’ve tested.

Here’s what that expensive-but-slow Apple charging cable looks like on the device.

And here’s what a fully certified Thunderbolt 5 cable looks like in the app.

Industry observers note that this little gizmo answers a few questions that the simpler tester can’t, including cable health (e.g., broken pins or shorted connections). With the latest firmware, it can report USB4 v2, PD 3.0/3.1 EPR, active-cable characteristics, Thunderbolt generation, and DisplayPort capabilities. If none of that jargon means anything to you, then this device might be overkill.

It also contains details about a chip included in some USB-C cables called an E-Marker, which electronically identifies the cable’s capabilities to the devices at either end. There is no way to divine the presence of an E-Marker chip from just looking at a cable.

A dock is an unusually demanding application for a USB-C cable, because that one wire can simultaneously be charging a laptop, sending high-resolution video to multiple displays, maintaining a high-speed Ethernet connection, and managing multiple USB peripherals and external storage devices.

As I discovered, choosing the right cable matters: a cable that works flawlessly for charging a laptop or connecting an SSD can fail when a docking station asks it to juggle all those tasks simultaneously.

Also: The top-selling cords, cables, and chargers readers bought this year.

Industry observers note that as for that concern when I connected the dock to the USB-C port on the right side of the Dell XPS 13 laptop? I went looking for a bad cable, but Plugable’s engineering team pointed me to this support article from Dell, which notes that the laptop might have concerns with the display when the monitor is connected to the USB Type-C port on the right side of the computer. “The issue is intermittent,” the support article notes. Intermittent failure modes are the most annoying to troubleshoot.

Which proves the point that cables matter, as do ports, and firmware, and indeed every link in the chain that carries data from a portable PC to a dock to an external device.

As rabbit holes go, this one was relatively fun to explore. It certainly changed the list of criteria I recommend that you look for in a USB cable.

Sources indicate that and then, follow this rule: When that new cable arrives, keep the packaging, and test it if you have the equipment. Most high-end cables these days are marked with a Thunderbolt logo, a USB4 label, or an indicator of power and data speeds. One reason I recommend Plugable gear is that every USB-C cable they include is clearly labeled. (Zoom in on the image at the top of this post to see an example.).

It has been revealed that if your latest purchase doesn’t have those markings, stick a label on it before you throw it into a drawer. Otherwise, in six months you’re going to pull it out of that drawer and wonder what exactly it’s capable of. Don’t go down that rabbit hole.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Microsoft has released newly introduced information explaining the massive outage that started Thursday morning and affected Microsoft 365, Copilot, and Outlook access in 74 countries, according to Downdetector.
  • According to recent reports, charles Lamanna, Microsoft’s executive vice president of Copilot, Agents, and Platform, posted early Monday morning that the outage was due to three factors, including a “latent defect” from a July revision to Microsoft 365 networking gateway servers.
  • Industry observers note that “A latent defect caused servers to become overwhelmed and unresponsive under certain load conditions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Microsoft has released newly introduced information explaining the massive outage that started Thursday morning and affected Microsoft 365, Copilot, and Outlook access in 74 countries, according to Downdetector.

According to recent reports, charles Lamanna, Microsoft’s executive vice president of Copilot, Agents, and Platform, posted early Monday morning that the outage was due to three factors, including a “latent defect” from a July revision to Microsoft 365 networking gateway servers. Low server capacity and peak traffic in the US brought the defect out of hiding, despite no prior reported complications.

Industry observers note that “A latent defect caused servers to become overwhelmed and unresponsive under certain load conditions. This was due to lock contention inside an internal process which caused the machine to become unavailable,” Lamanna said, noting that the patch was deployed safely worldwide without any issues for over three months.

He said Microsoft didn’t find the concern in testing due to “the different traffic and SKU mix used in our test labs,” because “our load testing tended to focus on our weaker hardware SKUs with fewer cores.”.

Also: Microsoft fixes over 1,000 Windows flaws – and one is being exploited.

Two other factors made matters worse, and left servers useless in less than two hours.

“A surge in load increased the likelihood for the networking gateways to encounter the contention,” Lamanna stated, explaining that Microsoft 365 maintains two gateway systems. Before the outage started, Teams failed from one to the other, which “changed its traffic patterns.” Simultaneously, he added, “nearly 14% of server capacity for the networking gateway was out of service due to an unrelated matter from the previous day.”.

According to recent reports, those two conditions collided and “caused the network gateway to encounter the latent bug from July,” Lamanna concluded. Requests eventually overloaded servers, at which point they stopped responding. At the outage’s low point, over 80% of its servers weren’t responding.

“When servers lose connectivity, our traffic management systems automatically route users to other healthy endpoints,” Lamanna said. “However, the redirected traffic increased the likelihood for the same problem to occur on the remaining endpoints. This caused a cascading failure from server to server as the same amount of load was spread across fewer servers.”.

Also: AI finds zero-day flaws for just $4 now – even mediocre hackers can cash in.

Before Microsoft issued an explanation, some suspected the outage may have been the result of a cyberattack, which both Lamanna and Microsoft’s status account denied.

It’s unclear how many people the outage affected, though Microsoft’s own numbers from January say Microsoft 365 “exceeds 450 million commercial paid seats,” illustrating the scale of the issue. Microsoft deployed an update to fix the outage and gradually applied it to groups of servers. Lamanna noted Microsoft would publish a full post-incident review with more details later this week.

Industry observers note that service might be restored, but customers aren’t happy about having lost nearly two full workdays. One think tank told CNN it estimated the outage — which lasted through close of business on Friday for some — resulted in $7 billion in losses, due to many businesses and organizations being unable to access their everyday systems.

Also: If the November Windows patch fails to install on your PC, here’s what to do.

The fact that Microsoft’s testing couldn’t find the July glitch ahead of time may leave customers wondering when the next dormant defect will strike, and whether the firm is prepared.

In a recent development, organizations across Europe have been leaving Microsoft in recent years, opting instead for locally-controlled, open-source alternatives. The former CEO of Github debuted a decentralized alternative called Entire earlier this year, citing developers’ need for something more reliable, as Github has similarly been plagued with outages.

For many, Teams was barely offline over the two-day period, or was the first service to come back online.

Industry observers note that “Several services like Teams, OneDrive, SharePoint, and Office apps failed out of the faulty network gateway infrastructure. That is why those services were restored earlier, with Teams chats and meetings functioning without glitch for most of the outage,” Lamanna explained. Other services like Exchange Online can’t fail out.

He added that fixing the outage was slow because waiting traffic hit servers as soon as they came back, rendering them unresponsive just as swiftly.

Industry observers note that “Our normally automated recovery processes were not designed to restore service from this broad unresponsive state,” Lamanna mentioned. “Additionally, since the main code defect was a latent bug from several months previous, our normal rollback, flighting, and feature flags were unable to promptly revert the change.”.

On Thursday morning, people began reporting problems with Outlook, Teams, and Copilot, according to Downdetector. By 1 p.m. ET, the number of reported Outlook outages was nearly 83,000 but had fallen to just under 75,000 by 2:38 p.m. ET. Teams and Copilot reports started dropping significantly by Thursday evening, but many individuals were still reporting issues accessing systems well into Friday morning on X and Reddit. Even Microsoft’s status page was down until around 3 p.m. ET Thursday.

Also: If the November Windows update fails to install on your PC, here’s what to do.

As late as Friday afternoon, the company didn’t yet have an ETA of when the outage would be fully solved.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Top chip manufacturer TSMC is ready to invest $1 billion in Anthropic and OpenAI. That would give the Taiwanese chipmaker direct stakes in leading AI developers, even as its own contract chipmaking business has profited enormously from the AI data center buildout.

The chipmaker’s board approved intends to invest up to $500 million in OpenAI preferred stock reserved for large investors and another $500 million to purchase Anthropic common shares at the latter’s expected IPO price, according to Reuters. Such an investment may give markets “a shot of confidence as the artificial-intelligence trade demonstrates signs of strain,” The Wall Street Journal reported.

But analysts also warned that such circular financing among investors, suppliers, and customers has made it difficult to evaluate real market demand for AI-related hardware and services, according to the Journal.

TSMC’s chip fabrication plants physically produce the vast majority of Nvidia’s chips designed for AI data center workloads and make most of Apple’s custom chips used in iPhones, Mac laptops and desktops, plus Apple’s planned AI computing server. Most of these fabs are located in Taiwan, but TSMC also operates fabs in Japan and China, and it has an expanding US manufacturing cluster in Arizona. It is also building a latest fab in Germany.

Industry observers note that meanwhile, Anthropic and OpenAI are both purchasing huge quantities of AI hardware manufactured by TSMC for their data center projects. So TSMC’s declared investment certainly seems to fit into the broader trend of circular financing that has become common during the AI boom, even as tech stocks have gyrated recently as investors have grown increasingly jittery.

According to recent reports, still, TSMC has plenty of money to spare on such a bet. Ongoing demand for AI-related chips has enabled the Taiwanese chipmaker to report six consecutive quarters of record profit, with the latest example being the company earning more than $23 billion in profit during the July through September 2026 quarter, according to Reuters.

It has been revealed that TSMC’s planned investment in Anthropic and OpenAI also pales in comparison with circular financing deals from major US tech companies. The most notable example is Nvidia, which has invested $30 billion in OpenAI and $10 billion in Anthropic so far, in addition to putting tens of billions of dollars into many other AI and robotics companies.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • There are limitations compared with Face ID, but this is much better than nothing.
  • There are limitations compared with Face ID, but this is much better than nothing.
  • According to recent reports, apple is testing adding face unlock to the iPhone Duo — not true Face ID, but something a little simpler and less secure.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There are limitations compared with Face ID, but this is much better than nothing.

There are limitations compared with Face ID, but this is much better than nothing.

According to recent reports, apple is testing adding face unlock to the iPhone Duo — not true Face ID, but something a little simpler and less secure. So far, it works great, and even with a few Apple-imposed security limitations, it makes the Duo quicker and more comfortable to use than relying on Touch ID every time. That’s one of my gripes with the phone taken care of.

In a recent development, the Duo’s foldable architecture means that Apple couldn’t fit in the full Face ID sensor array found on the rest of the iPhone lineup (though it reportedly hopes to change that by the second generation). Instead, it simply has two selfie cameras — one on the outer display, and another hidden under the inner one. Neither supports full Face ID, but after enough grumbling from reviewers and early adopters that using Touch ID alone feels cumbersome, Apple has relented.

The latest developer beta of iOS 27.3 introduces a upcoming option to “Unlock with Front Camera” — Apple is careful not to call it Face ID. Setup is similar, though instead of rotating your head in a slow circle, you simply have to turn it left, right, up, and down. It takes five seconds or so, and I even managed it under the jerky conditions of a moving London bus.

Industry observers note that the newly introduced face unlock brings convenience, taking just half a second to unlock, but Apple warns during setup that it “isn’t as secure as Touch ID or Face ID” because it lacks the infrared depth map of the TrueDepth cameras. That means it’s possible to spoof with a photograph or video clip, but I managed that only once in over 20 attempts. Crucially, after each failed attempt to trick the system with a photo, the phone demanded I use Touch ID for my next login — which it doesn’t require if it simply doesn’t detect any face in the frame. That means getting past this would require any would-be thief or spy to get the fake face right the first time.

In a recent development, lacking TrueDepth also introduces limits in low light, though performance is better than I expected. Walking around after sunset, I had to seek out especially dark spots before I could find anywhere where unlocking failed, like huddling behind a truck on a leafy street where the streetlights couldn’t reach me. It will fail eventually, but it does have to get quite dark for that to happen.

The iPhone Duo’s more annoying limitations reflect when you can use the feature. Face unlock works only for 45 minutes at a time, after which you’ll have to verify with Touch ID or your passcode the next time you unlock. Worse, it doesn’t work at all with the inner screen’s under-display selfie camera. Apple hasn’t stated why, though presumably it felt the lower resolution and quality of that camera made face unlock unsuitable.

I’d love it if Apple loosened its restrictions just a little — 45 minutes isn’t a very long time before requiring Touch ID again, and I’m sure I’ll regularly forget that the inner screen requires a fingerprint. But the Duo already feels more comfortable to use, letting me get straight into the phone rather than fumbling for the fingerprint sensor. It’s small, but it’s a welcome sign that Apple is listening to the Duo’s early users and is willing to adjust its grand vision to meet the world where it is.

It has been revealed that for now, face unlock is limited to the developer beta, but it could roll out to a public beta within a few days, and with luck will get a full launch along with the rest of iOS 27.3 in December. Now can we get the same option for MacBooks and iPads?

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that although the iPhone Duo was released just this fall, Apple is finalizing the foldable’s second generation. According to a Bloomberg report, Apple has already created prototypes for the second iPhone Duo, codenamed V78, and some include a sought-after feature: Face ID.

Apple reportedly wants to bring Face ID to the foldable, potentially integrating it into the outer display. However, Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman notes that Apple appears to be running out of time to finalize its aims for the Duo ahead of a fall 2027 launch.

Also: iPhone Duo review: Hard to recommend, even harder to put down.

iPhone launch events typically take place in early September, when Apple releases its new smartphone lineups. To have the iPhones ready for sale on the heels of their announcement, Apple must manufacture the new models well before the launch event.

Because of this timeline concern, Face ID isn’t guaranteed for the iPhone Duo 2, though it could come to a third generation instead.

Other planned uogrades — including an Action Button, a telephoto camera, and a thinner, lighter construction — are also noted in the report.

Industry observers note that apple reportedly wants to add an Action Button, the customizable button that performs an action when pressed. The iPhone Duo 2 may combine the Action Button and the Camera Control buttons into a single button, providing a useful physical shortcut instead of adding a new button.

Recent findings suggest that the report indicates that many users don’t use the camera control button as often as Apple expected. Combining the camera and action buttons gives Apple the real estate necessary to add both options in an already constrained space.

According to recent reports, apple also wants to incorporate a telephoto camera into the iPhone Duo, though this is likely to happen in one of the next couple of generations. A telephoto camera would give consumers greater flexibility to zoom in and capture clear photos of distant objects, which would be an upgrade to the Duo’s photography features.

According to recent reports, technically, equipping the Duo with a telephoto camera is feasible, but the biggest obstacle is space constraints. A telephoto camera needs more room than a wide-angle one, since it requires additional optical elements to magnify distant objects.

Apple already uses a tetraprism design in its Pro iPhones, which allows a longer optical path without too much physical depth.

Apple also wants to reduce the weight and thickness of the iPhone Duo, which is legitimately clunky and cumbersome. To do this, Apple needs to balance the large internal and outer displays, battery capacity, camera array, and the hinge mechanism.

Also: The iPhone Action Button you’re hardly using has a superpower.

For many people, reducing the weight and thickness of a passport-sized foldable could matter more in buying decisions than adding another button or camera.

Gurman’s latest report doesn’t mention any planned changes for the iPhone Duo’s hinge mechanism, even after concerns with the first generation’s durability. With manufacturing deadlines fast approaching, however, it’s unlikely that Apple will be able to make changes to the Duo 2 based on consumer feedback. More than likely, these changes would come with the third-generation model.

Sources indicate that CNET tested the iPhone Duo’s hinge mechanism and found that, after around 440,000 cycles, the hinge stopped opening flat on its own. Loosening and other signs of wear were evident after 390,000 folds.

Also: The best iPhone Duo cases: Expert recommended.

Given the thinner, lighter construction of a future Duo model, one could assume that changes to the hinge and the foldable’s internal structure are imminent, but this has not been confirmed.

It has been revealed that because Apple will not have enough time to gather feedback on the iPhone Duo before the manufacturing deadlines for the iPhone Duo 2, I don’t expect the second-generation iPhone Duo to be significantly different from its predecessor. We do expect a thinner iPhone Duo 2 and a way to incorporate the Action and Camera buttons.

#91. What Is Canton Network? The Privacy Blockchain Built for Wall Street

📅 14 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1087 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Decrypt ↗ Open Full Page

What Is Canton Network? The Privacy Blockchain Built for Wall Street

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1087 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Decrypt

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The majority of blockchains are designed in such a way that anyone can see every transaction, every balance and every smart contract call.
  • While that may work for retail crypto traders, banks, asset managers and clearinghouses can't work that way.
  • In a recent development, canton Network was built to fix that.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The majority of blockchains are designed in such a way that anyone can see every transaction, every balance and every smart contract call.

While that may work for retail crypto traders, banks, asset managers and clearinghouses can't work that way. They can't show their trading positions, client data or collateral flows to competitors, and privacy and confidentiality rules require them to protect client information.

In a recent development, canton Network was built to fix that. It is a public layer-1 blockchain designed for privacy-preserving transactions, in which data is shared only with the parties involved. Institutions can problem, trade and settle tokenized assets such as Treasuries, stocks, funds and stablecoins together on one shared network, and each party only sees the data it is entitled to see.

Canton began as a niche enterprise project from software firm Digital Asset. It now carries some of the biggest names in traditional finance, including the Depository Trust & Clearing Corporation (DTCC), the post-trade backbone of U.S. markets, which introduced its tokenization service on Canton and its own private network in October 2026.

This guide covers what Canton is, how its privacy model works, who is building on it and what its native token, Canton Coin (CC), does.

Industry observers note that canton Network is a layer-1 blockchain developed by Digital Asset, a Upcoming York firm founded in 2014 that has long built distributed ledger software for financial firms. Canton launched in May 2023 with a pilot group that included Goldman Sachs, Deloitte, Microsoft and others. Its public infrastructure, the Global Synchronizer, went live in July 2024 together with Canton Coin.

Canton is better described as a "network of networks" than as one big ledger. Each institution runs its own validator node and applications, and its node stores only the data relevant to it, according to Canton's documentation. The nodes connect through the Global Synchronizer, so assets and transactions can move between them atomically: a trade either settles fully on every side or not at all.

In a recent development, the network is governed by the Global Synchronizer Foundation, an independent body hosted by the Linux Foundation. A group of "Super Validators" operates the Global Synchronizer.

In a recent development, in June 2026, Digital Asset raised $355 million in a round led by a16z crypto. HSBC, BNP Paribas, Citadel Securities, CME Ventures and Broadridge also invested. That followed a $135 million round in June 2025.

Recent findings suggest that canton's key idea is sub-transaction privacy. Smart contracts on Canton are written in Daml, Digital Asset's open-source contract language. Daml spells out exactly which parties are signatories and observers on each contract. When a transaction runs, each participant's node receives only the parts it is involved in.

It has been revealed that think of a repo trade between two banks with a custodian in the middle. Each party sees and checks its own leg. Nobody else on the network sees the details, and the synchronizer orders and confirms the transaction without reading its contents.

This is very different from Ethereum-style chains, where every node replicates every state change. On Canton, the Global Synchronizer, run by the Super Validators, orders encrypted messages and confirms transactions without seeing their contents, while each institution's own validator node holds its data. Institutions keep control of their data, but can avoid much of the reconciliation that legacy systems require. In practice, most activity on the network is private: about 79% of the updates recorded on Canton in a 24-hour period in November 2026 were private, according to CantonScan.

In a recent development, "Atomic settlement" means both legs of a trade, such as a bond and the cash paying for it, move at the same moment. That removes the risk that one side delivers and the other doesn't.

According to recent reports, what sets Canton apart is who uses it. Recent milestones include:.

In a recent development, canton Coin (CC) is the native utility token of the Global Synchronizer. Users pay network fees by burning CC. Newly introduced CC is minted as a reward for validators, Super Validators and "featured" app builders who generate real activity on the network. This setup is called a burn-mint equilibrium.

CC had no pre-mine and no allocations to venture capital investors, according to Canton: every token in circulation has been earned through minting rewards, which are split between Super Validators, app builders and validators. Whether supply shrinks depends on usage. As of November 2026, the network was burning roughly 80% as much CC each day as it minted, according to CantonScan data, below the 1:1 ratio at which supply would start to shrink. Circulating supply stood at just over 40 billion CC.

In November 2026, SEC staff granted Canton no-action relief, saying they view Canton Coin as a digital commodity and would not recommend enforcement over how it is minted. In May 2026, 21Shares rolled out the first U.S. ETF offering direct exposure to CC.

Institutional custody is catching up. Ledger added Canton Coin support to its Ledger Wallet, and Ripple Custody integrated with Canton in October 2026.

In a recent development, CC trades on several major centralized exchanges, including Kraken, Bybit and OKX. CC perpetual futures are also available on Binance Futures, and Alchemy Pay supports buying CC with a card. On Canton itself, Cantex offers onchain swaps. CC is a native coin, not an ERC-20 token, so be wary of look-alike "CC" tokens on Ethereum-based DEXs. You can track Canton Coin's latest price on Decrypt's price page.

Availability varies by region, and nothing in this guide is investment advice.

Canton's next phase is moving from pilots to full production. DTCC's service is now live, and its roadmap adds onchain settlement, collateral management and digital cash. Derivnex and its partners plan to bring cash settlement and collateral management for derivatives directly onto Canton. Expansion in Asia is also picking up: Shinhan Financial Group, Hanwha Investment & Securities, LG CNS and Meritz Securities have all signed Canton deals.

Recent findings suggest that canton doesn't have a monopoly, though. DTCC aims to connect its tokenization service to Stellar, Circle's Arc and Solana in 2027.

Sources indicate that for CC holders, the big question is whether institutional activity grows fast enough that burns outpace issuance. Canton is betting that Wall Street wants privacy and interoperability on a public network, and it has signed up an unusually long list of major financial institutions.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • YouTube view counts will now include estimates of how many people are watching a video together on TV.
  • YouTube view counts will now include estimates of how many people are watching a video together on TV.
  • YouTube’s view counts will now include the number of people that it estimates are watching a video together on TV.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

YouTube view counts will now include estimates of how many people are watching a video together on TV.

YouTube view counts will now include estimates of how many people are watching a video together on TV.

YouTube’s view counts will now include the number of people that it estimates are watching a video together on TV. In an revision on Monday, the platform claims it’s bringing “co-views” to public view counts across long-form videos, Shorts, and live content to provide a more “complete picture” of how people are using its platform.

Industry observers note that youTube, which has become even more popular on TVs than phones, also indicates the change will help it align with “TV industry standards,” which similarly record views by estimating the number of people watching shows. The organization says it doesn’t use devices, like cameras or microphones, to estimate how many people are watching a video on TV. Instead, it estimates co-views using a “privacy safe statistical model” that takes into account “demographic patterns and viewing times.”.

This marks yet another patch to YouTube’s view count system. In August, the platform began counting a view as soon as a video starts playing. The tech giant mentioned at the time that creators will notice their view counts increasing faster as a result of this change, and it seems like adding co-views could boost these numbers as well.

According to recent reports, youTube notes that it will only apply co-views to new views on TV going forward, and that they won’t appear retroactively. Co-views also won’t affect a creator’s ad revenue, YouTube Partner Program eligibility, or revenue.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After shaking up the mountain bike world, DJI spinoff Amflow is hitting city streets with the UE Carbon and UE Carbon Pro — bringing 125Nm of torque, 82 miles of range, and Find My tracking — starting at $3,500.

After shaking up the mountain bike world, DJI spinoff Amflow is hitting city streets with the UE Carbon and UE Carbon Pro — bringing 125Nm of torque, 82 miles of range, and Find My tracking — starting at $3,500.

DJI spinoff Amflow has spent the last couple of years shaking up the electric mountain bike (eMTB) market with ridiculously high-torque, lightweight models. Today, it’s bringing that same overengineered energy to pavement with the UE Series, its first urban commuter line.

It has been revealed that the series consists of two models: the UE Carbon and UE Carbon Pro. Both pack 125Nm of torque, 1,100W of peak power, and an 8x max assist ratio capable of climbing 30 percent grades — all while operating quietly under 45dBA (quieter than a household refrigerator). A swappable 600Wh battery provides up to 132km (about 82 miles) of range and fast-charges from zero to 100 percent in 2 hours and 23 minutes.

Recent findings suggest that while most city e-bikes deliver their power modestly, Amflow is strapping a mountain-bike-grade motor onto a 20.9 kg (46 pounds) upright step-through frame — and pricing it slightly below its flagship trail bikes. The UE Carbon starts at €3,099 (about $3,500 USD), while the Pro will sell for €3,499 ($3,900 USD).

But this isn’t just another commuter bike. With its proprietary Avinox drivetrain, Amflow has been ahead of the curve in blending consumer gadget UX — features like wireless phone charging, Apple Watch proximity unlock, Find My integration, and camera controls — with serious hardware specs. That’s one of the reasons why The Verge’s own Thomas Ricker has been so bullish on the brand for the past few years.

It has been revealed that with 125Nm of max torque and 1,100W of peak power, the Avinox M2 in the UE Series is slightly more dialed back from Amflow’s 150Nm flagship eMTBs. That noted, 125Nm is still massive overkill for flat city streets — but it won’t hurt to have it when encountering any grades over 30 percent. A new Auto Boost mode automatically dumps extra power when starting at a traffic light or hitting a steep hill. And traction control will help prevent any spin-outs on wet asphalt.

It has been revealed that the 600Wh removable battery is good for up 82 miles in Eco mode — and likely less than that while relying on higher levels of assist. It’s worth noting that the 1,100W peak power and 8x assist ratios will likely be software-capped depending on where you live and what regulations allow.

Recent findings suggest that as a brand within the larger DJI ecosystem, Amflow loves to integrate a lot of tech into its bikes. A 1.4 inch touchscreen is integrated into the handlebars alongside a 15W wireless phone charger — plus a 20W USB-C charger, if you prefer. The cockpit also features plenty of Apple tie-ins, like the aforementioned Find My tracker and Apple Watch proximity unlocking. The UE can also pair with a heart rate monitor, allowing riders to set a target heart rate zone that will dictate how much pedal assist the bike provides. And, of course, there’s direct recording controls for DJI Osmo cameras, in case you like to film your rides.

In a recent development, additional security is provided by a built-in 10mm hardened steel wheel lock keyed to match the removable battery. And if the bike is paired with “Lost Mode” in the Amflow app, the user can remotely brick the drive system if the bike ever gets stolen.

There’s plenty of commuter-friendly touches, like a 65mm suspension fork, suspension dropper seatpost, and heavy-duty racks rated for 20kg (44 pounds) on the front and 27kg (60 pounds) on the rear.

The bikes are on sale globally starting today via Amflow’s website and retail partners. The organization states a smaller XS frame size is coming in 2027 for shorter riders.
