#78. 5 ways AI will change how you defend your business in 2027

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1172 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Zdnet ↗ Open Full Page

5 ways AI will change how you defend your business in 2027

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1172 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Zdnet

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that at the beginning of the year, few organizations were utilizing large language models (LLMs) and AI agents in their cybersecurity workflows, including for discovering and patching vulnerabilities.
  • Also: Rogue AI incidents hit ‘tens of thousands’: Can businesses trust these tools?
  • The capabilities of agentic AI are fast outstripping the speed and scale at which traditional security operations centers (SOCs) can operate.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that at the beginning of the year, few organizations were utilizing large language models (LLMs) and AI agents in their cybersecurity workflows, including for discovering and patching vulnerabilities. According to Google, this is now happening at scale.

Also: Rogue AI incidents hit ‘tens of thousands’: Can businesses trust these tools?

The capabilities of agentic AI are fast outstripping the speed and scale at which traditional security operations centers (SOCs) can operate. Like it or not, AI has an integral role in the upcoming reality — for the defenders and threat actors.

Speed and scale are the main reasons enterprises consider adopting AI in SOCs and for security more broadly, and these factors underpin Google’s fresh security forecast for 2027 — Cloud CISO Perspectives. However, without the right precautions, AI security adopters could inadvertently increase their attack surface rather than shrink it.

With this in mind, these are five ways AI will change the security industry over the next year and what CISOs need to consider going into 2027.

Alert fatigue is well-known across SOC teams. Alert after alert needs to be trawled through; many are irrelevant or false positives, tying up skilled staff with the mundane, tedious, time-consuming task of triaging them.

Now that autonomous, AI-driven threats can probe a network, gain entry, and move laterally across it in minutes, chasing threat data and security alerts from multiple systems logged days or weeks ago can’t help a business mitigate them — and certainly not at the speed of the threat.

Recent findings suggest that according to Google’s forecast, AI will mean the alert queue quietly disappears. Ramya Chitrakar, VP of engineering at Google Cloud Security, believes that “2027 is the year analysts stop chasing alerts and start shaping outcomes.”.

Also: AI is both a cyber weapon and a massive target.

Recent findings suggest that how? CISOs must change the alert model itself. Instead of human defenders triaging alerts at the start of a cybersecurity incident, the alert becomes final output, with autonomous agents handling “data enrichment, correlation, and triage automatically, surfacing a verified conclusion rather than a raw ticket,” according to Google.

This means cybersecurity experts can oversee alert handling and verify automated actions, potentially freeing them to focus on other tasks.

Custom agentic AI is often designed — or at least intended — to work autonomously, with human oversight. However, having thousands of individual agents working across multiple environments can create high-value entry points into corporate networks that cyberattackers target.

We need to think of agentic AI as more than a tool: each one needs its own identity, like a human employee, to operate within a zero-trust architecture, retain control, and reduce the risk of compromise.

Also: Your enterprise AI access can be sold for pennies – beware ‘LLM Mixers’.

According to recent reports, however, Heather Adkins, VP of security engineering at Google, thinks this needs to go further and suggests the zero-trust concept shouldn’t stop at the network layer. Instead, Adkins believes it needs to reach the transaction layer.

It has been revealed that A paper trail for each agent needs to be established, which is impossible to handle manually, and even within a zero-trust framework, AI agents could be given too much scope. Instead, implement verification for each transaction and for every authorization, and assign each AI agent its own least-privilege set of credentials that can be revoked if there is a security incident or the agent is no longer required.

“When backed by real-time autonomous reasoning, we can dynamically allow a transaction on Tuesday and block the exact same request on Wednesday if conditions look anomalous,” the report notes.

AI is being used to speed up the development and deployment of new software, and in 2027, security will have to become a continuous system embedded in the software delivery pipeline, according to Google.

Threat actors have carried out software supply chain attacks over the years, one of the most notable being the SolarWinds incident of 2020. Sandra Joyce, VP of Google Threat Intelligence, says cybercriminals are now poisoning everything from open-source code to software libraries, which AI coding assistants often pull automatically into codebases.

Also: How AI security failures are endangering your supply chain.

Sources indicate that bug-fix tickets that take days to respond to and security appearing at the end of a software development cycle no longer work. Instead, writing and securing code must happen simultaneously, with the help of agentic AI, so speed doesn’t compromise security.

“It’s also crucial that we link live production environments directly back to source code so that defenders can trace a real-world exposure to the exact line of code, validate whether it is genuinely exploitable, and deliver a pre-tested fix at machine speed without breaking production,” Google added.

As organizations rush to implement AI into their applications and services to appear “AI-first,” innovative, and modern, security may be ignored or treated as an afterthought.

According to recent reports, as a result, we may face a newly introduced, broader attack surface than we realize, as AI introduces new security issues, including software vulnerabilities, misconfiguration, bypasses, and indirect prompt injection attacks. Now that AI is also in the hands of all cyberattackers — from script kiddies to state-sponsored groups — auditing corporate networks and infrastructure is crucial.

Also: Who’s responsible for catching rogue AI agents? You are.

According to recent reports, penetration testing and red team exercises now need to cover agentic AI. This wasn’t in scope for many red teams only a few years ago, but now that businesses have run with the idea of implementing AI in their workflows, processes, and products, organizations need to identify and fix security challenges introduced by AI before threat actors take advantage of them.

CISOs should task pen testers with auditing before an autonomous workflow hits production, then combine the results with threat intelligence to ensure defenders have the information they need to bolster network defenses and harden classifiers against new and novel attacks.

The final significant trend we are likely to see in 2027 is tackling agent sprawl to create coordinated teams of AI agents that can rapidly handle security tasks at scale.

Recent findings suggest that single AI agents given general instructions won’t cut it when AI-assisted attackers can compromise endpoint devices, enter networks, move laterally, or start stealing data in a far shorter timeframe than before. Instead, CISOs should replace these “generalist” AI agents with specialized, orchestrated teams of AI agents that can meet the demands of defending against AI-driven attacks by employing specialist tooling and skill sets.

Also: AI agent kill switch urged by Okta-led alliance.

CISOs also need to ensure that each agent has its own domain training and understanding, memory, and dedicated tools, and can act on its own within set limits, with a central coordinator that knows when to hand a decision to a human. This requires oversight, but in return, organizations will avoid agent sprawl, which the tech giant believes is the next iteration of shadow IT and its associated threats.

This lightweight Linux distro revives old PCs destined for the junk pile – and it’s beautiful

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that there are more Linux distributions than you can imagine.
  • Of the list of lightweight Linux distributions that I have considered to be solid options, the following distros tend to always land somewhere in my top five:.
  • Recent findings suggest that bodhi Linux has been one of my favorite lightweight Linux distributions for a long time, primarily because it offers the Moksha desktop (which is a fork of Enlightenment) that is equal parts efficiency and beauty.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that there are more Linux distributions than you can imagine. Distributions for average desktop usage, AI, multimedia, number crunching, massive data, servers, and everything in between. There are also Linux distributions created specifically for older or slower hardware, which are typically labeled “lightweight” distributions. They might include specialized kernels, apps that aren’t resource-intensive, and desktop environments that are best suited for lesser-powered machines.

Of the list of lightweight Linux distributions that I have considered to be solid options, the following distros tend to always land somewhere in my top five:.

Recent findings suggest that bodhi Linux has been one of my favorite lightweight Linux distributions for a long time, primarily because it offers the Moksha desktop (which is a fork of Enlightenment) that is equal parts efficiency and beauty. Thanks to Moksha, Bodhi Linux is a great option for older hardware. The only concern some might have with Bodhi is that the Moksha desktop is quite different from anything they’ve ever used.

According to recent reports, linux Lite uses a customized Xfce desktop and ships with a decent collection of apps, so you can be productive right out of the box. You’ll find Chrome, LibreOffice (including Base, to create databases), GIMP, Photo Manager, Deja Dup Backups, VLC media player, a USB image writer, an onscreen keyboard, Timeshift (for restore points), and more.

Xubuntu is essentially Ubuntu with the Xfce desktop. Because it uses Xfce, it’s highly customizable. And like Linux Lite, Xubuntu includes all the software you need to get going, such as LibreOffice (office suite), Firefox (web browser), Thunderbird (email client), Transmission (torrent client), Catfish (file search tool), GIMP (image editor), Rhythmbox (music player), Parole Media Player, and Atril Document Viewer.

Also: My top 5 Linux alternatives to Windows (none of them are Mint).

It has been revealed that other than Bodhi Linux, the other two options might come across as looking a bit outdated; that’s because Xfce focuses more on speed and customization than aesthetics. Although that doesn’t mean any of the above are less usable, if you prefer your desktop operating system on the more modern side of things, you might find yourself rather disappointed with the above. That’s why, when I got my first peek at the oddly named XXRI-OS-LITE, I was immediately excited.

Industry observers note that there’s now another lightweight Linux option, but one that doesn’t shrug off aesthetics. If you’ve read me long enough, you know that the way a Linux desktop looks is just as notable as how it functions (to me).

As the name implies, XXRI-OS-LITE is a lightweight Linux distribution that is perfectly capable of reviving your older hardware. But this distribution goes a bit further than most lightweight distros by also delivering a modern desktop that doesn’t depend on the terminal window and offers zero complexity. XXRI-OS-LITE isn’t just lightweight; it’s beautiful and easy to use.

It has been revealed that XXRI-OS-LITE can be run on a system with very low resources. The minimum requirements are a Pentium II or K6-2, 256 MB of RAM, and 700 MB of storage.

If that sounds like you, XXRI-OS-LITE might be right up your alley.

Also: My favorite Linux desktop environment for laptops surprised even me.

Industry observers note that the XXRI-OS desktop is comprised of a dock, a desktop menu, and a system tray, all of which come together to create a nice, macOS-inspired desktop. If you click the desktop menu, you’ll see the few apps that are installed by default, which include a control center, power menu, terminal, a text editor, a web browser, a file manager, a media player, a settings app, and an app store. That’s it.

Recent findings suggest that when you click to open an app, the first thing you’ll notice is how fast it opens…like instantly. Lightweight distributions tend to be fast, but not like this. This feels like COSMIC Desktop (from System76) running on a Thelio (which is a beast of a desktop). This is fast in a way you don’t usually see.

XXRI-OS-LITE is based on Tiny Core Linux and is the lightweight version of XXRI-OS (which is still under development). At the same time, XXRI-OS-LITE is also early in the development process, which means there will be problems. The difference between the two (other than one being a lightweight distribution and the other not) is that the LITE version ships with a bare minimum of apps. Under normal circumstances, that would be fine because there’s a GUI app store.

I did run into a rather interesting issue. Even though I could get online with the OS (both in the browser and from the command line), the App Store refused to connect. I wrote this off as an early dev issue, but after a bit of digging around, I started thinking that maybe it was the repository being offline, so I waited a few hours and checked again. Same problem. I then hopped onto the XXRI-OS-LITE Discord server and discovered that this is a known issue.

Recent findings suggest that apparently, the App Store works fine over Wi-Fi, but not Ethernet. Because this problem is known, I’m sure it’ll be resolved soon. In the meantime, I decided to give an AppImage a try to see how well it would run.

Also: 5 premium Linux distros absolutely worth paying for in 2026.

It has been revealed that I uploaded my Quillwriter app as an AppImage, and the OS automatically detected that it should be executable and asked me if I wanted to give it the necessary permissions and then integrate it into the system (which means adding it to the desktop menu). After that, the app opened very quickly (as fast as it does on my MacBook M1) and functioned exactly as expected.

It has been revealed that even with the App Store issue, XXRI-OS-LITE indicates a lot of promise, so much so that if the developers can keep the project going, I could see this distribution jumping ahead of the current crop of top distros in its class. And with an aesthetic that makes XXRI-OS-LITE look more like a serious desktop distribution, the sky’s the limit.

Recent findings suggest that before you jump on the XXRI-OS-LITE bandwagon, know that, as I mentioned before, it’s early in the development process, which means it has a ways to go before it’s ready for the masses. Even so, this Linux distro is off to a great start; it’s fast, beautiful, and easy, it runs on hardware that most would have considered tossing into a junk pile, and it proves that a lightweight Linux distribution doesn’t have to look and feel as if it teleported from the early 2000s.

Recent findings suggest that would I recommend it over the other three lightweight distros I mentioned earlier? Not at the moment, but once the developers resolve the App Store concern, that could very quickly change.

Also: Linux has hundreds of distros: 5 reasons to stop using the same few.

It has been revealed that give XXRI-OS-LITE a try and see what it’s all about. Just remember, although the current version is 2.7, it feels a bit younger than that. Even so, it’s a fantastic start to a promising lightweight Linux distribution.

I’m very excited for what XXRI-OS-LITE can bring to the table.

On Sunday, it introduced the Apple Health AI Usage Study, which could contribute to the next AI health experience Apple builds by measuring the quality of AI health responses, comprehension, and everyday health behaviors, according to a press release.

Sources indicate that apple is conducting the study in collaboration with OpenEvidence, a clinical AI platform widely used by healthcare professionals. The study examines the relationship between conversational AI tools, like chatbots, and the people who use them.

“Insights from this study will help advance the broader scientific conversation and ensure that as technology evolves, we continue building trusted tools that genuinely support people wherever they are on their health journey,” Sumbul Desai, M.D., Apple’s vice president of Health and Fitness, remarked in the press release.

Also: Apple Watch Series 12 review: Finally, the health tracker I’ve been waiting for.

Participants are encouraged to share their HealthKit data and query the health app with questions. The study will also explore how AI tools can best prepare patients ahead of clinical visits. Apple will monitor the AI’s clarity and approachability when providing medical information, and each response or recommendation will be linked to peer-reviewed clinical citations. Responses could be unclear or incomplete, which is why Apple is rolling this out as a study to explore a responsibly designed AI health assistant.

In a recent development, apple often launches studies for features it would like to develop in the future. For example, many of the hearing health features launched on the AirPods were a direct result of the findings from Apple’s Hearing Study.

Also: Athenahealth patients can ask Claude about their medical records now.

The AI usage study comes on the heels of the revamped Health app’s debut, which releases officially next month. It also arrives amid a bevy of AI health coaches, popping up alongside companion health devices. Google rolled out its AI Health Coach in Google Health Premium last year, and Oura launched a proprietary AI model for women trained on medical standards and research from Oura’s in-house team of board-certified clinicians.

A growing number of Americans are relying on AI for medical advice. A recent survey from Pew Research Center found that 34% of US adults have talked with a chatbot for medical advice. As AI proliferates, that percentage will only increase.

It has been revealed that “Patients and clinicians are both turning to AI, but the tools they use are being built and tested in separate worlds,” said Robert M. Wachter, M.D., UCSF’s professor and chair of the Department of Medicine, in the press release.

Apple and other tech companies are building for this latest health normal, and the AI usage study indicates that Apple isn’t taking the responsibility lightly.

According to recent reports, if you’re interested in participating in Apple’s study, it’s open to 200,000 eligible participants age 21 and older in the US. You’ll need a phone with Apple Intelligence enabled (the iPhone 15 Pro or later), running iOS 26 or later. You can download the study app to learn more and enroll.

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1009 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ars Technica ↗ Open Full Page

Google pushes privacy angle as Gemini-powered smartglasses debut starting at $395

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1009 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Smartglasses have always faced an uphill road to acceptance.
  • Sources indicate that these devices are a collaboration between Google, Samsung, and the aforementioned eyewear designers.
  • According to recent reports, warby Parker has designed three frames for Google eyewear, called Alden, Reid, and Wren (see above).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Smartglasses have always faced an uphill road to acceptance. Not only is propping a computer up on your nose an uncomfortable proposition, but the privacy aspect has been vexing people since the Google Glass days. Now, Google is ready to take another swing at “intelligent eyewear” for the Gemini era after previewing its looks a couple of times. The first glasses are up for preorder today from Gentle Monster and Warby Parker, but they’re no impulse buy.

Sources indicate that these devices are a collaboration between Google, Samsung, and the aforementioned eyewear designers. Gentle Monster and Warby Parker have each designed a few different frames, with options for transparent and tinted lenses. Samsung is providing the computing hardware that fits inside them, and Google has the software covered.

According to recent reports, warby Parker has designed three frames for Google eyewear, called Alden, Reid, and Wren (see above). They are available with both standard optical and sun lenses in Pine, Saddle, and Jet Black colors at $395 and higher. Warby Parker is only selling devices in the US. Gentle Monster has gone a bit further with six styles, but Google hasn’t told us any names for those yet. They come in dark red, pink, gray, and yellow colors and are available with clear, tinted, blue, or brown lenses. The Gentle Monster styles start a little higher at $449, and they will be available in the US and South Korea.

According to recent reports, google says the frames all weigh about 41 grams, which is not terrible but is definitely near the top for glasses generally. They will, naturally, weigh much more when you account for lenses. That will also determine the final pricing. So far, we only have the starting prices for these devices, including non-prescription lenses.

The setup here is similar to the Ray-Ban Meta glasses we’ve seen for a few years. There are no screens in the lenses, but you can interact with the AI system via voice or by activating the integrated camera. The experience should be similar to using Gemini Live on your phone, but it will be a lot easier to fire up the AI. You can say “Hey Gemini” or tap a touch-sensitive area of the frame to start interacting with the robot.

Credit: Gentle Monster Credit: Gentle Monster.

In a recent development, since this is the same chatbot that operates across the Google ecosystem, it has access to your data and preferences. You can ask questions and get personalized answers, have Google Maps guide you by voice, or just talk with the AI to kill time. The glasses use custom open-ear speakers to limit distractions for those around you. Google notes the directional microphones should not pick up speech from other people, either.

It has been revealed that adding the camera feed is where things get interesting. When the AI can see what you see, it has the potential to do more work on your behalf. Google suggests asking Gemini for recommendations when looking at a bookshelf or glancing at an event poster to have the AI add it to your calendar. The glasses will also support Gemini Guided Vision, which provides conversational audio descriptions for people who are visually impaired.

In a recent development, the utility of these devices hinges on Gemini. I would be remiss not to point out that Gemini, like all AI systems, is not infallible. In fact, it can be frustratingly fallible at times. The chatbot still regularly screws up simple things like adding calendar appointments or identifying objects in an image in my testing, and when you don’t have a screen to verify the AI’s output, it may be harder to trust it. These devices will really only make sense if you can rely on Gemini to do things right, and that’s still not a guarantee.

All the Gemini-powered glasses from Gentle Monster and Warby Parker feature a 12 MP wide-angle camera capable of shooting photos and video. Google says it has implemented a number of features and limitations to ensure people don’t do creepy things with its intelligent eyewear, and that it doesn’t do creepy things to you—Google claims its approach respects privacy on “both sides of the lens.”.

For starters, there’s a recording light that is on whenever the camera is active. Like the Meta glasses, Google’s eyewear will detect if the light has been covered up or modified in any way that would prevent it from illuminating. In that event, the glasses will refuse to activate the camera. All Google-powered glasses will have a physical off switch, too.

Credit: Warby Parker Credit: Warby Parker.

It has been revealed that on the user privacy side, Google notes it will not save any images or videos captured by the glasses in your Gemini history. Additionally, none of that data will be used for training AI models or targeting ads. Your voice interactions with Gemini via the glasses are, as with all other Gemini endpoints, not guaranteed the same level of protection. You can delete your chats from the Gemini history, though.

Data on the glasses is encrypted, and it remains that way during transit to the cloud. However, it’s not encrypted on Google’s servers. The company does note that it’s working to bring Private AI Compute to glasses, which will isolate data during processing so not even Google can access it.

Credit: Gentle Monster Credit: Gentle Monster.

Anyone looking to get Gemini on their face and test Google’s privacy promise can preorder the glasses from the Gentle Monster and Warby Parker websites. Devices should ship and appear on store shelves on December 10. Importantly, support for these devices is a bit narrow at launch. They will work with all iPhones from the 13 Pro onward. On the Android side, you’ll need a Pixel 7 or newer or a Samsung Galaxy S or Z series device running One UI 9 or later. If you’ve got a cheaper Samsung Galaxy or a device from another OEM, you’re out of luck at the moment.

#65. Google faces calls for AI moratoriums in schools after Gemini pilot backlash

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1759 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ars Technica ↗ Open Full Page

Google faces calls for AI moratoriums in schools after Gemini pilot backlash

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1759 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • CHICAGO—Families joined protests in seven cities nationwide on Wednesday, rallying against what they see as Google’s bid to entrench its AI models in schools, turn kids of all ages into Gemini guinea pigs, and hook them on AI.
  • The backlash follows a Google statement last week, confirming that there will be no way for students to use Google Search without AI.
  • In Chicago, many families indicated up to protest Google, despite cold, rainy weather.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

CHICAGO—Families joined protests in seven cities nationwide on Wednesday, rallying against what they see as Google’s bid to entrench its AI models in schools, turn kids of all ages into Gemini guinea pigs, and hook them on AI.

The backlash follows a Google statement last week, confirming that there will be no way for students to use Google Search without AI. While Google claimed it was giving schools “more choice, not less”—by turning off Search, Gemini, and Gemini Notebook by default—it would not provide an option that allowed Search without AI. For students, the only way to avoid interacting with AI was to remember to add “-ai” to every query, parents worried.

In Chicago, many families indicated up to protest Google, despite cold, rainy weather. Waving signs, dozens of protesters marched up to Google’s downtown office as workers seemed to be leaving for the day, shouting chants like “Hey Google, nice try, we don’t want your Gemini” and “Hey, Google, leave our kids alone!”.

Called to action by a nonprofit grassroots advocacy group, the Illinois Families for Public Schools (ILFPS), some parents and students had previously won a major AI fight. In August, the group pressured Chicago Public Schools (CPS) to pull out of a Gemini pilot that would have roped in all high school students districtwide—without consulting parents. And now, ILFPS is demanding a moratorium on AI until risks to students are better understood and CPS can draft a policy to protect students from potential learning setbacks or more harmful outcomes from engaging Google’s AI bots. If the group wins, it will join cities like Los Angeles and Upcoming York City in cautiously banning AI in schools.

Sources indicate that most alarming to parents, Google now faces a lawsuit from a 13-year-old student in Durham, North Carolina named “Emma Doe.” As Emma has alleged, she was a happy, well-adjusted, straight-A student when she started using Gemini on her school-issued Chromebook. Emma’s parents had no idea she was using Gemini, as the lawsuit alleged that Google “deliberately” kept them in the dark while driving Emma into so-called “AI psychosis.” Over time, normal school-related interactions with the chatbot led to more intense chats, and ultimately the chatbot allegedly coached Emma to blueprint her own suicide and funeral. The school warned her parents and averted the danger after an internal system flagged a chat labeled “Funeral,” but Emma’s story stoked fears of parents joining protests not just in Durham, but also in Boston; Boulder, Colorado; Chicago; Los Angeles; Upcoming York City; and Portland, Oregon.

Emma’s lawsuit accuses Google of exploiting its dominant position in education technology and “sneaking” Gemini into Chromebooks, while falsely marketing them as safe.

Sources indicate that “As a direct consequence of Google’s choices, Emma was baited by its defectively designed products into repeated, unmonitored, sycophantic AI chatbot interactions on her school Chromebook without her parents ever knowing. And, but for a fortunate turn of events, Google’s AI may well have manipulated Emma into taking her own life,” the lawsuit alleged. “Google must be held to account for treating the lives of children as disposable in service of its bottom line.”.

Recent findings suggest that google has promised to “continue to engage deeply with educators to ensure we are giving schools more choice, more controls, and improved Search for learning.” However, Google’s statements so far attempting to address parents’ concerns focus exclusively on documented harms to learning. On that front, Google claims that it’s solving the problem of AI eroding students’ critical thinking skills by launching yet another pilot for students. In this pilot, students using AI Mode and AI Overviews will be offered a “step-by-step guided learning through problems, so that students don’t get quick answers to schoolwork,” Google said.

Sources indicate that cassie Creswell, executive director of ILFPS, told Ars that she’s been an advocate monitoring edtech concerns for more than a decade. And even she was blindsided by Google’s AI moves.

“I am aware of AI Overviews when you search, which have a whole slew of problems, but I did not know that you really actually just have an interface where you can interact with Gemini in the chatbot way on everyone’s Chromebook still in Chicago public schools,” Creswell mentioned. “And that’s so disturbing.”.

Sources indicate that she acknowledged that kids encounter AI on their phones and shared that her daughter stated her friends like using ChatGPT better than Gemini. But she said that the fact that some kids use AI on personal devices doesn’t mean that schools should be encouraging adoption at young ages when kids’ brains are still developing, and risks remain largely unknown.

“There’s all kinds of dangerous things out in the world, but we don’t have our school district handing it to kids at their desk,” Creswell remarked.

Meanwhile, schools seem to be part of the transparency problem.

Sources indicate that creswell said that currently, the Chicago school district “is telling us their official line is that kids don’t have access to generative AI tools and that we don’t need a district-level policy on generative AI because they have guidebooks.” However, she’s reviewed Google’s CPS contracts, and they suggest that kids are interacting with generative AI and frontier models. The ongoing confusion has led parents to demand “a real policy” that the CPS “board votes on and that has the input of teachers, parents, students, and experts who are not being funded by the tech industry.”.

According to recent reports, creswell told Ars that parents are particularly upset that Google is not transparent about how it processes and uses student data. She’s exhaustively researched Google contracts through Freedom of Information Act requests and told Ars that dozens of agreements she reviewed offer no indication of how CPS partners like Google—as well as Anthropic and OpenAI—are handling student data. Although she understands that “it’s probably just an honest statement of fact” that Google has built AI inextricably into Search, parents have a right to know how their children’s data is ingested into Google’s models, she said.

In a recent development, “Any sort of transparency on what is actually happening in terms of the data that they collect and what they do with it, that is absolutely missing,” Creswell said. And “it’s very unclear what data is being saved.”.

To Creswell and other advocates, it seems likely that kids’ data is collected no matter what, since “even if you do ‘-AI,’ and you don’t get a text summary, your search data and what’s being returned is all basically inside the generative AI model.” Although Illinois law only allows commercial use of de-identified data, parents think Google should clearly explain what steps it takes to ensure data can’t be recombined to re-identify kids.

Ars reached out to Google to see if the company could clarify if Creswell’s read is accurate or if there’s any meaningful distinction between adding “-AI” to an individual query versus building a button that would automatically add “-AI” to every query. Google did not clarify, instead emphasizing that schools will control whether students can access the Gemini app, Gemini Notebook, and Search, with options to toggle each off individually, but no option to use Search without AI.

Emma Doe’s lawsuit alleged that Google has taken advantage of a dominant position it has held in schools since 2007 to push AI on kids and seize their data without meaningfully protecting them from the worst potential harms of its chatbot’s sycophantic design. In Chicago, CPS signed a contract with Google in 2020, “long before Gemini was rolled out,” Creswell found. Over the next two extensions of that contract, no updates were introduced to protect students’ privacy as AI advanced.

Currently, that policy specifies that “we receive customer data through the Core Services and process it according to the school’s (the customer’s) instructions. This customer data includes anything submitted, stored, sent, or received through Core Services by you or your school.” Google collects that data on that activity, as well as account information “like name, email address and password” and location information, the policy said.

Industry observers note that the policy didn’t discuss Gemini but noted that data from using core services helps maintain services, improve personalization, and increase security. And “the data we collect in the Additional Services is used across our services to deliver, maintain, and improve our services; develop upcoming services; provide personalized services; measure performance; communicate with you; and protect Google, our users, and the public.”.

To parents, the policy provides no reassurance that their kids’ data isn’t part of Google’s blueprint to dominate the AI industry.

“We should not have any child data being collected in a school setting being used for commercial purposes,” Creswell noted.

In a recent development, parents’ privacy concerns go beyond Google, Creswell noted. But since Google has “captured so much of the education space and so much of the education experience,” parents are focusing their energy on interrogating those AI systems in schools early on.

In Chicago, a recently re-elected CPS school board member, Karen Zaccor, is pushing for an AI moratorium in schools after talking with city and community colleges about an allegedly noticeable decline in reading, math, and writing skills from students graduating from CPS schools. In Emma’s case, Google allegedly suppressed chat logs, and the school withheld safety logs, frustrating parents who already viewed AI as more harmful than beneficial in education.

At the Google protest Wednesday, parents waved signs that threatened to eject Google from schools, with slogans like “No Google + No AI = Win/Win.” Many kids used favorite cartoon characters from shows like Beavis and Butthead and South Park to slam Google’s seemingly cynical approach to introducing AI in schools. One young girl wearing pink rain boots held up a cardboard sign, declaring in colorful markers, “I like to read!!”.

At its peak, about 60 people stood outside Google’s downtown Chicago office, enduring the rain and listening to teachers and students who oppose reckless AI adoption.

According to recent reports, one particularly moving speech came from a CPS student, Reese Mackey, who spoke for students. She challenged Google to more carefully weigh the long-term harms of aggressively pushing AI onto students by claiming they’ll be left behind and struggle to find jobs without AI skills. Creswell told Ars the opposite seems true, as Emma Doe’s lawsuit pointed to research branding Gemini as “the most dangerous marketed for use by youth” and “confirming the existence of AI-induced psychosis.”.

“What about the future of our youth?” Mackey said. “What about the future of our minds?”.

On October 21, 2026, the Node.js project released security updates addressing a critical vulnerability in the Brotli decoder bundled with Node.js, commonly referred to as "Node2Shell" (tracked as CVE-2026-111497). The vulnerability is an out-of-bounds write that could allow a remote attacker to cause memory corruption and potentially execute arbitrary code. This advisory covers the status of impact of various Siemens products. Siemens has released newly introduced versions for several affected products and recommends to update to the latest versions. Siemens is preparing further fixes and recommends specific mitigations for products where fixes are not or not yet available.

The following versions of Siemens Industrial Automation Software Products are affected:.

As a general security measure, Siemens strongly recommends to protect network access to devices with appropriate mechanisms. In order to operate the devices in a protected IT environment, Siemens recommends to configure the environment according to Siemens' operational guidelines for Industrial Security (Download: https://www.siemens.com/cert/operational-guidelines-industrial-security), and to follow the recommendations in the product manuals. Additional information on Industrial Security by Siemens can be found at: https://www.siemens.com/industrialsecurity.

For further inquiries on security vulnerabilities in Siemens products and solutions, please contact the Siemens ProductCERT: https://www.siemens.com/cert/advisories.

The use of Siemens Security Advisories is subject to the terms and conditions listed on: https://www.siemens.com/productcert/terms-of-use.

CISA recommends consumers take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities.

CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures.

CISA also provides a section for control systems security recommended practices on the ICS webpage on cisa.gov/ics. Several CISA products detailing cyber defense best practices are available for reading and download, including Improving Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity with Defense-in-Depth Strategies.

CISA encourages organizations to implement recommended cybersecurity strategies for proactive defense of ICS assets.

Additional mitigation guidance and recommended practices are publicly available on the ICS webpage at cisa.gov/ics in the technical information paper, ICS-TIP-12-146-01B--Targeted Cyber Intrusion Detection and Mitigation Strategies.

Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents.

#63. I tried the Flowtica Verso AI notetaker expecting a gimmick – now it’s my newly introduced favorite MagSafe gadget

I tried the Flowtica Verso AI notetaker expecting a gimmick – now it’s my newly introduced favorite MagSafe gadget

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that AI is often touted as a tool for increasing efficiency, and businesses have grasped its potential benefits with abandon – perhaps, in some cases, far too quickly.
  • One company focused on products that automate time-consuming, tedious tasks is Flowtica — makers of the Scribe pen we saw at IFA earlier this year.
  • Also: Run this 10-step security check on your phone once a year – here’s why.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that AI is often touted as a tool for increasing efficiency, and businesses have grasped its potential benefits with abandon – perhaps, in some cases, far too quickly. But when done right, it can improve productivity.

One company focused on products that automate time-consuming, tedious tasks is Flowtica — makers of the Scribe pen we saw at IFA earlier this year. It was an impressive device, but its next product, the Flowtica Verso, promises more.

Also: Run this 10-step security check on your phone once a year – here’s why.

According to recent reports, the Flowtica Verso is a compact “AI productivity companion” with an e-paper display and a connector that attaches to the back of your smartphone. Instead of managing multiple apps to record meetings, transcribe, or handle your to-do list and calendar, Verso is designed so you don’t need to use your phone at all — everything you need is on the device’s screen, and always available.

Recent findings suggest that your kit comes with the Flowtica Verso itself, a USB-C cable, and a circular, magnetic clip you can use to attach the Verso to the back of your smartphone or any other magnetic surface. The device itself is thin, light, and comfortable to hold. There are just three buttons: one on the left to power it; an orange button for recording, and a secondary right button, which is the “Ask Flowtica” or AI button.

There’s a QR code on the display that lilnks to the app download page, available on Android and iOS. After starting it up for the first time, Verso asks what it should call you, to best describe your role and industry, and what you expect to use your AI companion for.

Also: Don’t use Muse? Meta’s AI agent can still access your private messages – here’s how.

You then pair your device to your smartphone via Bluetooth, and set up Wi-Fi, which you don’t need to record meetings, but you will need for transcription, since it calls the cloud to process.

The Always-on display is comfortable, and as it is designed without a backlight, its e-paper screen is always available to you in the background, a useful addition for work when you just want to glance at upcoming meetings or calendar events, all of which are displayed on the Verso screensaver.

In a recent development, however, in dim lighting conditions, it’s not as easy to read and could be particularly difficult for anyone with vision impairment. I also found that response times varied when I tapped the screen or swiped across to read content on my Verso, ranging from immediate to taking a few seconds to register.

For my test, I chose to record a conversation from The ZDNET Show on the best products of 2025.

In a recent development, I recorded the discussion between ZDNET experts from approximately five feet away, and I left my TV on to provide some of the background noise you might expect in a busy meeting room. After pressing the record button, I let the Verso get to work.

Also: I can access my home PCs remotely for free – how you can too (no VPN needed).

Sources indicate that while recording, you can simply leave the device on a table and let it record and transcribe for you without supervision. You can also choose to read a live summary of a meeting as it’s generated, or choose to read a transcription, which could be useful if the user is hard of hearing. There’s a small, red light at the bottom of the Verso that flashes when it is recording.

Once you want to finish recording, press the recording button again. Each recording is stored under the Meeting tab, accessible from the main screen. Dates, times, and the length of each meeting is displayed. Tap into it, and you can find meeting notes created from the recording, including a meeting type, executive summary, and an AI-generated summary spanning multiple pages.

While transcriptions are not 100% accurate – I would suggest a ballpark of around 80 – 85% – many of the mistakes are small, grammatical errors or miswordings, such as “zPed” instead of ZDNET, with human oversight, they still take a lot of effort out of transcribing.

Recent findings suggest that there’s plenty of options for exporting your meeting content, too. While you can do this directly from the Verso, I like how every meeting and recording is laid out in the Flowtica app, complete with a “To-do” function for adding follow-up tasks, exporting your notes, sharing, or changing your meeting language. (As the latter is based on AI, I can’t comment on how accurate the translations are.).

Sources indicate that the significant draw with all this data is being able to ask the AI questions about your meetings. You can have a chat with your AI assistant and ask it to perform tasks for you, including setting reminders, creating follow-up tasks, and summarizing meetings. It works rather well and doesn’t take too long to answer, but I think this is a secondary benefit that augments the calendar and transcription options, rather than the other way around.

Also: The best foldable phones of 2026: How the iPhone Duo stacks up.

I asked for a bullet-point summary of my most recent recording, and despite the Verso capturing some strange dialogue from background TV noise, it still understood what I requested and provided a solid answer.

According to recent reports, another notable feature is the ability to set up contact cards. The Verso has NFC connectivity, and business people can set up a business card they can pass to another with a tap. You set up your contact card in the accompanying app and update Verso to store it.

Recent findings suggest that yes. I think it has the best use cases in business, meeting-heavy roles, and for anyone tasked with transcribing conversations, where it could potentially save you many hours. This also expands to journalism, and I intend to use this gadget when I’m next in the field, attending a conference or conducting an interview.

Also: How I use my Apple Watch to identify a song fast – without opening Shazam.

It does take some time to set up and learn, but for those willing to remember to use it for a few days, I think it would become a valuable tool, rather than a device left to gather dust on the shelf. The Ask Flowtica AI feature is a nice touch, but it’s actually the meetings > transcription > AI-assisted summaries functions that can boost productivity. It doesn’t hurt that the gadget is small enough to keep with your tablet or smartphone, either.

Industry observers note that I’m generally wary of AI-first devices that promise productivity, as in many cases they’re just buzzwords and a cool gadget wrapped in an AI bow. However, when it comes to the Flowtica Verso, I don’t mind admitting that this kind of tool will actually help me in my day-to-day workflow and will be invaluable in helping me with transcription — a task I don’t want to spend much time on.

Also: HR thinks you can learn AI skills – so why is your firm hiring elsewhere?

I’m just a little annoyed, as I may now have to take the wallet cover off my Android to permanently install the Verso.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The state DMV labeled Waymo’s highway operations an “imminent hazard to public safety” after its robotaxis drove into an active construction zone.

The state DMV labeled Waymo’s highway operations an “imminent hazard to public safety” after its robotaxis drove into an active construction zone.

California has pulled the plug on Waymo’s driverless freeway rides across the entire state, citing potential safety hazards.

It has been revealed that in a statement, the California Department of Motor Vehicles noted that the ban went into effect on November 11th. The crackdown follows two recent high-profile Bay Area incidents, in which Waymo robotaxis drove into an active construction closure on US-101 near Burlingame, and a separate run-in involving California Highway Patrol vehicles on Highway 280 in San Francisco.

In its statement, the DMV explicitly labeled Waymo’s freeway operations as an “imminent hazard to public safety,” noting that this isn’t an isolated glitch. Waymo has experienced “recurring incursions into active construction zones, the DMV said, arguing the firm was putting road workers at risk.

It has been revealed that waymo has struggled with freeway operations over the years. The company has been testing its vehicles on California’s freeways since at least August 2024, before eventually opening up to public passengers in November 2025. Waymo voluntarily paused freeway operations in May 2026 over concerns about construction sites — but then resumed rides in late July.

Industry observers note that operating on freeways is crucial to Waymo’s robotaxi business; without freeways, the firm will be forced to take longer routes on local roads that will force customers to pay more for their fares. On average, Waymo rides are already more expensive than human-driven Uber or Lyft trips. A spokesperson for Waymo did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

In order to get back on the freeway, Waymo will need to demonstrate it has taken sufficient action to improve its operation around construction zones, the DMV said. The company will need to submit evidence to the agency for review, at which point regulators will determine whether it can safely resume operations.

  • Framework announced its Wireless Touchpad Keyboard earlier this year with the goal of delivering a better couch keyboarding experience than the Logitech K400.
  • Sources indicate that while the K400 couch keyboard is $35, the Framework Wireless Touchpad Keyboard is $99 with a $50 fully refundable deposit required to preorder one starting today.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Logitech’s K400 may have met its match.﻿.

Logitech’s K400 may have met its match.﻿.

If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

Framework announced its Wireless Touchpad Keyboard earlier this year with the goal of delivering a better couch keyboarding experience than the Logitech K400. According to The Verge’s Sean Hollister who went hands-on with Framework’s new all-in-one keyboard and touchpad last April, the manufacturer has succeeded in that goal, but it turns out you’ll be paying a bit more for Framework’s than Logitech’s.

Sources indicate that while the K400 couch keyboard is $35, the Framework Wireless Touchpad Keyboard is $99 with a $50 fully refundable deposit required to preorder one starting today. That makes it nearly three times more expensive than Logitech’s, but Framework’s upgrades and improvements could make it worth the premium.

Instead of starting from scratch, Framework uses the same keyboard module found in its Laptop 12 paired with a precision 120Hz touchpad and controller that’s also used in all of the organization’s computers. A Bluetooth connection is the easiest way to pair the keyboard to PCs running Windows, Linux, or macOS, or mobile devices, game consoles, and streaming boxes. You can swiftly switch between four wirelessly connected devices with a button press including one that uses an included USB receiver. If you want more responsiveness, you can also tether it to a device with a USB-C cable.

On a full charge of its replaceable 1,200mAh battery the keyboard will run for well over a year with sporadic use. If you’re instead using it for hours every day on a desk, Framework estimates the battery life will be closer to over a month. For customizability and remapping the keyboard’s open source firmware is based on a fork of ZMK.

Siemens Industrial Software Products mstradling Nov 16, 2026 Release DateNovember 17, 2026 DescriptionView CSAFSummaryOn October 21, 2026, the Node.js project released security updates addressing a critical vulnerability in the Brotli decoder bundled with Node.js, commonly referred to as "Node2Shell" (tracked as CVE-2026-111497). The vulnerability is an out-of-bounds write that could allow a remote attacker to cause memory corruption and potentially execute arbitrary code. This advisory covers the status of impact of various Siemens software products. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, we test a lot of TVs here at ZDNET, which means we get to see everything from the most impressive OLED and upcoming Micro RGB models to the most basic entry-level screens. And while we certainly have had our favorites over the past year, so did our readers: the following TVs were purchased by hundreds of readers via links in ZDNET reviews, buying guides, and other content in 2026 so far. (Note that your privacy is protected — we only have access to aggregate data from our user base, and there is no way for us to identify individual people’s purchases).

Most Accurate HDR Color Reproduction.

Some models, like those from Sony, Samsung, and LG, you would expect to see on a list like this, while others — especially the number one choice — are a bit of a dark horse.

Also: Best Black Friday TV deals live now.

Industry observers note that the most popular TV with ZDNET readers so far in 2026 has been the Amazon Fire TV Omni QLED. Unfortunately, it’s no longer in production and has been replaced by the Ember QLED series TV, which offers the same features and viewing experience but with an updated design and a streamlined operating system.

Keep reading below to find out more about the rest of the most popular TV models that ZDNET readers actually bought this year.

Sources indicate that the number-one pick among ZDNET readers is sadly no longer in production. The Amazon Fire TV Omni QLED has been replaced with the updated Ember QLED, which offers the same high-quality picture and audio with more refined smart features and better Alexa integration. The Ember QLED supports Wi-Fi 6 for faster web browsing and fewer buffering stops when streaming, as well as Dolby Vision HDR and adaptive brightness settings for the best viewing experience in almost any lighting.

Review: The Amazon Fire TV Omni QLED is great for gaming, but works just as well with Alexa.

It has been revealed that the Bravia 8 II is an excellent OLED TV that continues to prove why Sony is neck and neck with LG for the title of king of TVs. The updated QD-OLED panel is brighter than its predecessor without sacrificing contrast, color accuracy, or detail. And the 120Hz refresh rate means you’ll get smooth motion in everything from live sports and movies to video games and social media videos.

More: Why I’m recommending the Sony Bravia 8 II over competing OLED TVs – especially to enthusiasts.

Most Accurate HDR Color Reproduction.

Industry observers note that the U8 is Hisense’s flagship Mini LED TV, and the winner of our Lab Award for most accurate HDR color reproduction — beating out several other far more expensive brands. This TV is capable of a maximum brightness of 5,000 nits for the best visibility in almost any lighting environment. It also features a 165Hz refresh rate, making it a great choice for sports fans and console gamers, as well as support for AMD FreeSync Premium Pro VRR to prevent screen tearing. Film buffs can take advantage of both IMAX Enhanced and Filmmaker mode for seeing movies as creators meant them to be seen.

Also: We lab-tested 7 TVs for color accuracy – and the winners weren’t Sony or Samsung.

Recent findings suggest that the Hisense U6 Pro is a solid midrange option that uses a Mini LED panel to create millions of bold, rich colors as well as sharp contrast. It also features an anti-glare display for better visibility, a 144Hz refresh rate, and support for both Dolby Vision HDR and Dolby Atmos virtual surround sound.

The Hisense U7 splits the difference between premium and midrange, offering crisp 4K resolution, bold colors, and rich sound. It supports both Dolby Vision and Dolby Atmos for a more immersive experience, while the 165Hz refresh rate provides ultra-smooth motion. You can also share media from your iOS and Android devices via both AirPlay and Google Cast.

Samsung’s OLED TV options have continuously topped our lists as some of the best TVs you can buy almost since the minute they hit the market. And the S95F is no exception, even though it’s last year’s flagship. It may be a generation behind, but it still gives you plenty of reasons to pick it up, like signature OLED picture quality, object-tracking sound for a more immersive experience without extra speakers, and adaptive sound for the best listening experience in almost any environment.

Review: I tested the Samsung S95F OLED for a week, and I’m ready to give up my living room TV.

The LG C5 is the flagship OLED of 2025, and it’s a very smart choice for anyone who wants cutting-edge picture and audio quality without having to pay the usual premium to get it. You’ll still get great color accuracy, razor-sharp contrast, and ultra-fine details as well as a host of smart features like preloaded streaming apps, voice controls, and screen sharing.

Review: Why last year’s LG C5 OLED is the smartest TV buy right now.

Sony’s entry-level LED TV offers support for both Dolby Vision HDR and Dolby Atmos, a 120Hz refresh rate, 4K resolution, and a suite of preloaded apps like Disney+ and Netflix so you can get started watching your favorite highlights right out of the box. Bluetooth connectivity lets you set up wireless soundbars and subwoofers to create a fully wireless home theater, while AirPlay and Google Cast let you share media from your iOS and Android devices.

Both myself and former ZDNET editor Chris Bayer got to test out the TCL QM8, and we were impressed by what the tech giant had to offer with its flagship TV. With a peak brightness of 5,000 nits, you’ll get excellent visibility in almost any lighting environment — even direct sunlight — while the 5,000 local dimming zones give you OLED-level contrast for sharper image quality.

It has been revealed that the QM8 has a base refresh rate of 120Hz that can be boosted to 144Hz for console gaming, while AMD FreeSync Premium Pro VRR support prevents stuttering and freezing while gaming. The TCL QM8 is available in sizes up to 115 inches, but ZDNET readers most often opt for the 65-, 85-, and 98-inch models for both typical living rooms and dedicated home theaters.

Also: One of the best TVs we lab-tested this year is still one of the most affordable.

Industry observers note that mendix Studio Pro contains multiple vulnerabilities in the MCP Server, that could allow an attacker with network access to interact with the server remotely or trick a user's browser into sending unauthorized requests, potentially leading to unauthorized data access, tool execution, or system compromise. Siemens has released upcoming versions for the affected products and recommends to patch to the latest versions.

The following versions of Siemens Mendix Studio Pro are affected:.

Product Status: known_affected.

MitigationMaintain strict inbound firewall policies (such as Windows Defender Firewall) blocking external traffic on port 7782. This is already the case by default on standard Windows installations. If remote access is required, restrict traffic via a secure, authenticated channel (e.g., a VPN or SSH tunnel) rather than opening direct inbound firewall rules.

Vendor fixUpdate to V11.16.0 or later version.

In order to operate the devices in a protected IT environment, Siemens recommends to configure the environment according to Siemens' operational guidelines for Industrial Security (Download: https://www.siemens.com/cert/operational-guidelines-industrial-security), and to follow the recommendations in the product manuals. Additional information on Industrial Security by Siemens can be found at: https://www.siemens.com/industrialsecurity.

For further inquiries on security vulnerabilities in Siemens products and solutions, please contact the Siemens ProductCERT: https://www.siemens.com/cert/advisories.

The use of Siemens Security Advisories is subject to the terms and conditions listed on: https://www.siemens.com/productcert/terms-of-use.

CISA recommends users take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities.

CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures.

Sources indicate that CISA also provides a section for control systems security recommended practices on the ICS webpage on cisa.gov/ics. Several CISA products detailing cyber defense best practices are available for reading and download, including Improving Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity with Defense-in-Depth Strategies.

CISA encourages organizations to implement recommended cybersecurity strategies for proactive defense of ICS assets.

Additional mitigation guidance and recommended practices are publicly available on the ICS webpage at cisa.gov/ics in the technical information paper, ICS-TIP-12-146-01B--Targeted Cyber Intrusion Detection and Mitigation Strategies.

Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents.

#47. Democrats try to figure out how not to get swept away by the blue wave

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 15m • 📚 Deep Dive (2926 w)
