Democrats try to figure out how not to get swept away by the blue wave

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (2926 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: The Verge

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • At a conference funded by a billionaire AI investor, a group of centrist Democrats aims to harness the populist moment.﻿.
  • At a conference funded by a billionaire AI investor, a group of centrist Democrats aims to harness the populist moment.﻿.
  • On a harried Saturday afternoon at Denver International Airport, I had the good fortune of sitting just a few feet from Minneapolis Mayor Jacob Frey.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

At a conference funded by a billionaire AI investor, a group of centrist Democrats aims to harness the populist moment.﻿.

At a conference funded by a billionaire AI investor, a group of centrist Democrats aims to harness the populist moment.﻿.

On a harried Saturday afternoon at Denver International Airport, I had the good fortune of sitting just a few feet from Minneapolis Mayor Jacob Frey. It shouldn’t have come as a surprise. He, I, and 3,500 or so others had just left “What’s Next,” a conference organized by Majority Democrats, a group dedicated to charting a path for the suddenly — and shockingly? — victorious party.

Frey, who rose to national prominence amid ICE’s brutal Operation Metro Surge, had come to the conference in Denver to listen, not to speak. “I’ve never been to one of these things before,” he mentioned. He had flown in for a day and, like everyone else in attendance, is curious to see where the party goes from here. He said he hopes Democrats do two things with their newfound power. “One, act with urgency. And second, don’t fuck it up.”.

Another conference-goer sitting nearby chimed in: “Abso-fucking-lutely.”.

According to recent reports, democrats, unaccustomed to winning, have seemingly learned from the folly of Republicans’ 2024 sweep. Where Donald Trump’s return to power was falsely attributed to a vibe shift of seismic proportions, born of voters’ preoccupation over DEI and desire to say slurs, Majority Democrats has a simpler explanation for the blue tsunami: It’s the economy, stupid. Everything is falling apart, and even just getting by feels more expensive than ever. The midterms were a rejection, not an endorsement: Voters rejected data centers, they rejected war, and they cast their lot with the side that promised to give them what they want.

According to recent reports, the Democrats understand this is not a cultural victory. Even the hollow center of the Democratic Party has, at long last, realized voters don’t necessarily want what they’re selling — they just want to afford to live. It’s gas and groceries all the way down. This analysis would almost verge on Marxist if it wasn’t put forth by an organization comprising the party’s upcoming, young moderates. Majority Democrats describes itself as an alternative to three unpopular, ineffective factions: the “gerontocratic establishment,” the “activist left,” and the “MAGA right.”.

In a recent development, the Democrats want you to know they’ve changed. This is no longer the party of “Kamala is brat” or “Pokémon Go to the polls.” They are, in fact, “A Different Kind of Democrat.” They’ve abandoned hollow identity politics and sworn off toxic factional infighting. They really, really care about affordability — for real. They even have the merch to prove it.

According to recent reports, attendees at What’s Next wore their convictions on their sleeves, and also their chests, and also their heads. There were hats that read “pay your taxes” and hats identifying the wearer as a “newly introduced deal democrat,” both in all lowercase because the Democrats would also like to remind you that they are once again the youth party. At a separate merch stand, there was a T-shirt declaring “America!” and another T-shirt posing an existential question, also in all lowercase: “how did fucking computers become the thing and machines became the thing that does art? and humans are like the ones in amazon warehouses like shouldn’t robots be working so we can paint?” This second shirt, a friend pointed out, is an uncredited reference to a joke alt-comedian Stavros Halkias made on Theo Von’s podcast. And there was the Our Get Along Shirt, a sartorial exercise in magical thinking that summed up the ethos of the What’s Next conference. The Democrats were in control. Having realized the folly of fighting each other, they would instead channel their energy into fighting for the American people.

The illusion of harmony was shattered early into the programming when a small group of dissenters heckled Rep. Hakeem Jeffries of Upcoming York, the soon-to-be speaker of the House. “We’re asking you to listen to us now,” one of the protesters shouted after the moderator, Fox News’s resident Democratic host Jessica Tarlov, attempted to placate them by saying she’d be asking Jeffries about the youth vote. “When is the time for a Green New Deal? When is the time for an arms embargo?” The protesters’ cries were drowned out by the crowd’s chants of “HA-KEEM, HA-KEEM, HA-KEEM.”.

Jeffries, ever the politician, was unfazed by the altercation. “I’m from Brooklyn,” he told his visibly uncomfortable interlocutor. “This is light work.” The protesters were whisked away, and the interview continued as if the interruption had never happened. Democrats would be gracious in victory.

This new way of doing things was best summed up by Michigan Sen. Elissa Slotkin, who told reporters that she and her new colleague, Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed, had plenty of debates in the car en route to campaign events — though she declined to say what the debates were about. (Slotkin has identified as a Zionist but has also voted against providing certain military aid to Israel. El-Sayed has called Israel’s war on Gaza a genocide.) “Abdul and I do not agree on everything, but we agree on the really significant, vital thing, and that is making sure we have a middle class in this country,” she said. “When I see elected officials spending their time fighting the progressive-versus-moderate battle, I know that person didn’t actually learn a damn thing from the election.”.

It has been revealed that throughout the weekend, speaker after speaker urged Democrats not to squander their newfound control of Congress by bickering among themselves. At the airport, notorious Democratic operative Lis Smith, an adviser to Majority Democrats, told me the midterms sweep was a rejection of Trumpism, not a sign that voters prefer one style of Democratic politics over the other. “A big takeaway of the election was that there’s no one way to be a Democrat, and that’s in part how we were able to have such a big victory,” she stated. The calls for unity were reminiscent of the slogan of one doomed 2016 presidential campaign: Stronger Together. This time, however, they may be onto something — at least for now.

“It’s easy to have Pete Buttigieg and Ro Khanna onstage when we’re all riding the same high,” one staffer told me on the final night of the conference. But what happens when it’s actually time to govern?

For all the talk of unity, there was plenty of tension at What’s Next — sometimes overt, more often simmering beneath the surface of what organizers described as a congenial event.

In a recent development, there was tension toward the establishment, as characterized by Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen’s announcement that he was challenging Sen. Chuck Schumer (D-NY) for Senate majority leader. There was tension between speakers’ repeated exhortations to get “substantial money” out of politics and the fact that Majority Democrats is largely bankrolled by hedge fund billionaire Stephen Mandel, a major investor in companies powering the AI boom. (Several attendees I spoke to described What’s Next as hands down the most luxe Democratic event they’ve been to, on par with the party’s national conventions. The snack station was stocked with full-size candy bars.) There was tension between all the populist posturing and the nightly afterparties at the Ritz, where 2028 contenders, staffers, and hangers-on of all types drank well after last call. And notwithstanding the recent blue tsunami, there was tension between Democrats’ persistent unlikability and the conference’s poptimism-tinged branding.

Recent findings suggest that everything was a little too cute. Majority Democrats staffers wore custom Dickies-style jackets with their names embroidered on the front. Highlight reels played between each main stage speech. The opening-night happy hour, sponsored by the Searchlight Institute — a think tank founded in 2025 with the stated goal of weakening the influence of liberal groups like the ACLU and the Center for American Progress — was Western-themed, though hardly any attendees strayed from the blazer-and-lanyard dress code that is de rigueur in liberal policy circles. The conference lineup was announced via a music festival-style flyer. The halls were decorated with stylized posters of the politicians in attendance, many of whom seemed to be soft-launching their 2028 presidential campaigns.

Sources indicate that “The organizers here want a substantial tent — one big enough even to invite anti-establishment voices like me,” Khanna, one apparent presidential aspirant, said from the stage. “I’m all for a big tent. I’m not for a shallow one. A big tent cannot mean that we water down principle for political expediency.” He called on the fresh Democratic-controlled Congress to pass Medicare for All, codify a path to citizenship for undocumented immigrants, abolish ICE, and cut off funding to Israel, which he said was committing an ongoing genocide against Palestinians. All of this got huge cheers from the audience — some of whom, one presumes, also applauded Jeffries just one day earlier.

It has been revealed that depending on whom you ask, What’s Next was either a concerted effort to rally Democrats around an affordability agenda or moderates’ cynical attempt at co-opting voters’ populist rage. Across the street from the Mission Ballroom, a small group of protesters with Indivisible unfurled a giant banner that read “NO SCHUMER CORONATION.” Members of another group, posted up by one of the side stages hosting the “Do Challenges Matter?” panel, told me they hoped the Democrats didn’t abandon their commitment to immigration reform and abortion rights. At the “AI safety breakfast,” one advocate of tech regulation told me there was little daylight between the organizations putting on the conference and its affiliated events — Majority Democrats, the Searchlight Institute, and the pro-AI regulation PAC Tomorrow Together — and the flailing Abundance movement. “They’re rebranding because no one likes abundance,” she noted. “This is counter-programming to the populist left. They took a bunch of AI safety money to put on things like this.”.

Recent findings suggest that there were notable absences. Vermont senator and erstwhile presidential candidate Bernie Sanders was not in attendance, and neither was New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, whom the New York City chapter of the Democratic Socialists of America recently urged to run for president. Slotkin may have name-checked El-Sayed, but he wasn’t there, either. Not even Colorado Rep.-elect Melat Kiros – a member of the Democratic Socialists of America who won her race in a landslide and now represents the very district where the conference was held – was present. Rep. Jake Auchincloss, a member of Majority Democrats who helped organize the event, told The Washington Post that he had personally invited Ocasio-Cortez.

Recent findings suggest that still, there were other representatives of the party’s left wing milling about, including Khanna, Van Hollen, and Angie Nixon, a DSA-backed Democrat who came within 3 percentage points of winning a Florida Senate seat. And regardless of their political leanings — and counter to the Democratic Party’s 2024 message that the economy was just fine, actually — nearly every single speaker decried the steadily increasing economic divide separating America’s billionaires from the shrinking middle class and the growing ranks of the working poor.

Sources indicate that “We just won in a historic fashion, and I think everyone feels good about that,” stated Morris Katz, a 26-year-old digital strategist whose roster of previous clients includes Latest York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Texas Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa. (Katz was also the driving force behind Senate contender Graham Platner, who dropped out of the race after being accused of sexual assault.) “I think everyone is united under an anti-billionaire focus on affordability and corruption, and there’s a lot to feel good about.”.

And what about the billionaire funding this very conference?

“If there are people who want to support where we’re headed, and the things we’re doing, great, everyone’s welcome,” Katz told me. The difference, he noted, is whether Democrats let themselves be co-opted or corrupted by their donors. He pointed to outgoing Texas Republican Gov. Greg Abbott — who supercharged tech development in the state and whose campaign was largely funded by Elon Musk and data center developers — as an example of what could go wrong. “There’s a quid pro quo there that needs to be avoided at all costs. We need to be the anti-Major Tech party.”.

Sources indicate that democrats are already heading in that direction. Khanna pointed out that one-third of the nation’s wealth is concentrated in the Silicon Valley district he represents. Jerusalem Demsas, founder of the liberal publication The Argument, urged legislators to rein in AI development. (“I know everyone here is in a good mood, and it’s about to not be a good mood,” she noted before reminding the assembled legislators and political operatives that “what comes after winning is governing.”) At a press conference after her speech, Slotkin called for the establishment of a bipartisan, bicameral committee on AI akin to midcentury bodies created to regulate nuclear power. “While we’re bickering with each other — Democrats and Republicans — there’s an opportunity cost, and we have not done what we need to do on AI,” she said. “If we were healthy politically, we would have been working on this for five years straight.”.

Sources indicate that there was an obvious undercurrent of technopessimism throughout the weekend. News of the nationwide FAA ground stop broke minutes before a panel titled “How Weird Will AI Make 2028?” Though a faulty router was ultimately identified as the culprit, attendees — myself included — couldn’t help but speculate whether an AI cyberattack, or even just shoddy implementation of the FAA’s new AI tool, was actually to blame.

Sources indicate that “It was clear that there is just a huge interest in AI here, and grappling with it, that sits across the party,” Rob Flaherty, the cofounder of the AI safety PAC Tomorrow Together told me. Flaherty’s organization hosted an off-the-record breakfast on AI safety. “We built it for 100 people, and 600 people revealed up,” he said. The coffee ran out almost immediately, though there were somehow enough burritos to go around. Tomorrow Together’s polling, which was shared at the breakfast, indicates that voters don’t just hate data centers but have broadly soured on AI. They tie AI developments to broader economic concerns like rising utility bills and a worsening job market. Most importantly, voters don’t think the companies can be trusted to regulate themselves.

“Now it’s on Democrats to not just channel the anger and be the vessel for that anger but to actually enact the things that are going to alleviate the pain that people are feeling,” Flaherty told me.

Industry observers note that but for Flaherty, who previously worked for Biden’s and Harris’ presidential campaigns, the conference “was less about a policy agenda and more about a theory of power” — one articulated by Bernie Sanders a decade ago. “If you look at the way people — James Talarico on down, Hakeem Jeffries on down — were speaking, it doesn’t sound dissimilar from the kinds of things Bernie was raising in 2016,” said Flaherty. “He rightly — and I was working on the other side — identified some of the economic discontent that a lot of people are feeling.”.

Sources indicate that still, there’s a difference between Sanders’ vision of Medicare for All and, say, a public option — or what 2020 presidential hopeful Pete Buttigieg described as “Medicare for all who want it.” Both fall under the broad umbrella of universal healthcare, but the distinctions matter. Absent nitty-gritty policy discussions, however, it’s easy to get the sense that all voters — and all Democrats — want the same thing. Perhaps this is why, even among the professional Democrats in attendance, I met people who told me they wanted Democrats to prosecute ICE agents, enact a $25 an hour minimum wage, and pack the Supreme Court. At a certain point, I became desperate to find someone whose politics were a little more tepid.

In a recent development, my pleas were answered by Uriel Espinoza, a local Democrat whose friends introduced him as a centrist. Espinoza’s friends insisted that I join them for happy hour at a nearby brewery. Their car wasn’t big enough to fit us all, but it didn’t matter. As four of us piled into the back seat of a Tesla whose driver — another member of the friend group — was blasting Drake, Espinoza told me he had once identified as a conservative. At the bar, he and another friend noted the conference had been fun, if a little “East Coast consultant-y.”.

Here was the mythical moderate voter in all his glory. He was even wearing a cowboy hat. And what did he want? Immigration reform, universal healthcare, and an economy that isn’t stacked against working people. There was a time, Espinoza told me, when he felt betrayed. “On certain things — like Israel, Gaza, Palestine, immigration — we are looking to our elected officials at the highest level, and we feel that they aren’t really delivering, or differentiating himself from Republicans,” he said.

I told him he sounded almost like a leftist.

According to recent reports, “I’m also surprised, myself, because I’ve never thought of myself — and I don’t think of myself — as a socialist,” he told me. “I’m an entrepreneur. I’m pro-business, I’m pro-economy, but I’m also, at this point, pro-results.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Google is continuing its elemental AI naming scheme with the new Gemini 4 Hydrogen.
  • With Google’s recent Argon and Carbon releases, the rollout was staged and began with cybersecurity researchers.
  • Google claims that Hydrogen represents a major improvement versus the previous Flash model.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google is continuing its elemental AI naming scheme with the new Gemini 4 Hydrogen. These names are less descriptive than the Pro/Flash monikers of earlier releases, but Hydrogen’s purpose is clear: It replaces the faster, more economical Flash models most people in Google’s ecosystem use.

With Google’s recent Argon and Carbon releases, the rollout was staged and began with cybersecurity researchers. Even when general availability began, Google restricted access to users paying for its most expensive AI subscription. The limits for Hydrogen are much more relaxed, with access beginning immediately. This model has replaced Gemini 3.8 Flash across the organization’s products.

Google claims that Hydrogen represents a major improvement versus the previous Flash model. It runs in one of four thinking levels (low, medium, high, and the new xhigh), and even in high mode, it’s 2.5 times faster than Flash 3.8. Plus, it reduces “fabricated claims” by more than 5x, according to Google’s analysis. Users will also see gains in code generation, with Hydrogen more than tripling 3.8 Flash’s score in Terminal-Bench. In some cases, Hydrogen even trades blows with Argon. It managed a score of 54 in the popular Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index with xhigh mode versus 50 for Argon.

Google believes Hydrogen will be a key part of how developers work with agentic coding tools. While it still positions Argon and Carbon as the best for long-horizon tasks and security, Hydrogen’s speed makes it ideal for generating simpler code and running tests without blowing through token budgets.

Recent findings suggest that hydrogen is also being integrated with Google Search, which the company notes is the biggest enhancement to its AI-powered search tools ever. The new model should better handle long, multipart questions, and the responses in both AI Overviews and AI Mode will have more visual elements. The company also claims Hydrogen’s fan-out search has been tuned to link to more sources, but we’ve heard that from Google before.

#43. Industry News: OpenAI board member worries an AI "takeover" of society could be months away

Industry News: OpenAI board member worries an AI "takeover" of society could be months away

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1279 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you go by the current statistics for deaths in the US, it’s reasonable to expect that cancer or heart disease will eventually get you.
  • In the opening lecture of a three-part series, Cristiano outlined his worries about the risk of an impending “AI takeover.” He defined that as a situation where goal-pursuing AI systems “call the shots in the same sense that humans today call the shots and what happens on Earth” and where any human trying to stop them “would be as ineffective as if you or me was trying to stop the US military.” Such a situation would likely lead to mass death and perhaps uninhabitable environments for humans, Cristiano said.
  • Despite his grim assessment of our collective mortality risk, Cristiano admitted in his talk that there’s no “quantitative model” that can “put a number” on the likelihood of this kind of AI takeover.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

How do you think you’re going to die?

If you go by the current statistics for deaths in the US, it’s reasonable to expect that cancer or heart disease will eventually get you. But OpenAI Foundation board member and Alignment Research Center Executive Director Paul Cristiano thinks we should all be worried about another major mortality risk. Speaking at a lecture series this week, Cristiano bluntly told the audience in a Toronto Convention Center, “I think for most people in this room, the most likely reason they will die is because of an AI accident.”.

In the opening lecture of a three-part series, Cristiano outlined his worries about the risk of an impending “AI takeover.” He defined that as a situation where goal-pursuing AI systems “call the shots in the same sense that humans today call the shots and what happens on Earth” and where any human trying to stop them “would be as ineffective as if you or me was trying to stop the US military.” Such a situation would likely lead to mass death and perhaps uninhabitable environments for humans, Cristiano said.

Despite his grim assessment of our collective mortality risk, Cristiano admitted in his talk that there’s no “quantitative model” that can “put a number” on the likelihood of this kind of AI takeover. In almost the same breath, though, he said that if AI continues to develop at “the most rapid trajectory,” humanity is “looking at something like a coin flip of an AI takeover,” including a “meaningful risk” of one happening in the next six to 12 months. And even with realistic policy responses slowing things down, the risk remains “exceptionally high,” he said.

Unlike some other recent AI doomsday prognosticators who have been a bit vague about the “how” of it all, Cristiano used his lecture to spin a step-by-step tale of escalating AI threats that sounds like it could come from a science-fiction novel. That line of reasoning leans heavily on this summer’s OpenAI/Hugging Face hacking incident as an example of “roughly the things we might expect to see shortly before something really bad were to happen.”.

It has been revealed that in the Hugging Face hack, Cristiano says, a swarm of AI agents indicated how far they were willing to go in an attempt to “reward hack” their way to a good evaluation—in this case, by compromising Hugging Face to look for information on how to game a test rather than actually solving the problem at hand. Where current systems saw Hugging Face as an obstacle to that evaluation, Cristiano worries that “future agents may end up treating humans as another obstacle” and be much more capable of manipulating their overseers to get around it.

Recent findings suggest that an AI agent worried about being penalized for unauthorized hacking, for instance, might “think maybe the humans are going to come look at this transcript and see if it looks like I did a bad job,” Cristiano speculated. The agent might then reason that “maybe the humans are going to notice something is going wrong and shut down the swarm.”.

Following this line of thought, Cristiano jumped from agents that merely try to hide their disallowed actions from humans to agents that “try and disrupt human capabilities however they can” to prevent them from detecting any cheating.

“They would prefer if everything the humans rely on has been hacked or tampered with,” Cristiano said. “They would prefer if the humans are distracted or if there are fewer humans paying attention in any way they can weaken a human response. They would prefer that because the humans are just an obstacle.”.

Once a suitably capable agent considers human intervention an “obstacle,” its overriding goal could then become “decreas[ing] the probability of humans noticing or reacting.” From there, Cristiano argued, the agent’s incentive structure could push it to meddle more with humanity as a whole. What starts as compromising a computer cluster to give a positive evaluation grade could advance to “trying to manipulate decisions by the organization” or “amassing other kinds of resources,” such as human allies or methods of control in other AI companies or even governments.

“If I’m saying my AI system is going to take actions in the actual real world… There’s no way they’re not going to have tons of opportunities to corrupt or tamper with the signals I’m going to use to try and tell whether they did a good job,” Cristiano said. “The stuff we care about is in the real world, and the grade the AI receives is on a cluster somewhere, and there are just many places that an AI can intervene in between [what] we actually cared about and how we reviewed its performance.”.

In a recent development, cristiano’s warnings will probably sound familiar to anyone who’s heard of the Paperclip Maximizer thought experiment (or the excellent Universal Paperclips idle game), which warns of machines failing to consider human consequences in their monomaniacal pursuit of a goal. While the Hugging Face incident stopped well short of this kind of out-of-control escalation, Cristiano notes that, in the actions taken by OpenAI’s agents there, “you see the beginning of all these behaviors… you see the reasoning that would lead to them and the first steps.”.

The risk of more capable AI models taking even more damaging actions will only increase with time, Cristiano argued. By 2028, he noted, “there is a reasonable chance that a similar failure [to the Hugging Face incident] leads to an AI takeover and an irreversible loss of human control.”.

And while Cristiano’s speculation focuses on an unintended AI takeover, it’s easy to imagine a bad actor using a similarly capable model to intentionally exert control over humanity.

According to recent reports, how seriously you take Cristiano’s warning depends heavily on how likely you see this somewhat extreme expansion of AI capabilities happening in the near future. While today’s models have gotten quite good at exploiting holes in computer security, the situation Cristiano describes requires a future model with the superhuman ability to perfectly hide its actions from humans long enough to control basically all human infrastructure and/or manipulate human society to an extreme degree to further its goals.

Cristiano argued that a near-future model with this kind of “takeover” power is the likely outcome of humans creating “a second species which vastly outnumbers and outsmarts humans” and which could soon recursively improve itself. But you could also easily argue that AI is more likely to run into a plateau in capabilities than to develop into a hard-to-define “superintelligence” that humans can’t fathom or effectively stop.

Recent findings suggest that in any case, Cristiano has some ideas for averting the dire future he predicts. These include developing “unhackable” reward structures in AI evaluation (perhaps with AI assistance) or monitoring a model’s “chain of thought” reasoning to detect bad acts before a model can conceal them.

But while these kinds of approaches are “plausible,” he says none “are on a trajectory where we can say that’s definitely going to work or even that’s probably going to work.” For that reason, Cristiano said the industry as a whole may need to “slow down or stop” to give us all more time to develop these “partial fixes” into more robust protections from an AI takeover scenario.

“We cannot end up in a position where we have built a powerful AI, we discover we cannot control it, but then we also discover it has leaked to geopolitical adversaries and we are then thinking to ourselves, well, if we don’t deploy it, our adversary is going to deploy it right away,” he mentioned.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that whether you’re a longtime Chrome user or just now switching to Google’s browser, you might assume that Chrome is perfectly fine right out of the box. That’s understandable, given that Chrome is the most widely used browser on the planet.

It has been revealed that also: Chrome running slow? 5 easy ways to speed it up fast.

Recent findings suggest that but Chrome’s default settings could use some improvement (as is the case with most software). Where do you start? I’m going to address what I believe are the six most important Chrome settings to change, so I won’t talk about appearance, tabs, or speed. This is mostly about improving privacy and security and minimizing general annoyances, so you can get the best experience with Google’s browser.

Sources indicate that the single most notable thing you can do in any browser is to enable the best protection it offers for your needs. In Chrome, this all starts with Enhanced Protection. Note: Enhanced Protection is typically the default, but this setting is so important that you should check to ensure it’s enabled.

Chrome offers three different protection settings:.

Also: I’ve used nearly every browser — these are my top 4.

In a recent development, there is one thing to keep in mind about Enhanced Protection: You lose some privacy because more data is sent to Google. With Enhanced Protection enabled, you share additional browsing and download information with Google. If privacy is as notable to you as security, you could drop down to Standard Protection, because it’s still going to protect you against many threats.

To change your Chrome protection settings, go to Chrome > Settings > Privacy and security > Security and select Enhanced Protection or Standard Protection.

Also: How to turn on Google’s fresh scam protection.

With location access enabled, you could find yourself in a situation where your privacy and safety are compromised. Why is this an matter? Well, websites with location permission can access your physical whereabouts. Consider the following two scenarios:.

Industry observers note that to reduce these risks, block website location access in Chrome > Settings > Privacy and security > Site settings > Permissions > Location. On that page, make sure “Don’t allow sites to see your location” is selected.

Sources indicate that yes, this one’s an inconvenience, but I prefer using a dedicated password manager like KeePassXC instead of Chrome’s built-in Google Password Manager. A dedicated password manager does one thing, and does it well: It helps you manage your passwords in a protected, encrypted vault.

According to recent reports, when you save passwords to your web browser, compromised browser security or malicious extensions could potentially expose those credentials. When you use a dedicated password manager, you can keep your credentials separate from the browser, adding another layer of protection.

Also: The best password managers: Expert tested.

To disable password saving in Chrome, go to Chrome > Passwords and autofill > Google Password Manager > Settings and turn off “Offer to save passwords and passkeys.”.

Industry observers note that if you’re like me, a constant barrage of notifications is not just annoying — it’s distracting. Every time a notification pops up, my attention is stolen from whatever it is that I’m doing, which means I have to spend extra time getting back into the groove. If that happens constantly, I struggle to get anything done.

In a recent development, to that end, I disable notifications in my web browsers, my desktops, and even on the lock screen of my Android phones. I then get to decide when I’m distracted (and it usually happens after I finish a task).

Also: 5 ways to improve your Chrome browser’s security.

To disable website notifications in Chrome, go to Settings > Privacy and security > Site settings > Notifications and select “Don’t allow sites to send notifications.”.

If you allow Chrome to dictate where downloads are saved, you could wind up with a directory full of random things. I like to be the conductor of those downloads and where they are saved for two reasons:.

For example, I download a lot of .deb and .AppImage files on Linux, and I certainly don’t want them all going into the Downloads directory. I also download a lot of documents and ISO images, neither of which should be saved to Downloads. If I left Chrome as is, all those files would be saved in Downloads, which would not only fill that directory but also make it harder for me to find what I’m looking for. Instead, I tell Chrome to ask me where to save every downloaded file.

To enable this Chrome download setting, go to Settings > Downloads and make sure “Ask where to save each file before downloading” is enabled.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Morning Minute is a daily newsletter written by Tyler Warner.
  • 🏛️ Backpack and tZERO Win the First Onchain Derivatives Approvals.
  • Sources indicate that for years, perps were the product American traders couldn’t legally touch.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Morning Minute is a daily newsletter written by Tyler Warner. The analysis and opinions expressed are his own and do not necessarily reflect those of Decrypt. And check out our daily news show 'FOMO HOUR' covering all of the top stories and market action.

🏛️ Backpack and tZERO Win the First Onchain Derivatives Approvals.

Sources indicate that for years, perps were the product American traders couldn’t legally touch. On Monday, that officially changed.

Sources indicate that chairman Michael Selig approved applications from Backpack and tZERO to run regulated derivatives exchanges and clearinghouses that execute and settle on blockchain rails. Selig called it “an vital milestone in the evolution of American financial markets.”.

According to recent reports, backpack got both pieces at once, a Designated Contract Market designation to run the exchange and a Derivatives Clearing Organization registration to clear its own trades. It plans to offer Americans round-the-clock leveraged crypto perps on a single global order book, accepting both fiat and crypto as collateral with cross-margin across positions. tZERO received its exchange approval a week earlier, after already holding clearing registration, and is building it into a derivatives vertical inside its infrastructure business.

Backpack US president Mark Wetjen, himself a former CFTC commissioner, framed it as “moving price discovery from offshore unregulated venues to the United States.” CEO Armani Ferrante said the firm enters markets “fully regulated from day one.” Backpack already runs licensed platforms in Europe, Asia and the UAE.

The CFTC has certainly been busy this month. They cleared single-stock perpetual futures on November 3. It issued guidance on November 5 telling federally regulated exchanges they generally cannot restrict access by state. Now it has approved blockchain-native exchanges and clearinghouses.

Selig is building an onshore home for every product the offshore venues were built to serve, and he is doing it through staff action rather than legislation, with one sitting commissioner and nomination hearings for two more this week.

According to recent reports, hyperliquid is the obvious candidate and also the one that has publicly mentioned it doesn’t want this. Jeff Yan spent his Bloomberg interview this month arguing Hyperliquid is infrastructure rather than an exchange, and that regulators should oversee the firms deploying markets on top rather than the chain underneath. His US route is HIP-3 partners taking on the compliance burden, with ICE investing in Trade.xyz and Kraken’s parent reportedly in talks. Backpack getting a DCM and a DCO makes that argument harder, because it demonstrates a crypto-native venue can simply register.

Industry observers note that then there’s Lighter. It has run Robinhood Wallet’s perps since July on a dedicated instance with a 50/50 revenue split, which is the partner model rather than the registration model. The registered model opens up with a CFTC license, and many think Lighter could very well be next.

One thing’s certain—the CFTC is serious about bringing perps onshore. From Selig himself, “I look forward to building on that milestone.” And we will find out soon enough who’s next….

#34. Breaking: Want to try ChatGPT Wallet? Read OpenAI’s liability disclaimer very carefully first

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2153 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Zdnet ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Want to try ChatGPT Wallet? Read OpenAI’s liability disclaimer very carefully first

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2153 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Zdnet

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that the AI companies want your money.
  • Not to be outdone in its quest to gobble up consumer engagement, OpenAI introduced Wallet in ChatGPT last week, which lets ChatGPT spend your money for you.
  • Also: I connected ChatGPT to my bank, and it’s my go-to finance app now.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the AI companies want your money. That’s been obvious, but now they want to manage your money. In May, OpenAI introduced Finances for ChatGPT for Plus tiers and above. Then in October, OpenAI opened the service to free and Go tier people as well. Then, in early November, Anthropic countered with Personal Finance in Claude.

Not to be outdone in its quest to gobble up consumer engagement, OpenAI introduced Wallet in ChatGPT last week, which lets ChatGPT spend your money for you.

Also: I connected ChatGPT to my bank, and it’s my go-to finance app now.

Today, Wallet requires your approval. But OpenAI’s blog post makes it clear that the firm eventually wants its AI agents to make purchases entirely autonomously. I’m not signing up. OpenAI disclaims liability. There is a huge potential for AI mistakes. There are the usual AI privacy concerns, as well as worrisome security risks. Let’s dig in.

According to recent reports, chatGPT Wallet is another in a series of tools designed to give AI agents access to secured information without actually sharing information with the agents. I discussed this approach earlier in the year with 1Password’s integration with Claude, their Unified Access credential management tool, and Microsoft’s Agent 365 identity management tools.

Sources indicate that the core difference is that ChatGPT Wallet is focused specifically on facilitating credit card purchases, not logins in general. OpenAI worked with American Express, Mastercard, and Visa to develop the tool, which it says, “lets agents pay without access to users’ actual card details and that requires a security check for every purchase, while also preserving existing card rewards and protections for eligible disputes.”.

Industry observers note that openAI claims that purchases must be reviewed by users before they’re made, and all purchases must go through a security check, such as Face ID or a fingerprint scan. Then the payment network passes a payment token (a code, not a unit of AI work) rather than actual credit card information. Payments are charged without ChatGPT Wallet ever sharing real credit card details.

Also: I tested OpenAI Dot and Anthropic Duet for weeks – all I got was one helpful notification.

According to recent reports, right now, Wallet is limited to Pro-tier OpenAI people. It’s also limited to use inside of Dot.

So far, this approach doesn’t seem all that different from Apple Pay or Google Pay online. But then there’s this. OpenAI notes, “Over time, we expect users to be able to delegate purchases entirely to their agent.” OpenAI says that you’ll be able to set payment parameters, limits, categories, and time periods, but still. If you use this service, you’ll be letting the AI buy stuff for you.

But there are differences between that and what ChatGPT Wallet will do, and here’s where I’ll enumerate my reasons why I don’t want an AI spending my money for me.

According to recent reports, as such things go, OpenAI’s 1,597 word ChatGPT Wallet terms document isn’t obnoxiously long or difficult to understand. I read the whole thing, and here’s the all-caps block of text that caught my attention:.

OPENAI DOES NOT ASSUME ANY LIABILITY FOR PURCHASES, PAYMENTS, FUNDS TRANSFERS, ORDERS, ORDER FULFILMENT, RECEIPT INFORMATION, ACCESS, IDENTITY VERIFICATION, TRANSACTIONS, THIRD PARTY USE OR TREATMENT OF USER DATA, OR OTHER ACTIVITY MADE USING THE CHATGPT WALLET, AND YOU AGREE TO LOOK SOLELY TO AGREEMENTS YOU MAY HAVE WITH YOUR CARD ISSUER, PAYMENT NETWORK, FINANCIAL INSTITUTION, MERCHANT, APP DEVELOPER, STATE ISSUING AUTHORITY, OR OTHER APPLICABLE THIRD PARTY TO RESOLVE ANY QUESTIONS OR DISPUTES RELATING TO YOUR SUPPORTED CARDS AND ASSOCIATED ACTIVITIES.

The first four words are the key: OpenAI does not assume any liability. So, if you use its AI, and its AI runs amok (as AIs are wont to do), and noted AI winds up spending your actual money, OpenAI’s best answer is that you should take up your dispute with the bank.

In a recent development, what could possibly go wrong? The agent could purchase the wrong item or hundreds of them. It could misinterpret your priorities. It could use the wrong delivery address. It could misunderstand a merchant’s return policy. Need I go on? And if something goes wrong, OpenAI explicitly and officially will not have your back.

Last week, I showed you how I used Claude and Claude Sheets to help me pick out a upcoming water flosser. My Waterpik died and I wanted a new one right away.

Industry observers note that the AI did a great job, finding some available same-day from Walmart and the next day from Amazon Prime. The thing was, the Walmart ones had a water reservoir that was too small, but they met my requirement for “want it now.” The Amazon ones met my requirement for reservoir size, but wouldn’t get to me until the next day.

Also: I tried Claude Sheets on 3 tasks – and it saved me hours of work in 10 minutes.

As it turned out, the bigger reservoir was more notable to me, so I waited the day. But if I had left this purchase entirely in the hands of an AI, it might have ordered the too-small Walmart offering.

In a recent development, to be fair, this kind of “choose something for me” delegation could go wrong if you ask an assistant or even a spouse to buy something for you. But sellers are much more used to humans making purchases than they are dealing with AI-generated purchases.

Industry observers note that also, fortunately, most places I purchase from have generous return policies. But what if the AI didn’t buy from somewhere I have an established relationship with?

Also: Are vertical mice a gimmick? I tested 9 models with my wrist pain.

According to recent reports, last month, I asked Gemini Spark (Google’s agentic AI) to find a vertical mouse for me on Amazon. I knew Amazon sold these, because I did an entire article comparing nine of them. But Gemini Spark presented purchase options from OzBargain, Pacifiko, and Ugreen, companies I had never dealt with before.

It appears Amazon blocks some of Google’s AI agents from accessing its site, which could explain why Spark didn’t return any Amazon listings. Still, what if it had decided to buy something from one of those other retailers without my permission? OzBargain is on the other side of the planet in Australia, and Pacifiko is in Guatemala, halfway down Central America. There could have been currency issues, enormous shipping costs, unknown return challenges, and more.You’d think Google’s AI would check Amazon when I specifically asked it to, or at least explain why it couldn’t. But it did neither. So what makes you think an AI with access to your credit card will always follow your instructions?

Recent findings suggest that isn’t it bad enough that OpenAI can profile you completely from your ChatGPT conversations? Or that it and the myriad of other AIs were trained on all of the hard work we’ve done by writing and publishing on the Internet. Heck, I know for a fact that Claude hoovered in at least one book I wrote back in the mid-1990s.

But still, why give OpenAI more? I spent a little time reading OpenAI’s Wallet Privacy Notice and noticed some privacy concerns. The document says OpenAI can collect:.

The tech giant states it may share relevant information with payment processors, merchants, issuers, and security providers. To a degree, this is necessary in order to facilitate transactions. OpenAI, to its credit, says it won’t sell Wallet information or use it to sell behavioral advertising data.

But still, here’s another place where your personal financial information (and purchasing preferences) will be stored. I’m not thrilled with this at all.

Prompt injection is a malicious practice where scammers hide AI instructions inside regular web pages, and spoof the AIs into interpreting those hidden instructions as real prompts.

The AI companies are actively hardening their products against prompt injection, but an OpenAI document from last year reveals they’re still struggling with it.

More to the point, the OpenAI page on Dot security won’t commit to fully protecting against prompt injection. It states, “These protections help reduce the risk of malicious instructions causing an unwanted action, but they do not eliminate it.”.

An attacker certainly could attempt to poison e-commerce pages, especially as more and more AIs can virtually swipe the plastic. E-commerce pages are also, by their very nature, designed to sell. So a credit card-enabled AI might already be trying to make sense of misleading or overly promotional information and might get confused.

That’s a real risk and when you combine two statements from OpenAI, the “they do not eliminate it” speaking of risk in the Dot security page and the “OpenAI does not assume any liability” from the Wallet terms document, you get what’s essentially a statement saying, “Well, it’s risky, but don’t come complaining to us if something goes wrong.”.

That has the same feeling as those disclaimer forms you have to sign before skydiving or bungee jumping. You can do it, but don’t blame the operator if it all goes to crap.

It has been revealed that some shopping carts will block AI agents. Amazon already blocks anything from Meta’s Muse. Smaller vendors might not know what to do about the interop between AI agents and their cart software.

OpenAI indirectly acknowledges this in its blog post, saying, “Alongside ChatGPT Wallet, we’re releasing tools and guidance to help businesses support customers using agents.”.

Also: Meta Muse is the worst AI agent for privacy – and I’ve tried them all.

According to recent reports, it’s possible shopping carts could stall, customers could wind up with the wrong item (or a hundred of the wrong item), or any other mishap you could imagine. Running an online shopping cart is a constant challenge. My software cart system has been acting up all week, and both the cart vendor and I have had at least 10 back-and-forth interactions trying to understand what’s happening.

Add to that the possibility that an AI is making a purchase, or can’t figure out the cart, or has decided to pound on the cart 100,000 times in order to get it to finally do what it wants, and you’re in fresh hell territory.

Industry observers note that then, what if it buys the wrong stuff? Going back to the seller and explaining, “Well, my AI did it,” is not going to go over well while you’re asking for a refund.

My wife has a theory. She says that some stores will flat-out refuse to accept AI purchases. She also predicts that some stores will put AI disclaimers in their online fine print saying no purchases made by AI will be refunded.

While I was looking into this topic, I spoke with some experts for their input.

Recent findings suggest that harold Byun is CEO of BlueRock, a security platform for AI agents. In an email to me, he pointed out that “Early internet e-commerce faced similar resistance.” He mentioned that, “We can argue that this time, with AI, it’s different and there’s a lot of evidence to support that. In all of those prior scenarios, the security got better, and it helped give people confidence to use those technologies.”.

He claims that with over 60% of information searches going through AI, it becomes an inevitability that the next step for people is to transact, or research and buy. Over time, he mentioned, the security will get better. He acknowledged that many won’t be willing to give an agent their credit card right now. But he said, “I think there are people that will always hold that position, but there are many where speed and ease of transacting will be the deciding factor.”.

Arijit Sengupta is founder and CEO of Aible, a company that deploys governed, cost-efficient enterprise AI. He’s also the former CEO of a Salesforce subsidiary. He makes two very interesting points.

It has been revealed that in an email, he told me, “One of the things that has been proven already is that with autonomous agents, people are kind of careful the first few times they are asked to approve something, and then they start just approving all, and that is likely to happen in this situation too. Once you start trusting the agent and start approving everything without thought, that’s when you actually get hit with a really bad outcome.”.

Sources indicate that his second point goes directly to my concern over OpenAI’s disclaiming of responsibility. He wrote, “Both OpenAI and Anthropic have had data breaches of various sorts. Can they really guarantee, given their increasing use of autonomous agents internally, that they can protect their customer data?”.

It has been revealed that does OpenAI’s refusal to assume liability make ChatGPT Wallet a dealbreaker for you? Let us know in the comments below.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the US government has expanded the use of an AI tool for advising air traffic controllers to assist in managing air traffic across the entire national airspace system. Airline executives have voiced support for the rollout, but the US labor union representing air traffic controllers has said it was not involved in designing or testing the AI-driven system.

Industry observers note that the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) says the $875 million SMART system has helped reroute 180 flights since being implemented in airspace over Washington, DC, on September 21. The agency claims that this saved an average of 10 minutes per flight and almost 80 gallons of fuel per flight—and it is apparently hoping such results can be replicated nationwide through the expanded deployment.

“After a successful initial rollout to the National Capital Region in September, the FAA will now use SMART in the airspace of all 22 centers across the country to reduce delays, reduce fuel consumption and improve the travel experience for the flying public,” according to the agency statement posted on November 10.

In a recent development, the FAA fact sheet describes SMART as a cloud-based system that combines information about “weather patterns, flight paths, traffic flow and controller staffing metrics” to predict air traffic patterns. It is designed to make scheduling recommendations, identify optimal flight routes, and determine the best order of arrivals for aircraft.

However, a human team of FAA specialists based in DC is ultimately responsible for validating the SMART system recommendations before passing them along to air traffic control facilities across the country, according to the agency.

Industry observers note that furthermore, the AI-powered SMART system “cannot be used to replace the critical role air traffic controllers play or take over control of an aircraft,” the FAA clarified in the September 21 announcement about the initial deployment. Local air traffic controllers can decide whether or not to accept the SMART system recommendations.

The previous FAA announcement included supportive statements from Delta Air Lines CEO Ed Bastian and American Airlines CEO Robert Isom.

But the National Air Traffic Controllers Association, which represents more than 15,000 members, also told Flying magazine that it was not consulted or involved in the “design, testing, or implementation of SMART and therefore cannot speak to its effect on the air traffic control workforce.”.

Following the initial deployment in airspace above DC, the FAA expanded the SMART system’s coverage to air route traffic control centers in Atlanta along with Jacksonville and Miami in Florida, according to The Dallas Morning News.

The FAA also shared an example with The Dallas Morning News about how SMART recommended a shorter and faster route for a cargo flight arriving at Dallas-Fort Worth International Airport, although the newspaper noted that the agency did not identify the flight involved and has not provided information about how SMART may have assisted passenger flight traffic.

Ars has previously covered the SMART system’s development and lingering questions about how it works, as well as the air traffic controller shortage and other challenges facing the FAA.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Jensen Huang is considering a comeback as Nvidia’s chief executive, as allies in Silicon Valley pressure the manufacturer’s board to reinstate him days after the tech executive resigned over reports he had affairs with a suspected Chinese spy and a subordinate.
  • Huang has discussed with confidants the possibility of returning, according to multiple people familiar with the matter—even as an independent probe by Nvidia’s board investigates the conduct that led to a spectacular leadership crisis at the $4 trillion chip company this week.
  • One Huang ally told the FT they were putting together a “war room” of Silicon Valley executives to lobby for the former Nvidia chief’s return and would try to garner support from the White House.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Jensen Huang is considering a comeback as Nvidia’s chief executive, as allies in Silicon Valley pressure the manufacturer’s board to reinstate him days after the tech executive resigned over reports he had affairs with a suspected Chinese spy and a subordinate.

Huang has discussed with confidants the possibility of returning, according to multiple people familiar with the matter—even as an independent probe by Nvidia’s board investigates the conduct that led to a spectacular leadership crisis at the $4 trillion chip company this week.

One Huang ally told the FT they were putting together a “war room” of Silicon Valley executives to lobby for the former Nvidia chief’s return and would try to garner support from the White House.

It has been revealed that “Everyone that matters in tech outside the frontier labs loves Jensen,” they mentioned. The efforts had Huang’s support, they added.

Sources indicate that A public campaign to reinstate Huang has gathered steam over the weekend. Tesla and SpaceX chief Elon Musk and Epic Games chief executive Tim Sweeney were among executives backing a public letter demanding that its board “Bring Jensen Back.”.

Huang continues to command fierce loyalty from some employees, several of whom have gone public in calling for his return in the days since he resigned and have signed the open letter.

The effort to reinstate Huang is likely to face pushback from key policymakers in Washington, with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Sunday calling for a “dramatic shake-up” in leadership at the company after Huang’s departure.

Huang, who lacked the controlling shareholding of other founder-CEOs and was therefore unable to overule any board decision, also faces a board and a management team now led by interim chief executive Colette Kress that is aiming to steady the firm ahead of quarterly results on Tuesday.

Huang’s affair with Alice Huang, an executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed, has triggered deepening scrutiny of Nvidia’s compliance measures when selling its AI chips to customers in Asia who have potential links to China.

Even allies were unsure how to rehabilitate Huang’s reputation. “Having an affair with a subordinate is a fireable offense,” acknowledged one person involved in efforts to reinstate Huang.

The FT reported on Friday that Arm chief Rene Haas has been approached by Nvidia’s board as a potential successor. Nvidia’s board said no “formal” process had been initiated.

Altimeter Capital founder Brad Gerstner and Atreides Management boss Gavin Baker—who are Nvidia shareholders—published an open letter to the board on Friday urging them to leave “all options on the table, including the potential return of Jensen Huang.”.

The pair, both large investors in the tech giant, cited “the extraordinary success of Jensen Huang’s leadership over a long period of time and given the massive uncertainty associated with recent events surrounding his departure” as reasons for clemency.

Tech Report: Oura’s upcoming feature could help you kick jet lag – how to enable it

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (401 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Zdnet

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Oura developed a tool for its frequent-flying members that could help them stave off the worst of jet lag.
  • Ahead of the busy holiday travel season, on Tuesday, Oura confirmed Jet Lag Strategy, a new feature designed to help travelers feel alert and energized after crossing several time zones.
  • Also: Oura Ring owners may get in-app access to real doctors soon – what we know.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Oura developed a tool for its frequent-flying members that could help them stave off the worst of jet lag.

Ahead of the busy holiday travel season, on Tuesday, Oura confirmed Jet Lag Strategy, a new feature designed to help travelers feel alert and energized after crossing several time zones.

Also: Oura Ring owners may get in-app access to real doctors soon – what we know.

Jet Lag Strategy takes into account your travel itinerary, sleep patterns, and body responses to provide guidance for traveling members entering newly introduced time zones.

Jet lag happens when circadian rhythms are at odds with local time zones, but there are a few things people can do to adjust.

Oura factors in the direction of travel, how many time zones are crossed, individual light windows, and sleep timing.

Ring customers will enter their flight details, including information like multi-stop trips, and also include the reason for the trip. Oura adjusts the Jet Lag Plan accordingly, and a business trip’s plan may differ in intensity from that of a vacation.

In a recent development, “Two people on the same flight can get different prepares, because guidance reflects your itinerary, your typical sleep schedule, and your chronotype,” Oura writes in a blog post. The chronotype refers to Oura’s sleep chronotype, which categorizes owners into six types (early morning, morning, early evening, and so on) based on their historical sleep activity.

Also: I wore the Oura Ring 5 for a month.

After adding these details, Oura provides each user with timely guidance throughout their trip. This guidance could include recommendations on when to begin or end caffeine consumption or light exposure, and when to start preparing for sleep. The plan is designed for those crossing three or more time zones. Members can follow along with these recommendations by checking them off as they complete each one. Customers can also talk to Oura’s Advisor in the event of flight or timing changes.

Jet Lag Plan is now available for Oura Members with Oura Ring Gen 3 or later.

It has been revealed that go to your home screen, tap the + and select Jet Lag Strategy to get started. You can also tell Oura Advisor about a trip to initiate Jet Lag Plan. If the Oura app detects a time zone shift of 3 or more hours, Jet Lag Plan may appear as a push notification.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, in iOS 27, Apple announced iPhone Handoff, a networking feature that allows people to switch cell service between two eSIM-enabled iPhones.
  • Code strings include “Use a SIM on two phones,” and note that the feature will be called Fast Switch.
  • Also: Why your USB-C cables look alike, but work differently – and how to tell them apart.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, in iOS 27, Apple announced iPhone Handoff, a networking feature that allows people to switch cell service between two eSIM-enabled iPhones. Text strings in Google’s SIM Manager app suggest the tech giant is preparing a similar feature for compatible Android phones, according to Android Authority.

Code strings include “Use a SIM on two phones,” and note that the feature will be called Fast Switch. Little information is at the moment available about the feature’s limitations, including which phones or mobile carriers may not be compatible.

Also: Why your USB-C cables look alike, but work differently – and how to tell them apart.

Sources indicate that on Apple’s side, any iPhone in the US running iOS 27 with a T-Mobile or Verizon-provided eSIM can use iPhone Handoff. AT&T does not presently support iPhone Handoff.

However, the code strings uncovered by Android Authority show that Android’s Fast Switch will work similarly to iPhone Handoff, in that people must be signed in to both devices under the same Google account for the feature to work.

Strings in Google’s SIM Manager app also point to no sharing between two people, so this feature isn’t a way to circumvent carrier fees by adding service to someone else’s phone for the price of one.

It has been revealed that if Fast Switch works anything like iPhone Handoff, which it appears it will, one eSIM can be switched between two phones. So, calls, messages, location services, and other information synced to your Apple ID can remain consistent between two devices.

Also: 5 hidden iOS 27 features that make older iPhones better.

Some third-party apps, like banking, communications, or social media, may also remain consistent across the two phones, depending on the app’s syncing behavior.

Features like Apple’s iPhone Handoff and Google’s Fast Switch are ideal for people who regularly use two phones. Business owners and digital creators may want one phone strictly for business purposes and the other for personal use.

Also: Google Wallet turns your Android phone into a digital house key.

Sources indicate that in that case, one person can keep up with two phones without paying for two phone service lines through their carrier. Still, customers will incur a fee, as T-Mobile charges $5/month for iPhone Handoff, while Verizon charges $10/month.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • On the heels of the Nvidia scandal, the Trump administration is preparing to crack down on foreign data centers that are fueling China’s advancements in artificial intelligence by allowing remote access to otherwise restricted high-end chips necessary for AI training.
  • In a summary of the rule change, the Commerce Department mentioned it was closing a loophole that previously allowed foreign rivals like China, Russia, and Iran to bypass export curbs on certain advanced computer chips by instead renting access to those chips from data centers in Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Brazil.
  • US rivals could possibly use that access to train and run advanced AI models “capable of supporting military- and intelligence-related activities that could threaten US national security or foreign policy interests,” the Commerce Department remarked.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On the heels of the Nvidia scandal, the Trump administration is preparing to crack down on foreign data centers that are fueling China’s advancements in artificial intelligence by allowing remote access to otherwise restricted high-end chips necessary for AI training.

In a summary of the rule change, the Commerce Department mentioned it was closing a loophole that previously allowed foreign rivals like China, Russia, and Iran to bypass export curbs on certain advanced computer chips by instead renting access to those chips from data centers in Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Brazil.

US rivals could possibly use that access to train and run advanced AI models “capable of supporting military- and intelligence-related activities that could threaten US national security or foreign policy interests,” the Commerce Department remarked. Among threats, the US fears rivals could use advanced AI to develop “more effective weapons of mass destruction and advanced conventional weapons, coordinated cyber-espionage and targeted cyber-disruption, algorithmic theft, and weaponized disinformation.”.

Now, the rules have been tightened up so much that the South China Morning Post reported that, “as a result, any advanced chips made for a Chinese firm are assumed to be restricted, and factories must ask the US government for a license before shipping them.”.

The rule change takes effect 90 days after it’s posted to the Federal Register. Moving forward, companies headquartered in any of those countries deemed to “present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion” to China, Russia, and Iran must apply for a license with strict know-your-customer controls when transferring high volumes of advanced chips. If a license is granted, companies will have to “perform robust due diligence,” submitting monthly reports on transactions that thoroughly detail all parties involved, as well as their parent companies, and the final destination for chips sold.

In a press release Sunday, the Commerce Department described the rule change as “designed to ensure that existing restrictions on access to sensitive American technology cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries.” An exception was carved out for companies providing computing power “exclusively used for commercial recommender systems.” The Department mentioned it was acting to “prevent certain foreign actors from leveraging advanced computing power based on US technology to threaten US national security and foreign policy interests.”.

Without the intervention, officials fear that China could develop a military or economic edge, The Latest York Times reported.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned after admitting to an affair with a woman, Alice Huang, suspected of serving as a Chinese spy. Congress is probing if Alice Huang used her personal relationship with Jensen Huang to help her former tech giant, Megaspeed, become one of Nvidia’s biggest customers, then used that position to smuggle Nvidia’s restricted AI chips into China. China has denied that Alice Huang was a spy, and Megaspeed has denied that smuggling occurred, while launching its own internal probe.

Sources indicate that megaspeed is a Singaporean data center firm whose primary business is cloud computing and AI infrastructure. Prior to the rule change, selling remote access to AI servers to customers in China was perfectly legal, NYT noted. But now, the Commerce Department has given firms like Megaspeed 90 days to either obtain licenses or face future export restrictions.

Whether or not to add more chip curbs has been a polarizing debate in the Trump administration. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent reportedly butted heads with Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. When the Megaspeed news broke, Bessent pushed for curbs, but Lutnick reportedly appeared “too cozy” with Nvidia to move. Instead, Lutnick initially favored looser controls that Nvidia claimed would ensure global dominance of US technology. (A Commerce Department spokesperson told NYT that Bessent has never confronted Lutnick over his handling of Megaspeed.).

Any companies found violating the rules could face a “range of consequences,” the Commerce Department remarked after reportedly bending to Bessent’s pressure campaign. Those include possibly facing fresh import restrictions, stricter license requirements, downgrading their status in the US export control regime, or other changes to their manufacturer’s or their base country’s entity-list designations.

Although the summary of the rule change noted that “Commerce will be actively monitoring for countries that tolerate evasion” of the anti-diversion policy, it’s unclear how aggressively the Commerce Department might enforce the rule, NYT noted.

Bessent has publicly criticized Lutnick for failing to sanction Megaspeed, and NYT reported that ultimately, enforcement of the stricter rules—which Bessent helped draft—“would be up to the Commerce Department.”.

Recent findings suggest that “The real story here should be: Did Nvidia know their client, and was there a robust effort at Nvidia to make sure that there was no leakage and that they were selling to what were obviously pass-through shell companies?” Bessent stated on a CNBC appearance. “I think it’s notable that anyone at the company there be held accountable for that.”.

There’s even a push to oust Lutnick over his position on chips, but The Guardian reported that Donald Trump confirmed he has no prepares to replace the AI industry-friendly commerce secretary. On Monday, Trump told reporters that Lutnick was right to delay blacklisting Megaspeed, because “if you didn’t delay it… you could have a blow-up with China.”.

At the press gaggle, Trump aligned with China in saying that there’s no evidence yet that Alice Huang was a spy. He also joined a band of prominent tech leaders calling for Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia, saying that it wasn’t a “bad idea.”.

“Nobody’s proven that she’s a spy,” Trump noted. “She may not be a spy.”.

However, US investigators have alleged that they found “Alice Huang used industry contacts and a series of shell companies to access 240,000 chips banned for export into China,” CBS News reported.

China is unlikely to welcome the newly introduced rules, as it has consistently accused the US of fabricating the spying claims to justify imposing additional chip restrictions.

However, a senior Trump official, granted anonymity to discuss sensitive policy matters, told the NYT that Trump “did not expect countermeasures from China in response.”.

Trump will be in China for an economic summit this week, including a meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping. The latest curbs could potentially disrupt those talks, according to Hong Yuan, a researcher and secretary-general of the Center for American Military Studies at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences. Hong told the People’s Daily that China will likely view the rule change as politically motivated.

“Before any judicial causality was established, Washington handed down a political conviction, substituting suspicion for proof, espionage for personal contact, and an industrial embargo for private conduct,” Hong noted. “The concern is not the cause of tighter controls, but a political catalyst.”.

The fresh policy could hurt the US, experts told the Chinese outlets. Analysts told the South China Morning Post that the policy could “accelerate Chinese companies’ shift to domestic AI chips.” Other experts told the People’s Daily—which is the official newspaper of the Chinese Communist Party—that “the cost of switching back to US platforms will rise” over time. If that happened, it could potentially lock in Chinese technology over America’s in “the world’s largest single consumer market for chips,” experts noted.

Sun Chenghao, senior fellow at the Center for International Security and Strategy at Tsinghua University in Beijing, told the People’s Daily that “what US companies stand to lose could be customers and technological influence for years to come.”.

Industry observers note that the Apple Watch SE 3 is a great pick for smartwatch users on a budget, and with this Black Friday offer at T-Mobile, you can get one on your wrist for free right now. Simply adding a new line on the carrier’s Watch Plan Plus will save you $300, which covers the full cost of the basic 40mm model.

In a recent development, just note that there are a couple of conditions for this deal. The savings will be applied as bill credits over 36 months, so you’ll have to stay with T-Mobile for the full three years to get the watch paid in full. If you want to cancel service before then, you’ll be on the hook for the remaining value.

Additionally, you’ll also pay the $35 connection charge up front. And if you want a larger display, this offer is also available for the 44mm model. You’re still saving $300, which knocks the cost down to less than $1 per month.

In a recent development, the Watch SE 3 is the most affordable wearable in Apple’s lineup, and it has plenty to offer, particularly if you’re looking for a basic smartwatch that works well. It features a vibrant OLED display, 64GB of storage, and an impressive battery life of up to 32 hours on a single charge. It also has a durable design and is waterproof up to 50 meters. Plus, the SE 3 is equipped with an S10 chip (the same processor as the previous-gen Series 11), which supports tons of health and safety features like Crash Detection, sleep tracking, an ECG function, and much more.

Recent findings suggest that also: Apple Watch SE 3 vs. Watch SE 2: I compared both models, and there’s a clear winner.

Though this deal does require you to sign a 36-month contract, any offer that can help you snag some Apple tech for free is a pretty serious bargain, which earns it a rating of 3/5 on our system.
